Not long before one could see nothing but the Britannic. The very hills on the adjacent island seemed small. All that was left of the great hospital ship was a confetti of wreckage and a handful of filled boats, swimmers awaiting rescue and floating human remains. But for a mercy, help was close at hand. Mere moments after the ship had breathed her last, a small flatillaa of Greek fishing boats were on the scene to fish survivors from the water and lend what aid they could. Not long after that, the destroyers, HMS Scourge and HMS Heroic, could be seen on the horizon, sparing the survivors the grueling hours of torment that had been endured by those from Titanic. But how would they known to come if the ship's wireless apparatus had been damaged? It was later found that the damage to her wireless only caused failure on the receiving end. Her distress calls had been heard loud and clear. And in another stroke of good luck, the heroic had just passed by Britannic 1 hour earlier while leaving the Kia channel and turned around to render aid immediately with Scourge and French Tugs Goliath and Polyphimmis plus a nearby twler all following close behind. When Britannic founded, it was far from the nightmare the victims of Titanic had experienced. While Titanic sank during a cold April night with little shipping traffic in the area, Britannic, by contrast, sank on a warm, sunny day where survivors could quickly be spotted and fished from the waters by nearby ships. Reverend John Fleming later wrote of an officer on board whose young son fervently prayed for the safety of his father and all those aboard the ship and mused that the prayers of this young boy had prevented the worst from coming to pass. He himself had admitted to taking up the prayer of the man's son, saying that he had prayed that if the ship had to go down, it might be in daylight when the sea was calm and when land was not far away. There may be, he said, some who contend that this was mere coincidence, but many of us who were in the way of trial there felt that God was honoring the simple faith of a little child and teaching us vividly that more things are roared by prayer than this world dreams of. But the sinking was not without its horrors. The brutality of war being among the most evidence. Among the victims were nine members of the ship's medical personnel, non-combatant forces tasked with aiding the wars wounded. Despite the ship's paint scheme granting them immunity from attack, fate had dealt them a cruel hand that no White Hull and Red Cross could ever spare them from. The largest hospital ship of the Allied war effort was now resting 400 ft beneath the surface of the Aian Sea and would ultimately be recognized as the largest ship of any kind sunk during World War I. Mercifully, the quick thinking and the excellent training of the ship's compliment of nurses, doctors, and crew members resulted in the saving of all but 30 lives during the sinking. And while it had been a valiant effort, Bartlett's attempt to beach his ship and the subsequent breakdown of communication during the evacuation efforts had been responsible for all of the fatalities that occurred. Had the evacuation been halted as was ordered, or had the captain simply decided against the attempt to beach his ship, all 1,66 souls aboard Bratannic would have been saved. HMHS Britannic had been planned to go to sea with all the elegance and luxury of her two sister ships. Instead, she would never see a day as the palatial liner she was intended to be. a wartime tragedy with none of the Edwardian drama of her older sister. The Britannic sinking failed to capture public attention the way Titanic had. Instead, when Britannic was lost, it scarcely managed to make headlines, say for a piece on the front page of the New York Times, reframing the sinking as anti-German propaganda by erroneously painting the disaster as the work of two yubot and calling the sinking the latest reminder of German barbarity, whose wickedness topped even the sinking of the Lucatania. This spark of outrage failed to ignite and the loss of Britannic would go on to be little more than a footnote in the history of the First World War.

The matter went to Parliament, who had to approve the monumental loan to a private corporation at a time when many Britons were starving. In lengthy and impassioned appeals to reason, he cited the many corners of Britain from which Hull 534's components had come. The huge stem castings from Darlington, the turbines from Rugby, the high-pressure tubes from Wals, the 100,000 pieces of cutlery from Sheffield, the propellers from Milwall in London. He ended by saying that from 9,000 to 10,000 men will be employed right away from all over the country. Within a week in Clyde Bank alone, anything from 1,000 to 1,500 men will be started. This brilliantly turned the narrative from one of outrage and shock at a mammoth loan being given out to unrestrained capitalists to being a matter of job creation and national pride. Conservative politician Sir Joseph Null chipped in with his own take when he said that I well remember a little over a year ago coming back from New York in the Moritania. I do not think I've ever felt so depressed at the position which this country seemed to be occupying as upon a Sunday morning in a fairly still sea. With a mist the Moritania was running almost parallel with the Il France went away in the mist appeared the Bremen which in an hour had overtaken both ships. The old Meritania, still the fastest of the British ships on the North Atlantic run, was over 25 years old. Incredibly, the bill passed on March 27th, 1934, nearly 3 years since construction had started on the ship in the first place, and almost 10 years since plans for her had begun to be drawn up. All over Clydebank, letters were sent recalling men to work after years of inactivity. Over 1,000 men marched back to work again, being guided by pipers. and over them loomed the vast hulk of Hull 534. Rusted and inhabited only by colonies of seabirds and ravens. Soon she would be the site of extraordinary technological achievement, the height of luxury at sea. She would not be whole 534 forever, but the Queen Mary. It's April 1936 and just off the aisle of Aaron, Scotland, a huge ocean liner is being put through its paces. These are the ship sea trials, and on board are representatives from both the ship builder, John Brown & Company, and the future owners, the Kunard Line. On the bridge is the vessel's captain, Sir Edgar Britain. He had started as a young man at sea aboard a thousand ton sailing ship. Now he commands an 80,000 ton behemoth. As the liner's engines are worked up to full power, her name gleams in the sunlight. Queen Mary. This was a triumphal moment for all involved. But just a few short years earlier, the great ship's hull had sat empty and rusting on the slipway, unfinished thanks to the Great Depression. This is the story of how the master ship building company John Brown turned that Hulk into one of the greatest oceanliners of all time. The mighty RMS Queen Mary. John Brown was a legendary ship building company and they had built some of the world's largest and most famous ships from ocean liners like Lucatania and Aquitania to the warships HMS Hood and Renown. They were situated in Scotland at Clydebank, which is a little over 9 km or 5 mi from Glasgow on the Clyde River. Here's an overhead view of the shipyard in 1934. You can see that Queen Mary is being constructed here. In the spring of 1934, you could have stood over here across from the fitting outwarf and watched the mighty hull of the Queen Mary taking shape. For over 2 years now, the ship had loomed over the town like a giant. Now it was up to John Brown's workers to finish the vessel and send her on her way. To understand the magnitude of the task ahead, we first need to get some understanding of what state the Queen Mary was in by that April of 1934. At the time they had put down tools way back in 1931, Queen Mary's hull had only just taken on its fundamental form. As with all ships, the workers had started with the Keel in 1930. This was the ship's backbone and it comprised a steel girder running the majority of the ship's 1,019 ft length and it was riveted at top three layers of keel plate which was about 3 and 1/2 in thick. Flanking either side of the keel was seven longitudinal girdters and then a web of floors were riveted to these and plating installed on top of the structure and underneath. This formed the ship's double bottom which was cellular and largely watertight. And from here, the huge transverse frames could be attached. These steel beasts gave Queen Mary's hull its shape, and they were spaced apart 36 in amid ships, narrowing to only 24 in at the extreme bow and stern. This was to give the ship some flexibility when sailing through rough seas. A more rigid construction, brought about by frames being too closely spaced, could cause catastrophic failure and a broken back. Every third frame on Queen Mary was a web frame, which was heavily reinforced by plating to provide some additional rigidity. Because of Queen Mary's immense size, she would have more web frames than was usual. Long support structures called stringers were riveted to the frames, and all this steel would form a basis for a ship that was both immensely strong and very flexible in heavy seas. Then came the hole plates. Huge flat pieces of steel riveted together to form the ship's skin both inside and out. They originated at the keel plate and individual hull plates were lined in vast rows called strakes. The one either side of the keel was known as the garbage strike and then each strake from there received its own letter designation in alphabetical order as they worked their way up the hull. The plates were riveted together with dozens of rivets each, often in two or three rows. And all of these rivet holes had to be individually punched out of the steel by specialist machine with pinpoint accuracy. Then the riveters would get to work pounding red hot iron rivets into the holes and therefore fastening the steel together. This work continued down the length of the ship, and as the plating continued, wood logs were put in place to shore up the ship and make sure that it couldn't move on the slipway. Scaffolding then slowly began to rise stories into the air so that workers could continue to rivet the hole together. Meanwhile, at the extreme ends of the ship, two monumental pieces of engineering achievement were fitted. These were the stem castings and they formed the very tip of the ship's bow and stern. They were actually the biggest yet made and the forge that produced them, Darlington, had to make some considerable investment in their works to even complete the order. This was a master stroke of engineering and pure craftsmanship. The castings that arrived by rail in sections at John Brown were immense. The bow stem casting itself being 130 ft long and rising to about the height of a 10-story building once assembled. In between the frames, holes were cut into the shell plating for the thousands of port holes which would provide light into the ship's hull for stateooms and public spaces. Even at this stage of construction, millions of rivets had been used. And eventually a total of some 12 million rivets weighing a combined estimated total of 4,000 tons would be needed to hold the vast ship together. The rivets alone weighed almost as much as the total displacement of two Fletcherclass destroyers. This work, laying the keel, assembling the frames, and plating the hull, went on and was about 80% complete when the shipyard was forced to shut down thanks to the Great Depression in December of 1931. When John Brown and company's workers finally returned those 2 years 4 months later, they picked up from where they left off, and the ship's hull was complete and finally ready for launch by September of 1934. Even though the hull was empty and carried none of the immense boilers and machinery that would power it through the water, she already weighed as much as 36,000 tons. Getting this enormous mass safely into the water for the first time would be no easy feat, and it took a significant amount of planning and preparation in itself. The Queen Mary was being built on the slipway here. But at 1,09 ft long, there was a real danger that she would run ground on the opposite side of the Clyde River after launching. To remedy this, two things had to happen. First, 5 acres of the Clyde and cart banks had to be dredged to widen and deepen them enough so that the Queen Mary wouldn't become stuck. And secondly, thousands of tons of dead weight would need to be fixed to the ship's hull so that it was tethered to the slipway and would stop dead in its tracks as soon as it was afloat. 2,350 tons of drag chains would therefore be used to keep the ship from running ground. Careful calculations were poured over by the John Brown team. With an empty hull weighing some 36,000 tons, they estimated that she would travel 1,194 ft. And this had to even be tested with a model. Then after launch, the ship would be guided by tugs here to the fitting out basin so that all of her heavy machinery could be installed as well as her lavish interiors. On September 26th, 1934, the big day finally came and a huge crowd of some 200,000 people flocked to see the event, even though it was raining. To convey the ship's sheer scale, John Brown employed an old tactic, painting the hull a brilliant white so that she would stand out more against the drab city background in black and white photographs. King George V and his wife, Queen Mary of Tech, ascended the launching platform. Until then, the ship's name had been a secret, and it had only been referred to as hull number 534. But then, Queen Mary of Tech cut the ribbon, announcing the ship was named after her instead. The name having been picked as a break from tradition and a step in a fresh new direction. There was a loud cheer as a bottle of Australian sparkling wine smashed on the ship's bow and then a dull rumble as the ship's huge hull began to slide down the slipway which had been coated in tallow to make the task easier. This was a critical moment. The hull was about to undergo huge stresses, more than it ever would in its entire career at sea. The builders held their breath as Queen Mary hit the critical point with half of her hull a float in the river and the other half still up on the slipway. This caused her hull to bend up by almost 8 in and then eventually sagged down by two. A weaker ship could have probably broken in half, but Queen Mary's builders had stiffened the hull with girders, and they had also delayed cutting openings like windows and doors into the superructure on top of the hull to provide additional support. In about a 100 seconds, the vast white hull of the Queen Mary was afloat for the first time, and cheers filled the air. Her bulk sent up a two-foot wave, which flooded out the spectator stands on the opposite side of the river. And in the end, the launching model had proved incredibly accurate. Her builders had predicted that she would travel 1,194 ft before coming to arrest, and in reality, she only exceeded this distance by 2 ft. With Queen Mary at the fitting out wararf, workers could finally swarm aboard to begin outfitting the ship's machinery. And what machinery it was, everything about the Queen Mary was of immense scale and incredible accuracy. Her rudder was the largest yet built and weighed 150 tons by itself. The four manganese bronze propellers each weighed around 35 tons and stretched 20 ft across. The slightest error in their casting would have cost the ship builders more than $330,000 in today's money. Five 60 ton gear wheels for the turbine engines had their teeth ground in to a thousandth of an inch of accuracy over the course of 2 months each. The anchors were the largest built for a liner and weighed 16 tons each. And to lessen the effect of wind resistance, a cutout was made so they could sit recessed into the hull. Huge cranes lifted the immense boilers up and down into the ship's bowels. 24 Yarrow boilers went in as well as the four Parson's turbine sets. Steam from the boilers would be superheated to 700° F and course through the lines at 400 lb per square in. This steam would send the turbines rotors, which themselves weighed 40 tons, spinning at 3,000 revolutions per minute, and the engines could output 50,000 horsepower each. Down into the ship's bowels went the four we condensers, massive units with 41,000 square ft of cooling surface designed to turn exhaust steam back into water and recirculate it. Then there were four turbo generators by British Thompson Houston, which would power Queen Mary's lights. And there were even installed two emergency kerosene generators that on their own could provide power for all the ship services for 36 hours in the case of an emergency. All of these huge pieces of machinery, each of them extremely expensive and specialized, was lifted with care into the Queen Mary and fixed into place. Then work could commence on the superructure and the interiors. Public rooms had their walls or bulkheads riveted into place. Corridors and vast interior rooms suddenly appeared as walls were installed. A network of ventilation trunking provided fresh air to the ship's inside, and these would be connected to enormous intakes and fans on the boat deck, which could suck in immense amounts of air to adequately ventilate the Mary's 80,000 ton interior space. This work at the fitting outwarf went on for 20 months, and slowly but surely, the Hulk was turned into a ship. Then three funnels, each of them wide enough to drive three locomotives through a breast, were lifted and riveted into place. All three of the funnels were actually of different heights, and they got shorter sequentially, but the forwardmost funnel was the height of a seven-story building. They were fitted with steam powered typhen whistles whose deep rumble could be heard more than 10 mi away. They were tuned down to the absurdly low pitch of bass A so as not to disturb passengers on deck and to convey Queen Mary's huge size. Each of the three whistles weighed a ton by themselves. While all this work was going on outside the ship, work was intensifying inside as well. Hundreds and hundreds of passenger stateooms, bathrooms, and public spaces had to be constructed to the highest possible standard, and no expense was spared. The ship's interiors would be decorated with dozens of species of timber, including ebony, jackaranda, zebra, mahogany, violet wood, sycamore, elm, birch, about 56 species in total. Then there was the art. Vast oils, carved gesso panels, etched glass and bronze reliefs, murals by painters and cartoonists. The first class verander grill, for example, featured a mural by Doris Zincisen that was 1,000 ft square. Down on D-D was installed the two-story palatial tiled swimming pool completed with balconies and a simulated mother of pearl ceiling. And in the cabin class restaurant, a monumental map depicting the North Atlantic with a miniature crystal replica of the ship indicating its exact position on the route. The interior decor was, for one of a better word, a bit weird. Kunard ered on the side of tradition as always, but they did not want to put Queen Mary to sea with the kinds of stately Edwwardian interiors you'd expect from the Aquitania. The result was a mix of deco and modernism and traditional Britishness, said one critic at the time. The pictures and sculpture are varied in kind and quality, and not all of them fit happily into their setting. The general effect is one of mild but expensive vulgarity. At the time, this gave Sir Percy Bates, Cunard's chairman, cause for concern. But in the end, the strange combination proved endearing, and passengers found Queen Mary to be comfortable and homely. The exterior architecture of the ship was also a curious balance of old and new. Her three funnels echoed the design of her running mate, Baronia, but they were proportionally squatter. She didn't have Aquitania or Moritania's massive goofy cow vents, but in their place, she had massive rectangular units instead. Her bridge front also echoed Moritania and Lucatania with its elegant sweeping curve. And instead of an Edwwardian Clipper stern, she sported a modern cruiser type stern instead. With the ship nearing completion, 20 lifeboats, each the size of a motor yacht, powered by diesel engines, and with capacity for 145 people, were installed on modern electric gravity davverts, which could be lowered quickly and safely. Two additional boats with reduced capacity could carry their own wireless sets, and two more lifeboats were kept ready for emergencies, such as a man overboard. A single lifeboat from the Queen Mary could carry all of the passengers of the Cunard Line's first steam ship, the Bratannia. Constructing the Queen Mary was a monumental achievement, one that was almost never finished. But finally, in April 1936, the ship was guided down the Clyde by tugs for her sea trials before departing on her maiden voyage. Her engines roaring at full power, Captain Sir Edgar Britain's eyes must have smarted against the chill Scottish spring air as Queen Mary glided through the waves at speed. She was a shipbuilding triumph, a win for Britain as a whole and undoubtedly the pride of Scotland. May 27th, 1936, the RMS Queen Mary has departed Southampton on her maiden voyage. Board her are 1,849 passengers and 1100 crew. The cream of society has sought desperately to board this ship for the special occasion. And as the ship's turbines are run up to full power for the first time in her service career, Queen Mary's bow slices through the water like a knife through hot butter. The question on everybody's mind is this. Will the ship beat the Normandy? Just one year earlier, France's new Super Liner had taken the honorific blue ribbon by beating the Italian liner Rex's speed record in carrying out the fastest transatlantic crossing, reaching New York from Southampton in just 4 days and 3 hours. Britain had to answer this challenge, and it would be the Queen Mary that would try it. But could she beat the French liner? Would the engines be powerful enough to pull it off? What design features of the two ships set them apart? The world held its breath and watched the start of one of the greatest shipping rivalries of all time. This epic story has its start in the time just after the First World War. As always, wartime had been a proving ground for new technologies. Before the war, many passenger ships had been built with triple expansion steam engines. These beasts comprised towering pistons driven by steam, but they were mechanically complex and could only achieve moderate speeds. The turbine had been introduced and adopted by many shipping companies before the war as a replacement. It was immensely powerful, relatively compact, and could achieve enormous speeds. The war had proved the turbines dominance. Battleships, cruisers, and destroyers had traveled great distances at high speeds powered by turbines. They would be the way of the future. At the same time as this heady technological era when the sky was no longer the limit, the victorious Allied powers, France, Britain, and America were riding a surge of patriotic nationalism at home. Britain and America had incurred huge shipping losses and were rewarded three of the most modern ships built by Germany, Imperator, Fartterland and Bismar, which were also by far the largest ships afloat. By contrast, France was left with an aging ocean liner fleet. Company General Transatlantic, also known as the French line, had lost 30 ships in the conflict and rushed to replace them with some clapped out freighters. They were not awarded one of Germany's super liners, but three small freighters and another three smaller steam ships. The country that had lost 1,700,000 dead, almost 5% of their entire population was left to pick up the pieces themselves, and French Line had grand plans. The early 20s saw the company planning and building a series of increasingly impressive ships. First was the SS Paris of 1921, the new flagship. She was not the largest or the fastest ship in the world. French Line was not in a position to challenge those titles, but she was magnificently appointed and finally built. This set a pattern for the line and they applied this formula throughout the decade to their other liners. The Degrassi in 1924 and the vaunted Il France in 1927. By contrast, Britain's major passenger carriers like Cunard and Whitestar were still relying heavily on their famed pre-war fleet as well as the newer German additions. Kunard had Moritania, Aquitanian, and Baronaria, a trio of liners totaling some 130,000 odd tons of shipping, while White Starline boasted the largest trio of ships by tonnage in the world and 137,551 gross registered tons. The Olympic, the Homeriic, and Majestic, the largest ship in the world. These were transatlantic heavyweights and the ships were household names. Almost everyone a legend in their own right. French Line's offering was extremely modest by comparison, but if the company was to compete on the world stage, they would need to build a ship the likes of which had never yet been seen. She would have to be the largest and fastest ship in the world. From the ruin of wartime, French Lines's fleet of humble liners had proved profitable. By the end of the 1920s, the company was well placed to challenge the British competition and plans were laid for France's own superliner. At first, she was called only T6, and the hull that began to form on the Shantier Atlantic slipway at Staint Nutsair, France, would have looked totally alien because of its bizarre shape. The hull's flared curves and strange shape was the brainchild of a Russian immigr. The engineer had started out working in Russia on dreadnaugh battleships for the navy after the Russians lost their fleet in the infamous 1905 battle of Tsushima. During this time, Yorgovich seized upon hydrodnamics and how water impacts ships as they sail through it. Ship's hulls below the water line until then had been nice and streamlined, but there was a limit to how streamlined they could be. The ship's bow needs to have enough mass so as to be buoyant enough in heavy seas and actually float. Streamline the hull beneath the water enough and it would cut through the ocean like a knife. But the ship would be dangerously unstable, prone to pitching up and down and easily submerged in heavy seas. Yokovich sought to solve this by providing a broader midship section and exaggerated tumble home where the hull gets progressively wider as it reaches the waterline. By the 1920s, he was living and working in France, a fitter and a turner at the Renault car factory. But everything changed when he was taken on as a draftsman at Shantiier at Lontique shipyard. When he found out the French line was working on initial plans for a super liner, he approached them with his hull design. The company was at first skeptical, but he received backing from a Russian French admiral, and the company agreed to test his hull with models in a tank in Germany. The results were fascinating. His hull design was capable of achieving high speeds with 20% less power than a more traditional design. His concept was formally adopted in 1929, and France's new liner would feature this radical new hull form. Here's how it was supposed to work. For a ship designed for speed, the enemy is always drag. Drag can come in three major forms. Below the water line, at the water line, and above it. Below the water line, the ship's massive hull has to push through the ocean at a rate of knots. So, the hull form has to be sleek and streamlined to make this as easy as possible. Meanwhile, at the waterline, the ship experiences the destructive interference of waves. The bow itself creates a wave which breaks along the side of the ship, creating drag and slowing it down. Then, the very shape of the ship's hull and superructure above the water line is moved through the air at speed and creates aerial drag. Everything must be made as efficient as possible if the super liner is going to be able to beat the standing speed record. One single knot or 1.15 mph could make all the difference. To solve for the first of the three main drag creators, Yorovich provided the new ship with a knife edge bow of extremely thin profile. Normally, this would of course lessen the ship's buoyancy, but to account for it, the ship's hull featured an enormous midsection. Normandy boasted an extremely long and fine bow below the waterline that suddenly flared out to its full amidship's width. As well as this, the bow above the water line flared out and up, providing more mass and ensuring the ship would not be at danger of pitching dangerously up and down. By contrast, the Moritania, a ship which had long held the transatlantic speed record, featured a conventional hull design with no flare and a prow or very front, which was almost perfectly straight. With so little mass at her bow, the ship was known as a pitcher and would often alarmingly drop straight down and seemingly at random, even in relatively calm seas. This new French ship, by contrast, would provide a smooth ride, and the wide midsection would reduce rolling from side to side as well. Next, Yorovich solved the wave problem as well. The new ship's hull featured a bulbous bow. Conventional ship's boughs carved their way through the ocean and threw up enormous waves as they did it, which broke along the ship's side and slowed them down. The French liner's bulbous bow would act ahead of the ship's prow, disrupting the flow of water and canceling out the bow wave, thus reducing drag. Even at full speed, Normandy would create only the tiniest of bow waves as it glided through the water. Last, there was the above water drag. Normandy superructure, which was extremely long thanks to the ship's huge midsections, some 734 ft, or over 70% of the ship's length, was dramatically curved at the front end. And the funnels, instead of being cylindrical, were constructed in a teardrop shape to better channel air as it flowed past. The third funnel, a dummy of sorts because it wasn't connected to the boiler uptakes, was so placed to disrupt the flow of air and more efficiently displace it along the ship's massive length. Every aspect of the ship's layout worked in conjunction to provide greater efficiency, and there was good reason for it. Britain and America's shipyards had output some of the most modern ships a float, and as longtime adopters of the steam turbine, they had simply perfected the art. British and American steam turbines were easily the most powerful and effective aloat and French line may not have felt fully confident in challenging this dominance. A more radical propulsion method was chosen. The new ship would be turbo electric with steam turbines creating electricity for motors which would then drive the ship's propellers. The system allowed for full power to be used in reverse without the need for dedicated stern turbines or complex and delicate gearing. And it was quieter and more easily maintained. Instead of relying on brute horsepower, the new ship's sleek hull would mean less power would be needed to break the speed record. What French Line introduced to much fanfare in 1935 was easily the world's largest ship. White Star Lines RMS Majestic was a 56,000 ton steamer, but the new French ship dwarfed her at almost 80,000 gross registered tons. The ship was essentially a floating palace kitted out with the latest art deco interiors and the very finest fittings French craftsmanship had to offer. Early on, her construction, heavily subsidized by the government, had been a huge source of contention in France. But now, as this new super liner proudly steamed out on her maiden voyage with the tririccolor fluttering in the breeze, it all seemed worthwhile. She was named Normandy, the largest ship in the world to be sure. But would she be the fastest? Departing Southampton, Normy's engines were gradually worked up to full speed, and her hull barely made a ripple as it sliced through the waves. From the outside, the ship looked incredibly elegant, but deep down, there were actually problems. The ship's stern section vibrated badly, even at half power, and the cause was as yet a mystery. And then, on the first day, a condenser tube ruptured and drained the ship of 25% of her power while works were carried out. But despite this, Normandy recorded more and more miles every day. On day two, it was 718 mi, but by day four, it was 754. The ship's passengers and crew were sure they'd broken the speed record and won the symbolic blue ribbon. And on June 2nd, the passengers dressed in blue, and 98t long blue banner was flown from the mast. Normandy glided into New York Harbor only 4 days, 3 hours, and 2 minutes since passing Bishop's Rock at an average speed of 29.98 knots. She had done it. France had won the blue ribbon, and Normandy was the largest and fastest ship in the world. For the Cunard line, this French victory was a bit of a blow. From the outset, their proposed new pair of super liners, what would eventually become the Queen Mary and the Queen Elizabeth, were intended to be the largest and fastest ships on the transatlantic trade. Traditionally, the route was serviced by trios because it made the most sense. Think of it a little like a bus route. In order to offer the most reliable and regular passenger service, three ships work best. Sailing at 20 to 25 knots on average, the ships could make decent time. And with three liners, one ship could be sailing west to America, another sailing east to Europe, and a third crossing in either direction or in for repair with no major impact on the schedule. Kenard wanted to shake this up and replace the three large ships they already operated with two larger, faster ships that would be big and quick enough to maintain a regular service on their own. The design philosophy behind the pair was outlined by Kunard chairman Percy Bates who said that the speed is dictated by the time necessary to perform the journey at all seasons of the year and in both directions plus the consideration of the number of hours required in port on each side of the Atlantic. The size is dictated by the necessity to make money by providing sufficient sailable passenger accommodation to pay for the speed. So in this way the speed drove the ship's size. But from the outside, making the largest and fastest ships in the world wasn't just good PR for Cunard. Bait said that instead of just competing for size and speed for the sake of it, the two new ships would really be the smallest and slowest which can fulfill properly all the essential economic conditions. But this was a little disingenuous. The British government was backing the construction of the Queen Mary and had saved it from cancellation during the Great Depression. The expectation was that the new ship would maintain Britain's dominance over the transatlantic trade and all eyes were on the John Brown shipyard where as Normandy made its record-breaking dash across the Atlantic, the Queen Mary was being finalized. From the outside, the differences between Queen Mary and Normandy are stark. Normandy bears little resemblance to the ships that came before her. Queen Mary, on the other hand, deliberately borrowed and expanded upon design cues from older ships like the Moritania, like the very front of the bridge here. On top of this, where Normy's decks were clean and open with most of the big fans and ventilators obscured behind paneling or in the funnels, Queen Mary's decks were cluttered full of huge air vents and equipment in the tradition of older Cunard liners like the Aquitania. Cunard was not in the business of reinventing the wheel or breaking with tradition. So when it came to Queen Mary, very few radical decisions were made. This was most evident in the hull design. Queen Mary would not have a bulbous bow and her lines would be long and traditional. Where Normandy featured a sweeping super fine bow profile beneath the waterline, Queen Mary's was comparatively thicker. The Mary's hull was sleek and streamlined to be sure, and it had actually been tested with 22 models in water tanks over the course of 8,000 tests. The bow flared out and featured a prominent rake, which meant pitching up and down would be minimalized. But at sea trials, the ship threw up an enormous bow wave, almost the height of a three or four-story building at full speed, meaning the hull form lacked the refined efficiency of the Normandy. In fact, it was down in the engine room where Queen Mary's trump card lay. Normandyy's turboctric engines were novel and fairly advanced and output around 160,000 horsepower in total. But Queen Mary was fitted with four massive Parsons turbines tried and tested and capable of putting out some 212,000 shaft horsepower, the equivalent of 7 million rowers. The arrangement required an enormous power train comprising four primary boiler rooms each containing six massive yarrow boilers for the propulsion, an auxiliary boiler room with three scotch boilers to generate electrical power for the ship services, two turbo generator rooms, and then the two engine rooms. This power plant consumed the majority of the space of the bottom four or five decks of the ship for its entire 1,09 ft length. In May 1936, Queen Mary was ready at last for her maiden voyage. Sea trials had proved promising, and the ship hit in excess of 32 knots. But the question still remained, could Queen Mary beat Normy's speed. Unfortunately, the maiden voyage would not provide the answer. Initially running at a decent speed, the Mary encountered fog on the final day of the crossing, and she reached New York only 2 hours behind Normy's record. Queen Mary had not decisively crushed the French ship's speed on her inaugural crossing. But even in the face of fog and delays, she had come dangerously close. French line was sweating. Despite the fact it had been such a close-run thing, there was an air of gloom around Mary's inability to beat Normandy on that first crossing. Kunard swore that they had not even been trying to do so. But even then, the pressure was on. The Mary's monstrous turbines were worked up to full speed again in August 1936 for another crossing. And the Normandy's record was finally beaten by 2 hours and 35 minutes. French Lines directors were dejected, but they would not give up hope. One of the greatest maritime rivalries of all time had begun, and the margin of victory, just over 2 hours, was very slim. Improvements were made to Normandy throughout the winter of 1936 to 1937, with boiler efficiency increased, and a new set of four-bladed propellers fitted to the ship instead of her older three-bladed ones. And the result was impressive. Normandy beat Queen Mary's time in May 1937, crossing the Atlantic in just 3 days and 23 minutes. Her engines pushed to output power very close to Queen Mary's turbines. On the return voyage, Normy's turboctric engines actually output 195,850 developed horsepower on the final day. Clearly, the improvements had worked. Normandy once again held the blue ribbons, but Kunard and Queen Mary had an answer. See, Normandy was not the only ship to receive modifications to help her speed along. A set of four 18 ft wide manganese bronze propellers were crafted for the ship, more efficient than her original set. And in August 1938, Queen Mary's crew again pushed her engines to full power, and the ship ended Normy's reign, cruising into New York over 2 hours earlier than the French ship's fastest time. Normandy skipper sent a message through, "Bravo to the Queen Mary. Until next time." But there would be no next time. The great speed that Kunard chairman Percy Bates and considered crucial in maintaining a regular peaceime transatlantic schedule would now see the two sister ships become some of the most highly valued Allied troop transports of the war and the most sought after target of Hitler's navy. It's July 24th, 1915, a Saturday in Chicago, Illinois. A surprisingly mild day in the middle of summer. Just the day before, it had been 10° higher. Thunderstorms swept sporadically across the city, keeping many inside. But down at the Chicago River between Lal and Clark Street, the riverfront was bustling with activity. Hundreds of people are crowded, excitedly stepping aboard an excursion steamer that's going to take them for a day of fun. Directly across the river looms the red brick facade and the beautiful clock tower of the brand new Reed Murdoch and Co. office building. Those working through the weekend there have a good view directly opposite as the excursion steamer loads its human cargo. But any keen eyed observers might have noticed it beginning to wallow in the water, leaning this way and that. No matter. Small steamers came and went from here every day. With loading about complete, one final passenger jumps between shore and a ship. On the upper deck, a small band plays lively ragtime tunes. Then, as the little white ship begins to cast off from the warf, it rolls sluggishly, but quickly enough to catch the musicians off guard. The music stops as they fall, and the ship lurches heavily in plain daylight, within full view of the Chicago Riverfront and the workers across the way. The ship has capsized. It had barely cleared the warf. The sinking of SS Eastland has become legend in Chicago, where its sudden violent loss is an unusually horrific chapter in the city's history. The sinking was bad enough, but the revelations that would come later, the causes of the disaster would outrage the public and shock even to this day. This is the tragic story of the sinking of the SS Eastland. The Great Lakes are like an immense inland sea, providing a vital waterway to link major cities like Chicago, Buffalo, Michigan, Detroit, Milwaukee, Cleveland, and more. For generations, Chicagoans have taken to the lakes on fairies and daytrip steamers. But the lakes are no picnic. They can be whipped into frenzied rage by winter storms or blotted out entirely by dense, impenetrable fog banks. It's thought that between 10 to 20,000 ships or more have been taken by them. In the early morning of July 24, 1915, the sleek white hull of an excursion steamer rose up from the Chicago River. On the bow of the unusually tall hull in neat, small letters was the name Eastland. And of the hundreds of people who crowded aboard that day, not one of them knew that a series of ill-informed decisions and poor design choices had ensured that this morning would probably be their last. The SS Eastland was a passenger ship designed for the lakes known as the Great Lakes Speed Queen. She was launched in 1903. For decades, there'd been a bustling passenger trade across the lakes, so countless feries and steamers were built to capitalize on the demand, operating voyages to link rail heads and stop at towns and cities along the way. Aside from operating a regular timetable, fairies could be chartered for events and functions as pleasure cruisers and day trips became more popular. The SS Eastland's design and construction was a little unorthodox, and the seeds for the disaster that would occur over 10 years later were sewn from the start. The contract for the ship's construction was awarded to the Jinx Ship Building Company of Michigan. Now, the shipyard had a history of building freighters and tugboats, and Eastland would be their first and only passenger ship project. Sydney Jensen, the yard's chief designer, consulted with his naval architecture professor from Cornell University on the project, and the pair came up with the outline for their ship. It had a dual purpose, a cargo vessel and a passenger ferry, and it needed to maintain a good turn of speed to keep up the demanding schedule. Capacity for passengers needed to be 500 for overnight voyages housed comfortably in cabins. But critically, Eastland needed a shallow draft, that is the amount of ship that's below the water line to allow it to enter into those shallow ports. The design was finalized and calculations on the ship's metacentric height and center of gravity were completed. These all dictate the stability of the ship's final design. But then the shipyard Jinx, probably at the request of the steamship's future owners, shortened the length by 60 ft and added a passenger deck. Now, this would obviously have a huge impact on the calculations on balance and stability, but apparently no recalculating was done and no further inclining tests on the ship stability were carried out. The result was a long, thin, tall ship with a design top speed of 20 knots and some quirky habits. From the beginning, Eastland was known to be topheavy and had a history of stability issues. She would roll this way and that something passengers found funny as the steamer limped into or out of port. It meant for the captain and his engineers, operating the ship was a never-ending game of pumping water into and out of ballast tanks to straighten the ship up. Now, this instability was primarily due to Eastland's relatively narrow beam, or the ship's width, in comparison to its length and height. It made it prone to listing from side to side. The narrow beam was a reflection on Eastland's purpose, speed, and efficiency. The beam was one thing, but even more alarming was Eastland's shallow draft. To compensate for a high center of gravity, designers can give the ship more draft. That's simply more of it under the water line to ensure stability. Back then, designers of the age set about 60% of the hull below the water line, but this created more drag and the engines had to work harder. Now, Eastland's draft was already shallow, far less than the usual 60%. But after her inaugural season in 1903, the ship's draft was reduced even further in an effort to gain even more speed. The ship was built for efficiency. As an engineer later put it, the idea was to save coal by keeping the hull as much out of the water as possible. The draft was cut in two. Instead of 60%, only 30% of Eastland's hull could be found below the waterline. Now, the 1903 to 1904 refit reduced the ship's draft and added even more weight above the water line. Worst of all, Eastland was regularly sailing with well over 2,000 passengers. Measures were taken to try to fix the ship's bad behavior. The ship's passenger compliment was lowered by 200 and some stateaterooms were taken out. Then a couple of years later, the remaining cabins were removed because they sat way too high up in the hull and the funnels were cut down in height. Two tons of concrete were added lower down to try to balance things out. But still, when loading passengers, the ship was known to dip down in the water by as much as 25°. In August 1913, naval engineer John Deo York took a voyage on Eastland and was appalled by what he saw. He said in trying to make the harbor, it was like steering a log of wood. She wouldn't obey the helm. He quickly wrote a letter to the US harbor master of the city's port saying, "You are aware of the condition of the SS Eastland, and unless structural defects are remedied to prevent listing, there may be a serious accident." But he got no response. Now, that was already bad enough, but then things got even worse. In response to the Titanic disaster in 1912, new maritime safety regulations were enacted, requiring ships to carry enough lifeboats and rafts for all passengers. For the Eastland, this meant adding additional lifeboats, which would be shipped on the top weather deck. This added tons of weight to the uppermost part of the ship. Now, obviously, this couldn't go unnoticed as the already unstable Eastland was renowned for its funny tendency to roll to one side. A a chance, general manager of the Detroit and Cleveland navigation company, petitioned hard against this change because as a ferry operator himself, he knew the danger. Eastland was not a unique case. Many of the Great Lakes ships were designed and built in a similar way. If their upper decks were crowded with lifeboats, they were likely to capsize if the conditions were right. He told Congress, "The extra weight of the lifeboats and rafts would make ships of the Great Lakes topheavy and unseaorthy, and some of them would turn turtle if you attempted to navigate them with this additional weight on the upper decks." Eastland's owners and operators, the St. Joseph Chicago steamship company complained about the change as well with the general manager writing to the secretary of commerce in Washington and saying if it were possible to put this amount of equipment on the Eastland the weight that would be added to its upper deck would make the boat difficult to handle. Now this all sounds very noble on behalf of Eastland's owners. But now they had a choice to make. With an unmoved government, they could prove that passenger safety was truly at the heart of their complaints by operating Eastland with fewer lifeboats, but a reduced passenger capacity. Now, fewer passengers meant, of course, lower revenue. Or they could accept the danger, fit more lifeboats, and apply for a permit to raise passenger capacity and earn more revenue. Now, Eastland's owners, of course, chose the latter. Increased revenue at the expense of their passengers safety. With Eastland already topheavy, dangerously unstable, and crammed with massively heavy boats, the St. Joseph and Chicago Steamship Company made a critical modification that upset her even more. The old wood floor had been ripped up and replaced with a layer of thick concrete. That plus another concrete pouring further after added up to 20 tons of weight above the waterline. The end result was a very cranky ship indeed, and the stage had been set for a disaster of tragic, almost unfathomable proportions. Around 7,000 tickets had been sold for the function. Western Electric was just that big of an employer for the city at its surrounds. Eastland's captain continued the departure though and the ship's stern began to swing away from the dock. Now this and the ship's band which continued to play tricked passengers into thinking that all was well and they began to move away from the starboard side railing to watch the departure. The stairs collapsed altogether, and there was no way out. Then the water began to roar in. It wasn't a gentle, gradual fall. It was sudden and violent. The jaunty panled interior just moments earlier, a sight of excitement and happiness was turned suddenly into a scene from hell as people were flung off their feet into one another and then white water roared in around them. Either stunned by the impact or held down by a desperate drowning victim. Boille would be the only victim to die that day who hadn't been aboard the Eastland. Meanwhile, on the Theodore Roosevelt nearby, passengers erupted in panic at the sight of the other ship's loss, and they fought their way off their ship in a frenzied hurry. All around the Eastland's hull, tragic scenes of human suffering were playing out in full view of a stunned crowd ashore. With the crew hauling people out to safety, a steady, sad stream of people who'd been fortunate enough to make it out and onto the Eastland's overturned hull in time began to march their way off their ship, onto Kenosha, and then onto the warf. Frank Blaha and his mate just waited until a boat came over to get them. They simply stepped off the overturned hull to safety. But others weren't so fortunate, and they had to be bodily hauled out. FW Willard was a superintendent of the Western Electric Cable Works. And instead of standing frozen in panic, he rushed to grab a line and started throwing it out to anybody that could catch it. Nearby, another Western Electric man, Howard W, did his best to haul people out of the brackish cold water. "I pulled one old fellow out," he said, on a 2x4 that was at least 2 ft underwater, hanging onto an armchair, which refused to sink, so he was floating along about 2 ft under. I got him to the raft and pumped some air into him and then hoisted him on deck of the Posski. And when I got up there, he was sitting on the cabin floor with his arms around his daughter whom he had also pulled out, crying and asking for two sisters and the mother who were missing. The rescue effort had been tremendous and instantaneous with absolutely no warning or coordination. Bystanders, passengers, and crewmen alike had sprung into action to do their best to help. made all the more remarkable because nobody knew if the boilers, which had had steam on them, would explode or not. One group of heavy industry workers nearby had rushed aboard a clapped out tug and somehow got the old engine to work despite having no formal qualifications or seagoing experience themselves. They still managed to pull in about 50 people from the water. Soon, very soon though, it became clear that all that could be done outside had been done and hundreds were missing. still trapped inside the steel coffin-like hull. Inside the ship, divers soon got to work, but they soon realized their mission had become one of body recovery. The interior was confusing and extremely disorienting, with everything now rotated 90°. Dozens and dozens of bodies were found jammed in the bottleneck that had formed at the main staircase leading out of the hull. Some had claimed from the outside they could still hear faint tapping and cries from within. So it became clear that the ship would need to be cut open, and a settling torch wielding workers began to slice into the steel, but not without complaint from Eastland's own Captain Pettison, who had survived and watched on appalled at how his ship was being treated. "Here, stop that!" he had allegedly cried as the steel was rent open, but one worker brushed him off in disgust. My orders are to save lives, he had said, not be careful of the boat. What workers found inside was nightmarish. The result of the sinking had been horrific. 844 passengers and crew killed. In fact, more passengers died on Eastland than had died on Titanic 3 years prior. Nearly 240 victims had been teenagers. 58 were little children. 175 women went home that day as widows. 84 men lost their wives. Whole families were gone. 500 or more Western Electric employees had been wiped out. It had all happened just feet from the dock. And safety footage from the recovery is so distressing I can't even show you today 110 years later. It's just that horrendous. But over the coming days, workers struggled to haul people up from deep within the ship while pressman and film cameras snapped away just feet away from them on the riverfront. The brand new red brick reed Murdoch and co-off building and warehouse directly across the river suddenly became a morg with dozens of unidentified dead lining its ground floor. Now, the news was a sensation, and even as bodies were being pulled out of the overturned hull, newspapers ran sorted headlines and indicted owners and ship builders alike. Engineer John Deo York, who had written that letter in 1913 to the Chicago Harbor Master, warning of impending disaster, passed his letter on to the local media, furthering the outrage. Of course, the resulting scandal caused furious, justified questions from the outraged public. How could this have happened when Eastland's design was well known to have been dangerous? Why did the owners operate the ship? And how were they allowed to have operated it at all? Questioning began with Jensen, the designers and builders of the ship. Now, it soon became clear that standards of ship building on the lakes had been lax. Sydney Jenx, Eastland's designer, testified that his vessel had only been designed for 500 passengers for the original owners. He said, "I had no way of knowing the quantity of its business after it left our yards." Now, damningly, no inclining test on the ship's stability was ever performed. He said that because the ship had been launched on its side, lent over 45°, and then writed itself again, that it had demonstrated its stability just fine, and that was apparently enough. With six members of the St. Joseph Chicago Steamship Company indicted for conspiracy and negligence. Judge Clarence Sessions said that there is no proof which tends even to a slight degree to fasten such guilt upon any of the respondents. Every act charged and proved against these respondents was done in the usual and ordinary course of business. In fact, the company's knowledge of Eastland's bad past behavior seems embarrassingly basic. Back in 1913, during discussions around the sale, no mention of the instability was ever made, nor the major listing incidents from early in the ship's career. At an inquest, Walter C. Steel, the company's secretary treasurer, said, "I didn't know much about the boat except that we had got it at a bargain. All I do is to sign blank checks." So, what had happened? Well, in brief, the government had ordered the installation of additional lifeboats if the company had wished to maintain the massive passenger capacity, something Eastland's original builder later testified she'd never been designed for in the first place. In retrospect, we know that Eastland's owners had complained about their ship seaworthiness with additional lifeboats fitted. But clearly, in opting to fit additional lifeboats to boost passenger capacity, they had chosen profit over safety. In the event when Eastland rolled over, the lifeboats were basically useless and more of a hazard than anything else. Many of the St. Joseph Chicago Steamship Company executives had avoided extradition to Illinois, staying in Michigan instead to avoid federal charges, and their extradition was barred by the same judge who had said that every act charged and proved against those respondents was done in the quote usual and ordinary course of business. If they truly had no knowledge of their ship's strange behaviors and top heaviness, then surely they need only have looked at the thing as it pathetically limped and listed 10, 15° from side to side, or even read reports from engineers who are tasked with furiously pumping water in and out of tanks to maintain balance. If they were truly concerned for passenger safety, thanks to the additional lifeboats, as they had stated earlier, then surely they should have conducted stability and inclination tests on their ship with the lifeboats fitted. But they never did. Now, if not guilty of deliberate manslaughter, then surely Eastland's owners and operators were guilty of extreme incompetence and negligence, but they were never found guilty and escaped unscathed. Unforgivably, they blamed Eastland's chief engineer, Ericson, for the disaster and maintained that his counter flooding of the ballast tanks and attempting to mitigate the listing was the cause of the accident. Cases dragged on and on for two decades. In 1919, Erikson, the chief engineer, had died, and he became an easy scapegoat for the disaster. In 1933, the matter was closed at a limitation of liability hearings that concluded astoundingly that Erikson's mishandling of the ballast tanks was the cause of the disaster, and the Eastland was quote, on the morning of July 24th, 1915, seaorthy in every respect, fit for the carriage of passengers if properly handled. The civil trial determined that a payout to the families of victims should equal the value of Eastland's hull, about $50,000 at the time. But first, the owners had to pay out the salvas of the hull. That cost 35,000. Then another 15,000 went to creditors. So by the end, there was nothing left. Aid for families actually came from the Western Electric Company, the city of Chicago, and the Red Cross. But that was it. There was no watershed reform of maritime safety. In fact, there was no regulatory result at all. Eastland and her 844 victims slipped from the headlines and slowly faded from memory while the St. Joseph Chicago Steamship Company and its owners and officers escaped Scott free. This infamous disaster didn't result in any major precedent of law, although it damn well should have. The Eastland sinking serves as a tragic reminder of what happens when businesses are allowed unchecked and unregulated to maintain unsafe standards of practice. In Chicago today, as people hurry and bustle past the Lasal Street Bridge on their way to work, they could be completely forgiven for missing the metal plaque installed in 2003 that commemorates the tragedy. It's hard to imagine that there in the middle of that vibrant town, a disaster had taken over 840 lives. There on the other side of the river still sits the red brricked Reed Murdoch and Coing, a silent sentinel and witness to one of history's most tragic maritime disasters. The day the Eastland rolled. Here the Queen Mary slides into Southampton after another transatlantic run. A royal lady come home once more. Once upon a time, if you wanted to get anywhere in the world, across the roaring Atlantic mid- winter, where the waves stand the height of apartment blocks or way down to Australia over the Indian Ocean and its blistering sun, you would have to board an ocean liner. These magnificent pieces of technology were the toast of their era. And from the 1800s, when they were first introduced until the mid- 20th century, they evolved and grew to gargantuan proportions. They served their respective countries heroically in wartime. They transported celebrities and migrants alike in their hundreds of thousands and they cut the journey across the Atlantic from weeks and weeks to just 3 and 1/2 days. Then they disappeared. Quietly in the background, a technological war had been waged. For half a century, the airplane had grown and evolved too. And then when the ocean liner was right at its absolute height, the unthinkable happened. Almost overnight, the world's great ocean liners were made redundant. Passenger bookings dropped to nothing. Once celebrated, ships were pulled unceremoniously from service and sat rusting, awaiting their fates. Overhead, the roar of jet engines sang their swan song. Just how this played out, the key players and companies, is one of the most interesting technological tales of our times. It's a sad tale of redundancy. What happens when the times move on and leave the marvels of the past behind? This is how the ocean liner died. The New York Chelsea peers. Since the turn of the 20th century, this was the gathering place for a veritable who's who of the world's largest and most glamorous passenger ships. From the Cunard darlings Moritania and Lucatania at pier 54 to the later magnificent Queen Mary and Elizabeth at pier 90, the spectacular Normandy of the French line at pier 88 and the record-breaking SS United States at 86. The ships that frequented these peers were celebrities in their own right and they helped the peers earn their veryat nickname beginning in the 1930s, luxury liner row. In the post depression era, luxury liner row was home to a near constant flurry of activity as passengers of all kinds made their way to and from these grandiose vessels with transatlantic services offered multiple times per week across several fleets of ships. These ships were capable of whisking travelers across the ocean in around 4 and 1/2 days with the speed queen SS United States offering a trip across the Atlantic in a ripping 3 and a half. Most passengers look forward to their voyages, which in many way were like holidays all of their own. Travel by sea had come leaps and bounds since the days of rickety and dangerous packet sailing ships. And in just a few short decades, luxury liners had evolved and transformed, making once dreaded sea travel a stylish and savvy way to cross the Atlantic. The steam engine meant big ships could propel themselves over the world's oceans at previously unthought of speed and regularity. Sailing ships had been doomed to sail only when the weather permitted. But steam ships didn't have to worry about that. They could just forge ahead. The humble, fair-paying passenger could look forward to a relatively easy few days at sea where every need was met and then some. For the wealthy, it meant traveling in luxury that rivaled their favorite hotels ashore, like the Ritz and the Seavoy. For the poor, it meant amenities and comforts few had ever seen before at all, like flushing toilets, electric lights, and three square meals a day. It wasn't just a matter of convenience either. Crafting the world's largest and fastest ships was a matter of national pride for their home countries. And celebrities and society's elite were all known to have their preferred ships, their favorite stateooms, and even captains, making a crossing on a luxury liner into a star studded event. It wasn't just the transatlantic crossings, either. Passengers could get all the way from England or America to Australia, New Zealand, or the Far East on a single ship on a single voyage. It would take weeks, but it would be a comfortable and enjoyable escape, especially for those who weren't seasick. The ocean liner had enjoyed an unrivaled dominance of the world's ocean highways. It hadn't always been smooth sailing, though. Some tough lessons had to be learned along the way. There had even been attempted interlopers when zeppelins had briefly offered trans ocean services, but that had eventually ended in disaster and it wasn't pursued further. Ocean liners were the undisputed monarchs of the ocean. But then in 1957, just south of Seattle, Washington, something momentous happened that would change the world forever. To understand this, we need to wind the clock back. in my flying upg. >> Throughout the 1920s, while travel by steamship was just beginning to reach the heights of absolute glitz and glamour, aviation was still well in its infancy. Travelers around the world were becoming more and more curious about air travel. And buzz began to circulate as this seemingly futuristic bit of engineering started to gain widespread notoriety. But much like ocean travel in the 1800s, aviation at the time still left much to be desired. While they had come a long way since the days of the Wright brothers, helped along massively by the huge technological advancements gleaned in the First World War, early passenger airplanes were cramped, cold, noisy, slow, and dangerous. Many aircraft could only seat around 20 passengers at a time versus the thousand or more that could travel at once on board an ocean liner. And the unpressurized and unheated cabins made flying a frigid affair, especially at higher altitudes. Passengers bundled up in hats and coats to combat the freezing air with almost nothing in the way of insulation to fend off the bitter temperatures outside. Frequent refueling stops extended already sluggish flight times. Passenger aircraft were also slow. Most could only muster around 100 mph, still much quicker than a ship. But then they needed to stop every few hundred miles to refuel. During the peak years of the ocean liner, travel by air was still prohibitively expensive, too. With some trips costing about half as much as a brand new car, this meant that in its early years, flying remained reserved for only the most wealthy or daring of society, and daring they needed to be. Early aviation safety record would give any traveler pause for thought. In the late 1920s, the accident rate was one aircraft lost for every million miles flown. Now, at the same rate, in today's world, that would equal around 7,000 fatal plane crashes annually. Navigational instruments were simple. Aircraft engines were relatively underpowered. They were completely at the mercy of the sky and its temper, and many simply disappeared. The aircraft showed promise, and the number of passenger flights slowly grew, but they couldn't yet hope to match the comfort and the luxury of the world's beloved palaces at sea. By the year 1926, only 6,000 souls were brave enough to take to the air in these primitive commercial aircraft. Clearly, there was much progress left to be made if travel by air could ever hope to rival travel by sea. And the ocean liner enjoyed an easy lead because big ships could benefit from centuries of lessons learned at sea. While the airplane was really breaking new ground, the 1930s saw some truly revolutionary aircraft begin to turn the tide, though. The Boeing 314 Clipper, a flying boat aptly named after the great fast sailing Clipper ships of old, did something once thought only as science fiction when it carried passengers and male across the Atlantic in 1939. Only a dozen were ever built, and the route took nearly 30 hours with multiple refueling stops. But for the 40 or so passengers, it was the quickest way yet to cross the Atlantic. This was the sign of things to come. But then the world erupted into a global conflict and the transatlantic passenger service both above and on the water was rudely halted for 6 years. This was the crucial moment the airplane had needed to get ahead. Because while the construction and development of ocean liners had virtually stopped overnight in late 1939, the development of aircraft engines and technology was absolutely paramount. Many things came out of the second world war that changed the airplane and travel forever. The first was the jet engine. The development of fighter aircraft like meashmmit 262, the glouester meteor and the locked P80 proved the jet engine as a supremely powerful propulsion system. Something that could propel aircraft up to incredible speeds. But arguably the most important development for passenger comfort especially was cabin pressurization. In 1940, the Boeing Stratliner had introduced the system that enabled passengers to breathe and live comfortably at much higher altitudes. The system was perfected in the B-29 bomber. Now the airplane could fly incredibly high up over the bad weather which had once tormented it. 1952 would prove to be a critical year for the ocean lighter. It benefited from wartime lessons, too. And the SS United States was designed and built in the postwar world with technology that had been seen on modern American battleships. Superheated boilers and advanced propeller design saw the new ship snatch the speed record from the old Queen Mary in July that year and bring the transatlantic crossing down to just 3 days and 10 hours. An incredible feat. This was the fastest an ocean liner had ever been. But it was also the fastest an ocean liner would ever be. Because although the United States designers didn't know it yet, even as they were preparing their ship for its triumphant maiden voyage, another vessel's first trip was underway. But this one was above the clouds. Introduced as the world's first commercial jet airliner by Britain's BOAC, the Deavlin Comet shook the world's merchant marines to their core. While its predecessors had been sluggish, cold, and uncomfortable, the Comet promised a new era in air travel with its quiet, pressurized cabin, expanded passenger capacity, and unprecedented fuel efficiency, range, and speed. All thanks to its advanced jet engines. What was once a nightmarish mode of travel now seemed positively cushy by comparison. And that's to say nothing of that speed. Suddenly, a crossing which once took days could now feasibly be undertaken in just hours. Ship owners were initially nervous, but they may have been somewhat heartened by a series of crashes which shook public confidence in the comet. By the mid-50s, though, the kinks had been ironed out of the comet and the playing field had been leveled. It was a showdown. Ocean liners against airliners. At first, Cunard and the great shipping lines thought they could weather the storm. Passenger numbers stayed steady in the early and mid 1950s, and things look good. But then, as the decade wore on, something changed. The series of comet hull losses in the early 1950s, two of them fatal, had forced the company back to the drawing board to address severe issues with the pressurization of its cabins. These overhauls in the design of the aircraft would ultimately result in the Comet 4, in which designers applied all the lessons they had learned from their early efforts to create something that would go on to revolutionize the world of aviation. On October 4th, 1958, the Comet 4 became the first jet airliner to complete a commercial transatlantic flight. Not just one, but two aircraft undertaking the journey simultaneously. One bound for New York and the other for London. The westbound plane touched down after just over 10 hours, including a single brief stop in Gounder, Newfoundland to refuel. The eastbound flight completed its journey in just 6 hours. The new jet liners were proving to be to the ocean liner what the ocean liner had once been to the sailing ship. Even if it seemed a losing battle, it was still a battle. The great passenger lines tried to stem the falling passenger fairs. Cunard, especially with a dozen liners still in service, hoped to sway customers away from this new and speedy mode of transport with one director quoted as saying, "Flying is a fad. It will pass." Cunard was still operating two of the world's most popular passenger ships, the Queen Mary and the Queen Elizabeth, with 10 other ships accompanying them in the fleet. But they were hardressed to convince the public to opt for a six-day crossing when a 9-hour flight was now entirely within reach. In October 1958, passenger numbers for airlines eclipsed those of shipping lines for the first time with 1 and a half million travelers crossing by air versus a comparatively pitiful 882,000 by sea. It was just a sign of things to come because that same year, 1958, delivered a death blow to the ocean liner with the introduction of a realworld beater. An aircraft that would bring air travel to the masses. The year prior, it had taken its first flight just south of Seattle, Washington. It was the Boeing 707. This was the aircraft which would define the jet age with a 600 mph service speed, capacity for 181 passengers compared to the comet's 70 or so, and an overall safer service record. The Boeing 707 completed its own crossing from New York to Paris on October 26th, 1958, and a total of 8 hours and 40 minutes, including the refueling stop in Gander. It would have taken a liner days to cover the same distance. There could be no more denying it. The jet age was well and truly here. This was truly a nightmare scenario for the world's ocean liners and the companies that owned them. Almost overnight, what had once been considered the foremost option for travel was now functionally dead. Nowhere was this more evident than the once glittering New York Chelsea peers. By 1960, the once lively peers were already beginning to fall into disrepair. And where they had at one time been the home to the hustle and bustle of merry travelers and the luxurious liners they sailed on, now the peers were mainly relegated to handling cargo ships. But even this era was short-lived, and the last of the cargo ships had left the peers by 1967. It was a sorry sight. The peers fell into disrepair and abandonment, an ugly stain on the Hudson Riverfront. Airports had taken their place, becoming the epicenter of the bustling travel world. Dramatically impacted by this shift was the United States line, who throughout the 1950s had enjoyed nearly unprecedented success with their record-breaking super liner, the SS United States. The United States was the largest ocean liner ever built by the Americans and the fastest liner ever, too. But even she was no match for the Boeing 707, which was capable of cracking the equivalent of a staggering 521 knots to her 38. It was a fight that the shipping world was sure to lose. While a running mate for the SS United States had been planned, Congress could no longer justify putting millions of dollars behind what was by all accounts a dying industry. Funding was withheld and the SS United States successor would never materialize. In 1961, the United States had to cancel a crossing because only 350 passengers had booked. A series of strikes in 1965 saw all of the ship summer voyages canled. She was permanently pulled from service just 4 years later. The SS United States had been a technological triumph, but she only saw service for 17 years. And even then, nearly eight of those had been a struggle just for survival. While the rest of the shipping world could do little more than bork at the disastrous cards they had been dealt, the everindustrious Kunard line decided to operate under the old adage, if you can't beat them, join them. In fact, a few decades prior to the aviation boom, Cunard experimented with the world of air travel. This was still well before the dawn of the jet airliner back in 1937. So Percy Bates, then chairman of the company, was approached by Imperial Airways, who came in with a very tempting pitch. Put simply, with the world still relying heavily on sea travel and the Great Depression putting a damper on much of the travel industry's innovation, he failed to see what the company could stand to gain by expanding from sea to air. But nearly 10 years later, in 1946, Bates's successor, Sir John Brocklebank, seemed to be a more forwardthinking sort, and he was willing to revisit the idea. Brockbank's plan included an in-house airline to add to the company's fleet, bolstering their position in the everanging travel world. In 1960, with airlines now exerting their dominance more and more, Kunard Inc. a deal with Eagle Airways to purchase a 60% share in their company. This 30 million pound investment would lead to the introduction of Cunard Eagle Airways. And with the acquisition, the company hoped to cement themselves as a lasting presence in the travel industry despite declining numbers in their oceangoing fleet. It seemed a natural response for the company in the face of dwindling ocean travel. The very next year in 1961, Cunard Eagle was operating daily transatlantic flights to accompany its continuing trans oceanic schedule. This seemed to do the trick. Eventually, Kunard Eagle was operating flights to destinations all around the world. In 1962, the venture caught the attention of BOAC, who in turn offered Kunard a 30% stake in their own company. Kunard Eagle became BOAC Kunard. Eagle Airways pulled out of their side of the agreement a year later, but with tidy profits in 1964, BOAC and Kunard both held on with high hopes for a successful partnership in the long run. The unfortunate truth was that while partner BOAC had both feet firmly in the aviation business, Kunard was still operating a fleet of ships and a pricey one at that. Meanwhile, aircraft was still evolving. And with the powerful Boeing 747 on the horizon, the company knew they lacked the capital to continue to finance both seagoing and airborne vessels, each becoming pricier with every new iteration. By the late 1960s, despite decades of attempts to position themselves as a travel juggernaut on both sea and air, reality had finally set in and the overextended Cunard admitted defeat. Even with the ocean liner dying out, QE2, as she would one day be affectionately nicknamed, was designed to maintain a liner's transatlantic service. But she could also run cruises thanks to her clever layout. She was a new ship for a new era. If passenger ship companies were to survive at all, they would have to look to the growing leisure cruise market instead. Other shipping lines found their own ways to try to stay afloat in the face of airborne adversity.
