And even the largest fleet in the world was not immune to the overwhelming shifts brought on by air travel. With the 10 lb palm scheme at its end and passenger numbers continuing to nose dive, by the mid70s, PNO had scrapped virtually all of its great pre and postwar liners and moved away to cargo and cruisers instead. Interestingly, while many companies were desperately trying to expand away from shipping to stay alive, some clever business owners were doing just the opposite. and they were finding success. Chandras Lines was founded in 1960, just 2 years after the comet's first successful commercial transatlantic flight. Much like PO, the aim of the Chandras Line was to capitalize on the still profitable immigration trade to Australia. The MO was simple. Buy retired ocean liners at minimum cost and work them hard for maximum profit. They did this well and their ships Oustralis, Elinus, Bratannis, and Patrice became well-known migrant vessels carrying thousands for new lives down under. But the business strategy worked, and even as aircraft dominated many major routes, Chandras Lines ships sailed well booked with passengers even into the late 1970s. It was the late60s that saw the real end of the era of the ocean liner. The retirement of the Queens heralded the real end of an era. The ocean liner had finally died. But adaptable companies like PNO, Charrus, and even Cunard began to sense a new opportunity to keep some of their fleet in service. Cruising was actually nothing new at the time. The 1960s though had seen a huge uptick in demand for leisure cruisers even as demand for travel by air was reaching new heights and cruising offered an experience the airlines couldn't hope to match. A leisurely holiday at sea where one could wh away the hours with any number of activities offered on board all with the freedom to move around the vessel instead of being restricted to one single seat in the cabin of an aircraft. While airlines offered an efficient mode of travel, cruisers offered an actual enjoyable experience. And it was this very experience that kept the world's ships at sea, even in the face of an industry which threatened to make them obsolete. Many of the remaining great ocean liners found new lives as cruise ships. Probably the most successful was the SS France. She'd been built too late to capitalize on the golden age of the ocean liner. A triumph for her home nation though she was. France was introduced just a few years after the first commercial flight of the Deavlin Comet. She saw only 14 years of service with French Line and that should have been the end except a new and budding cruise line had other plans for her. Norwegian Cruise Line picked France up and transformed her into the SS Norway. What had begun life as a transatlantic passenger liner designed to operate a schedule as ruthlessly and efficiently as a train ended her days as a beloved cruise ship running pleasure voyages around the world. The transition to cruising wasn't easy on all ocean liners, and some just couldn't cut it. The Italian liners, Christophoro Columbo and Leonardo da Vinci, were just too expensive to run. They had been built to absolutely burn through monstrous amounts of fuel to run at breakneck transatlantic speeds, not swinging around on joy cruisers. Not only that, but their class segregated interiors became a confusing maze once the ship was converted to oneclass cruising with staircases that skipped decks, corridors that seemed to go nowhere. By contrast, other ships have been designed with this future in mind. The Dutch SS Rotterdam used a genius system of folding panels that could separate classes during a crossing or be folded down to open the ship up for oneclass cruising. She had a long and successful career with her original owners and beyond into the 21st century. The first half of the 20th century saw the ocean liner at its absolute peak. The world was connected like never before and passengers could be carried across entire oceans in record times and in unmatched comfort. Countries took pride in producing the biggest and the best vessels the world had ever seen. consistently outclassing one another in terms of size, speed, strength, luxury, and efficiency. But as history has shown us time and time again, technology is constantly finding new ways to change and evolve. So it was little wonder that the ocean liner's days were numbered. Looking back at the success of the SS United States and the blue ribboned holders who came before her, one fundamental truth rings clear. In the eyes of a fickle traveling public, speed comes above everything else. It seems obvious then that for all its wonders, this stately and beautiful mode of travel was bound to be eclipsed by the miracle of flight. And by 1958, that was exactly what had happened. Despite the best efforts of the most illustrious shipping lines of the time, travelers were largely ready to move on from the ocean liner and onto the next big thing. They simply voted with their wallets. The results were disastrous for an entire industry and way of life. The Chelsea peers, once the glorious sight of ocean liner row, fell into disrepair in the60s, rotted in the 70s, and then completely collapsed in the 80s before they were fully dismantled. Today, the waterfront has been rejuvenated with parks, bars, and luxury hotels. And only the facade of Cunard's Pier 54 remains of the massive original structure. At the other end of the route in Southampton, the magnificent customuilt ocean terminal building designed specifically for the big male ships like Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth had worked as a kind of lounge and baggage handling facility with a massive train station so passengers could easily step foot from off of their train and onto their ship. It was finished in the ' 50s but scrapped in the 80s already a relic of a bygone era. But within a decade, the cruise industry had exploded, and Southampton once again found itself needing exactly the kind of ocean terminal building it had demolished. Today, if you want to board a cruise ship from the port, you won't do so from a beautiful deco building, but from a series of Spartan sheds instead. Such is the March of Progress. The oceangoing greats that had once won the hearts of millions, few remain today. The Queen Mary has been preserved as a museum in a hotel in Long Beach, California, but Queen Elizabeth caught fire and burnt to a crisp in the 60s before her university overhaul ever bore any fruit. The Rotterdam has been remarkably well restored and now acts as a museum and a hotel in the port of her name in the Netherlands. France served for years as the cruise ship Norway, the sweetheart of tens of thousands of passengers before being finally scrapped in 2006. United States. The brilliant record-breaking speed demon has sat rotting for years at a dock in Philadelphia. And now, instead of being preserved for future generations, it looks like she's going to be sunk to become an artificial reef. There is just one glorious ship at sea upholding the old traditions. Kunard's Queen Mary 2, a remarkable special ship built in the early 2000s. She was designed to fulfill the role her forebears had done so well before her. With 40% more steel than your standard cruise ship at much greater construction expense, the Queen Mary 2 can take the worst the Atlantic can throw at her. Once recently, in a terrific storm, most Atlantic traffic was stopped in its tracks, including ships of the Navy who were beused to spot on their radar screens one vessel making good headway into the huge seas. "What are you?" they radioed out. The reply was simple and concise. the Queen Mary. They said, "Imagine this. You've had to abandon your ship loaded heavily with aviation fuel after it was set on fire in an attack. You and your comrades took to the ocean in two lifeboats. But in the chop and the darkness, you've been separated. Now your boat drifts aimlessly and a full day later as a storm is just beginning to blow a light is spotted off on the horizon. You pull with all your might on the oars and you even rig a sail hoping for rescue and you find to your absolute surprise that the light is actually a ship on fire. It's the ship you abandoned yesterday, but it's still a float and it hasn't sunk yet. This is the exact bizarre scenario that the crew of the MV San Ditrio found themselves in in late 1940. Caught out in an assault by a German pocket battleship, the vessel had an epic comeback after its men abandoned it to burn and presumably explode, only to come across the thing, still burning happily the next day. What happened next is one of the great feats of maritime daring dew from the war. This is the incredible true tale of the San Ditrio, the ship that rescued its own crew. Late 1940, the war has been raging for a full year now. Since Nazi Germany's Panza twos and threes rolled over the Polish border after the Phony War had come, the invasion of France and Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Britain was on the ropes. But the Battle of Britain had shown that Germany's forces could be defeated. The island nation held out under intense nighttime raids by the Luftvafa. While at sea, the Creeks Marines, Ubot, and warships hunted with near impunity. The strategy had been to starve Britain into submission, to deprive it of the critical materials it needed from friendly powers across the sea to keep the war machine humming. Merchant ships bunched up in convoys for protection. But the protection the Royal Navy could actually offer was often pathetic. Their most powerful ships were tied up in the Mediterranean, and even a destroyer could hardly be detached from fleet work to do something as mundane as escort duty. So, merchant ships were given little 3 and 4 in guns or QF12 pounders and told essentially to hope for the best. Now, one of these convoys was HX84. It had steamed from Halifax, bound for Liverpool on October 28th, 1940. Made up of 38 ships, oil tankers, and freighters. The convoy had originally been protected by the ancient Wixclass destroyer Colombia and the Clemson class St. Francis, which were both built in the last war. But alongside those ships was Jarvis Bay, an ocean liner converted through the addition of guns no bigger than 6 in and dating to the late 1800s into an armed merchant cruiser. Now, recent history had shown that ocean liners make for shocking auxiliary cruisers, but the Royal Navy was tied up and the Admiral was in a desperate position. So Jarvis Bay and many like her were called up to pull off a task that could suddenly often turn brutal. So HX84 set off with Colombia and St. Francis both peeling off after a day of escort duty clearing the coast. The convoy plotted on until November 5th when they were about 800 m or 1300 km southeast of the tip of Greenland in Mid-Atlantic a smudge of smoke was spotted on the horizon. Now, we've covered this story before in some detail, but you can only imagine the convoy's collective horror when the smudge materialized into the massive heavy cruiser Admiral Shear. The kind of fast miniature battleship that was ideally suited for hunting down and killing convoys. With its fast acting 11-in main guns and a top speed of 28 knots, there was simply no running. with a main belt of 80 mm or 3 in of steel armor. There wasn't a single gun between any of the ships in the convoy that could possibly hurt her. But still, the escort Jarvis Bay peeled off to draw Admiral She's fire and a kind of desperate self-sacrifice that many have since described as reckless, but which in my opinion at least served to tie the German warship down long enough for the convoy to scatter and try to escape into the dusk. Now, Jarvis Bay was hit and basically taken to bits by the German gunfire, and the Shere turned its attention to the panicked and fleeing convoy ships. One of them was a tanker absolutely loaded with aviation fuel. Now, there are certain cargos you just don't want to be carrying if you're hit. And right at the top of that list would have to be gasoline and fuel. The tanker was a floating keg. The San Deitrio was a modern kind of tanker built back in 1938 with 8-cylinder diesels and a hull that was about 463 feet or 141 m long and about 8,73 gross registered tons. She wasn't a giant ship, but she was a modern and utilitarian workhorse that had been built for the Eagle Oil and Shipping Company in peace time, but now found itself in one of the most dangerous and unforgiving battlefields in the world. On a bridge was Captain George Wait, who'd already experienced hell at sea because in late 1939 he'd been the skipper of the tanker San Alberto that was caught and torpedoed by the U48. He now watched on appalled as Admiral Shear sped straight past the now silent and burning Jarvis Bay and turned her guns on the convoy. It was every man for himself. The New Zealand liner Rangutiki was hit, but she dropped a dense smoke screen that hit her well enough to make an escape. Others weren't so fortunate. German shells slammed into them and wait on the Sanjitrio had to try to steer his vessel to safety. With the light failing, he hoped he might escape into the night and he altered course to starboard to clear the main body of fleeing merchant ships. But there was a shout of alarm from a lookout because a ship to their right off on the starboard bow was attempting to do the opposite and seemingly steer directly into them. Fortunately, collision was just avoided. Then wait and his men felt Sand Demetrio tremble underfoot because she was hit. Night had fallen, but a big moon was illuminating the horizon ahead of the German cruiser, which could easily pick its prey out of the darkness. It fired on, and the crew of the Sand Demetria, only being able to see flashes in the dark from far behind them. Shells rained down all around. The ship they had narrowly avoided colliding with was hit first, and the screams of the wounded drifted across the water. Then it was Sand Demetrio's turn. Hit after hit, shell after shell struck home, and soon the vessel was burning fiercely. After only 1 hour since the Admiral Shear had started the attack, San Demetrio was presumed a total loss, burning completely out of control. She become a giant petrol bomb just waiting to go off at any moment. Now, this wasn't diesel fuel. It was fast burning high octane aviation gas that threatened to detonate into an allconsuming enormous fireball. Captain Wait knew the game was up and he wasted absolutely no time at all. He ordered his ship hastily abandoned. A handful of boats were swung out and lowered, but one was swamped, leaving just the forward starboard and port boats bobbing together in the darkening night. One loaded with 26 men and the other with just 16. Now briefly tethered together, a plan was formed to get away from the tanker as quickly as possible. But now they had another issue. Ships from the convoy were tearing past them from every angle in a desperate bid for escape. They were badly at risk of being run down by one of their own ships. The men rode like demons to get out of the way. But when the danger had cleared and the night became still, the two boats had been separated and set out into the night. Most alarmingly of all, the wind was freshening and it looked like there might be a storm on the horizon. Admiral Shear hunted and fired on vessels well into the night until she finally disengaged about midnight. Five merchant ships were sunk outright, not including Jarvis Bay, which herself had gone down with nearly 200 lives. Sand Demetrio had been abandoned to burn into the night. But the rest of the convoy had scattered and would survive. Cold comfort for the men in the boats who had to spend a night being tossed around the ocean like a cork. Next morning brought a full gale with huge waves. The open top boats were battered and thrown around filling with water. So the men had to bail nearly non-stop just to stay afloat. Our efforts now, recalled apprentice John Jones, were just survival as the seas swamped the boats and often we bailed for our lives. As conditions grew worse and they were seriously at risk of sinking with no help at hand, the boat loaded with 16 men was treated to an enticing sight. A call from someone announced a dark shape off to Winwood, a ship somewhere off in the distance about 4 miles away. The men shouted, lit flares, and tried to wave her down, but there was no response. A brief period of depression followed, wrote Jones, which we soon realized was a luxury we could not afford, and the fight for our lives resumed. More flooding and endless bailing. It went on and on until the afternoon when the storm seemed to calm, and then again another ship could be seen, but this one was tailed by an ominous, greasy cloud of smoke. The men hoisted a sail to catch the fresh breeze and try to run the ship down for rescue. But the closer they got, the more familiar the ship appeared. It took a while, Jones recalled, to recognize that this was our own ship. Sand Demetrio had not exploded. Instead, it had burnt through the night and now continued to burn, but it was bearing down on the boat as if to swing past for a rescue. Faced now with the prospect of sinking at sea in their open top boats, the men decided to try reboarding their own tanker to see what could be done. They bore down on it with sail set, but afternoon was slowly turning to evening, and with the failing light, a hard decision had to be made. Reboarding the ship in a big sea was tough enough, but to do it in the dark was insanity. We've spent a lot of time on this channel talking about the ocean liner, big passenger carrying steam ships from the mid 1800s. Something that as a piece of technology completely changed the way the world traveled. It's actually kind of hard to convey just how big a change this was. Naturally, to demonstrate things, we need to look at what life was like before. Before the ocean liner. Here's a spoiler alert. It's not a pretty picture. Without exaggeration, it can be said that for hundreds and hundreds of years of our history, going to sea was like rolling a dice to see if you'd make it or not. It's that dangerous out there. Line was an experienced Scottish shipping firm that was set up in the 1860s and came to acquire a fleet of 25 then modern iron hullled sailing ships that combined all the centuries of knowledge we'd learned in operating sailing ships and the huge technological developments that metal hulls had brought. But the truth of it is that times were just tough. And in the 1800s, so many ships were lost that it's actually hard to choose which stories best explain what those risks were like. But I've picked two, and the first one in particular is chilling. The first one happened not too far from me in Australia. She was called the Kataraki. Kataraki was a sailing ship, a bark built in England in 1840. She was absolutely typical of the hundreds, if not thousands of ships of that kind, that were sailing to and from Australia at the time. See, in the mid 1800s, Australia was still a relatively new British colony, and the government was keen to establish more of a foothold on the continent. Assisted immigrant schemes were put into place where families seeking to establish a new life away from the grime and mark of England cities could try their luck in an entirely new continent and society. There were a few downsides though, especially the trip out. The voyage to Australia was really tough and conditions were nothing short of awful. The ships leaked and rolled violently in the high seas and passengers not yet used to traveling at sea were sick the entire way. The decks ran thick with vomit and passenger quarters were cramped and dimly lit. Many sailing immigrant ships simply disappeared in storms, never to be seen again. To sail to Australia was to risk your life. Kataraki was tiny, only 138 ft or 42 m long and 802 tons. But still, in April 1845, into her decks were crowded 369 immigrants and 41 crew. 120 of the hopeful immigrants were married with families and the ship carried 73 children. The crew knew that they were approaching the south coast of Australia and plotted roughly where they thought they might make landfall. Meanwhile, down in the passenger quarters, the two ship's doctors, both brothers named Carpenter, had been hard at work. On the voyage, five children had been born and six others had died. And if a shell went through the belt, it would hit the flat walls and damage important machinery spaces within the armored citadel. Because of this, ship designers angled the sides of the armored deck to form a slope thicker than the deck amid ships. If the penetrating shell were to hit this slope, it would have a higher chance of ricocheting up and away. Not only that, but sloping armor increases the thickness of material that a shell actually has to penetrate. At 22°, Bismarck's turtle back armor had a relative thickness that went from 120 mm to 320 mm for any shell meeting at flat from the side. A shell striking Bismar flatly at close range would need to penetrate the main belts 320 mm and then punch through another 320 mm on the turtle back, 640 mm, 25 in of steel. However, by the interwar period, many designs had dropped the turtle back armor scheme. As more effective fire control systems were developed and stronger guns were built, engagement ranges increased. The main threat now was not shells penetrating the armored belt from the side, but plunging fire coming down at range from above. Bismar's turtleback scheme was susceptible to heavy damage from long-range engagements as her deck armor was weaker than her contemporaries in the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. But these navies would have to fight in the Pacific as well, where long-range engagements were common. Marina designers built Bismar for the North Sea and the North Atlantic, where she was intended to get up close and personal and engage the enemy on her terms at closer ranges. To make up for it, her builders constructed a very buoyant hull with a wide beam or overall width. To bring her heavy guns and armor into battle without suffering from significant rolling to protect her guns and their massive equipment as it burrowed down into the magazines far below, Bismar was fitted with those four huge turrets. Here is where some of the heaviest armor was fitted. The turret fronts were some 360 mm or 14.7 in thick, the sides up to 220 mm, and the roofs 130. The idea behind this array of fire control computers was fairly straightforward. One of each pair would be used to compute for the main 38 cm guns while the second could cover the 15 cm secondaries. There was built-in redundancy. If one computer's direction was knocked out, then the other could take over. And by changing the ballistics information, the computer that had been working for the main guns could easily switch over to the secondaries and vice versa. In fact, if one whole computer room itself was destroyed or damaged, then the other could take over entirely. But in keeping with the German doctrine of plotting multiple targets at once, all stations could be working to engage two or more enemies at the same time. Bismar's hull was split into messes and birthing for petty officers and other ranks, appropriately segregated into large compartments. Of course, the Japanese Yumato and Mashi dwarfed her in size. The American Iowa class fielded much more advanced radar, and they weren't much smaller. But that's been conflated with legend and myth which has painted Bismar out to be the ultimate warship when she certainly wasn't. Events would soon show that the day of the battleship was over and the aircraft carrier was supreme. But Bismar was still very scary. In May 1941, she and Prince slipped the net. The new battleship Prince of Wales, the mighty battle cruiser Hood rushed to engage them. Bismar's gunnery system finally went into action with devastating results. Now, if that seems a bit reckless, fear not, because her maximum service speed was limited to just 2.5. The Farad Bruno's crew was made up of 45 officers and enlisted men who were squeezed into her 182 ft, 55 1/2 m long hull. When people described the construction of monitors as being cheap and cheerful, they're not embellishing, but Fardy Bruno was quite unique, even in comparison to other monitors of the time. Her flanks and decks were built to a prismatic shape like the armored shell of a turtle with the sides angled downward to guard against incoming shells and her extremely low freeboard making her harder to sight and hit. Her deck surface was bare in typical monitor fashion but featured a towering tripod mast which rose up behind the main gun turret and supported a protected bridge. Speaking of main gun turrets, yeah, wow. The massive 15-in 381 mm guns were housed twinned in a revolving turret. I seriously cannot even imagine what it would have been like to be aboard this thing when those guns went off. Her hull, in addition to its prismatic shape, also had a concrete coffam 9 1/2 ft or 2.9 m thick for added protection. Far Bruno was expected to engage enemy shore installations, so it was thought she'd need to be protected mostly from field artillery. So to that end, her protection was quite well thought out. It would be pretty hard to hit this thing from a couple of miles away with your 8 cm field gun. Despite their unusual design, construction, and purpose, Italy actually invested in 14 monitors for their navy. They were designed to specifically meet three requirements. First, in being able to carry heavy longrange artillery to disrupt the front line and allow a breakthrough in the AustroHungarian lines because the big battleship caliber guns had a maximum range of nearly 20 km or 12 1/2 miles. Second, there'd need to be stable gun platforms to maximize accuracy and fire effect. And finally, they needed to be able to operate in extremely shallow coastal waters. To that end, Farty Bruno, despite having virtually nothing above the water line, featured only 7 ft or 2.2 m of ship below the water line. Now to offset the dangerous propensity for rolling and even capsizing, she was given the beam or the width of an ocean liner or battleship. Even though she was shorter than a destroyer, the Fi Bruno and fellow monitor Alfredo Capalini did play a small role in the 11th of 12 battles of Iso. These were a series of conflicts between the Austrohungarians and Italian armies fought in the latter part of 1917. The father Bruno and Alfredo Kapalini along with two British monitors bombarded the Austrohungarian positions just as they had been designed to do. And although the battle was a victory for the Italians, the role of the monitors probably had very little to do with it. A few months after the battle of Isanzo, the Fardy Bruno was hit by a storm, driven ashore, and badly damaged. Now, perhaps signaling her importance to the Italian Navy as a whole, she was left stranded and not salvaged for almost a year. The Far Bruno was decommissioned in 1924, but returned to service as a floating battery under the name GM1 194 at the beginning of World War II. The aging vessel was towed to Genanoa, where she would spend the rest of the war. She was there when the Royal Navy bombarded the port in February 1941 and even fired off three shots in return. But that was all. After the Italian armistice, the strange vessel was captured by the Germans, who somehow thought she might be of some use and wanted to turn her back into a monitor, but the war ended before those plans ever came to pass. Ultimately, Far De Bruno was scuttled in 1945 and dismantled. She was a strange ship, to be sure, with her rectangular profile and her sluggish maneuverability, but in some ways, she should be considered a success because she'd been designed to be a stable gun platform for the big 15-in battleship rifles, and she was able to do just that for nearly 30 years. But as far as unhinged warship designs go, it's hard to think of anything more off-the-wall than Italy's first proper monitor. Often with technological advancements, you have a before and after and the slightly awkward in between. Battleships were no exception, and we've had a lot of fun talking about the weird time in the Royal Navy when wooden sailing ships, which had basically been perfected over hundreds of years, gave way to iron steam ships, which often left a lot to be desired. One fun example of these is Britain's Colossus class battleships, ironclads, which implemented a few firsts for the Royal Navy and the world. The Colossus class battleship was born out of an era where the French, British, German, American, Russian, and Italian navies rushed to compete with each other with each successive class of battleship. In a running skirmish between guns and armor, the British had a series of successes and failures. HMS Ajax had been a class-leading battleship when she was laid down in 1876, but it took four years to complete her. And even then, on trial, she was found to exhibit some bad behavior. Such was the pace of design and the frantic construction schedule at the time that even before Ajax was finished and his service, designs were already put into place for an improved class of battleship. Now, the key to Colossus' development was the introduction in the Royal Navy of breach loading guns. These had been tested years earlier, but they proved dangerous and unpredictable. But the development of an automatic safety device meant breach loaders were at last capable of being fired with reliability in mind. The simple fact was that a breach loaded gun was a bigger and more powerful gun than a muzzle loaded one for the fact that large shells and bags of powder could be more easily fed into the brereech at the back instead of being stuffed down the muzzle. This resulted in the development of a big 12-in 25 caliber gun. The Navy just needed something to put it on. Colossus was originally proposed to be significantly longer than any other British battleship in service, but the Admiral T settled on a more modest 325 ft length, but still her slightly longer hull and shallower beam meant she could squeeze an extra knot of speed out over her contemporaries. Colossus' true pioneering chops lay in the fact she was the first to use steel rather than iron for nearly all of the hull structure, aside from the stem and sturm castings. and she was the first truly modern battleship to field big breach loading rifled guns in turrets. The guns were impressive for the time. In trials, Colossus managed a blistering four rounds in 6 minutes from one gun and even scored three hits on a target at full steam. Breach loaders were just fast like that. In a naval battle, the amount of time and labor saved can make all the difference. On their sea trials, both Colossus class ships performed well and vastly exceeded their contract design speeds. with Colossus underloaded hitting 16 1/2 knots which threw up an enormous bow wave described as being like a solid wall of water 13 ft long. Crucially, they improved on the Ajax classes sea handling characteristics, but they still left a lot to be desired. Gunports were only 12 ft above the water line, and if the ship rolled just 13°, the gun's muzzles would kiss the water if they were trained to the side. They had a quick roll which required the fitting of large tanks down below to stabilize them. But their massive height meant they were liable to catch the wind and be carried off course with the helmsmen not paying attention. In fact, this is why Colossus has made this list for the most unhinged warship designs. She towered high out of the water with a hull that stood up like a steampunk wall stories tall. And there in the center of the ship were her twin gun turrets, which thanks to the raised folks and stern, had to be offset to fire forward or aft. For good measure, she was fitted with a ram bow, a device that did much more to act as a bulbous bow and cut down her fuel consumption at speed. While the technological achievements of the Colossus class are notable, her career and that of her sister was more mundane. The pair engaged in training and testing, but were rendered obsolete just a few short years after their introduction. It must have been an exciting time to be a naval architect in the British Admiral Dy when the government poured funds into creating the biggest and baddest warships the world had yet seen at an exponential rate. While they were definitely not without their growing pains, the Colossus class of battleship was a success, even if it was a short-lived one. With their towering hulls and funnels, the class certainly lived up to their name. They were true steam leviathans of the Victorian world. Now, we've talked about this next ship on the channel before, but I just had to bring it up again because the story is so fascinating. That one time the US Navy converted a passenger carrying paddlehe steamboat into a fullyfledged medalinning aircraft carrier, and it actually worked. In the early years of the Second World War, the United States had a bit of a problem. Its aircraft carriers were tied up in the Pacific theater, seeing desperate action in huge battles like Midway and the Coral Sea. They'd gone from mere curiosities to becoming the backbone of the modern Navy, and they had to be protected at all costs. But back home, pilots needed training for carrier operations, which came with their own quirks and immense dangers. Pilots landing on aircraft carriers faced a whole host of dangers their land-based colleagues didn't have to. For one, the weather was totally beyond the crew's control, and it could shift drastically on approach to the carrier. Chief among quirks for training carrier pilots was the length of the landing zone itself. Land-based pilots could enjoy runways thousands of feet long, but carrier pilots had just a short few hundred feet to work with. They had to put their aircraft down with pinpoint accuracy, usually just above stall speed. Of course, then the runway they were landing on was moving by itself as well. The early carrier pilots were their own breed of gutsy daredevil. But without an actual aircraft carrier to train on, pilots would be woefully underprepared when they got to the actual theater of operations. This is where some Navy planners got a clever unhinged idea. The SS CNB was a grand passenger steamer launched in November 1912 by the Detroit Ship Building Company in Michigan. Named using the initials of its owners, the Cleveland and Buffalo Transit Company, CNB, get it? The CNB boasted accommodations for over 1,500 passengers. At 500 ft or 152 m in length and 58 ft or 17.6 m in beam, she was among the largest and most opulent passenger steamers on the Great Lakes. And she was in fact the largest sidewheel steamer in the world at the time, a fact that would come in very handy for the Navy. She had boasted an impressive array of amenities aimed at passenger comfort, including stateaterooms, elegant dining saloons, and spacious prominard decks. In fact, the decision to use old-fashioned inclined steam engines was taken specifically for passengers who wanted a good night's sleep on board. The engines could develop impressive horsepower at low revolutions, creating less vibration and making for a more comfortable trip. She was an impressive, quirky ship, to be sure, and the SSC CNB served the Great Lakes region for over two decades. But then came the second world war. Navy commander Richard Whitehead had come up with the idea of making use of lake steamers for training purposes. But it took some time for the seemingly ludicrous idea to catch on. Remarkably though, the SSC CNB was acquired by the Navy in March 1942 and underwent a radical transformation. Her impressive length and beam made her an ideal platform for use as a training aircraft carrier and Navy workers got started on converting her. Her luxurious accommodations and superructure were removed and in their place a flattop flight deck was installed along with a small island superructure. She was fitted with resting cables that would seize landing aircraft. And it was reported by the Buffalo Courier Express that 45 mi of welding and 45,000 bolts went into her. Commissioned as the USS Wolverine in August 1942 because Michigan is known as the Wolverine State, Go Spartans, the vessel became one of two freshwater aircraft carriers alongside the USS Sable tasked with training naval aviators in carrier takeoffs and landings. In fact, Sable had once been a Sidewill Steamer 2, the SS Greater Buffalo built in 1924. The choice of the Great Lakes for these operations was strategic, too, offering a safe, controlled environment away from the threat of enemy submarines and allowing for nearly year round operations, albeit limited by winter ice. It was also a question of convenience, making the least impact on Navy resources. If Wolverine had been training on the open ocean, for example, instead, then an escort force of destroyers would be needed every time she left port. Operating primarily out of Chicago alongside USS Sable, the Wolverine played a crucial role in the training of thousands of Navy pilots. The two unusual ships came to be known as the Cornbelt Fleet. These aviators would go on to play a pivotal role in the Navy's aerial campaigns in the Pacific, contributing significantly to the Allied victory. The training operations aboard the Wolverine were not without their challenges, though, including navigating the unpredictable weather of the Great Lakes and accommodating the limitations imposed by the vessel's original design. They weren't real aircraft carriers, after all. There were no hangers or storage decks, elevators, or anything like that. Plus, the ships weren't fast enough to create the adequate wind conditions required for safe landing. So, on calm days, operations had to be halted entirely. But despite these hurdles, the Wolverine and her semi-sister ship, the Sable, provided invaluable service in preparing naval aviators for the rigors of carrier operations. The USS Wolverine was decommissioned in November 1945, shortly after the end of World War II. It had been an unusual end to such a unique ship, but CNB had served her country well and was scrapped after a successful three decade long career. As a fun little footnote, it turns out that the owners, the CNB Transit Company, had vastly inflated the value of the ship when they sold it to the government, who when they found out, we're not happy and hunted down more than a quarter of a million dollars from CNB stockholders. Wasn't very patriotic of CNB, wouldn't you say? Sometimes a design looks good and practical on paper, but this may not carry over into the real world once the thing is made out of iron and steel. Enter the strange Russian circular ironclads, the Nogarod and her halfsister, Vitz Admiral Popov. The basic idea behind these defensive monitors was based on the theory of Scottish ship builder John Elder to shorten the hull of the ship and widen the beam or its width, thereby reducing the total area needed to be covered by armor while also improving maneuverability. Russian Vice Admiral Aa Popov took the idea and ran with it, widening the beam so much that the ship became almost completely circular and flattening the bottoms entirely to totally minimize the draft. That is, how much of the ship sat underwater. This design would also allow for thicker armor overall, as well as the ability to carry larger and more powerful guns. That sounds great, right? Well, in the 1870s, for better or worse, the Nogarod and the slightly larger Vitzer Admiral Popov, a pair of ships, also known as the Papovkas, were built and were fully in service by 1877. Now, while the ships certainly looked a bit unusual, the concept itself is actually nothing new. In ancient Mesopotamia, India, and Asia, round floating platforms had been used to transport people and cargo across waterways. Even in Great Britain and Ireland, small round basket boats with flat bottoms called coracals [music] have been used for centuries as something of a simple vessel designed for use in swiftly flowing streams. These vessels were obviously more primitive, being made of interwoven willow rods tied together with bark. Animal skin was used as now to layer with a thin layer of tar to make it waterproof. These circular flat bottom single passenger boats were easy to maneuver, lightweight, and hardly disturbed the water below, making them a very clever sort of fishing vessel. However, applying the same design principles to a warship would prove to have some unfortunate, almost comical consequences. Despite their peculiar design, the Papovkas did operate well under certain conditions. They were found to be very stable gun platforms with easy roll in good weather. They would also be capable of firing in a full 360°. On top of this, they were extremely well protected for their time due to their heavy armor. The rounded deck made use of 2.75 in or 70 mm of armor consisting of three layers of plating. The lower section of the funnels at the base of the engine room skylight had armor plates that were a whopping 6 in or 150 mm thick. They also had decent firing capability. While the rate of fire was slow at about one round every 10 minutes or so, the guns could effectively penetrate 11 in or 28 cm of armor at a distance of 800 yd or 731 m. Initially, the Imperial Russian Navy liked Papov's idea so much they ordered a fleet of 10 of the things, planning to use them as coastal defense ships in the Kirk Straits in the mouth of the Denipa River. However, this plan would prove too expensive, and in the end, probably fortunately, only two were ever commissioned. Once the ships were built, it was found that they suffered from some rather serious design flaws. Firstly, steering was nearly impossible with the comparatively light hull and slow speeds proving ineffective against the rather strong currents in the Den River. Fred T. Jane, the famous warship historian, was quoted as saying, "On a trial cruise, the Nogarod and the Vitzer Admiral Popov went up the Deniper very nicely for some distance until they turned to retire. Then the current caught them. They were carried out to sea, whirled helplessly round and around with every soul on board helplessly incapacitated by Vertigo. They're also prone to rapid rolling and anything but flat calm in the Black Sea, which itself was known for its rough and turbulent weather. In severe cases, heavy storms would cause the ship to pitch enough so as to lift her propellers out of the water. And on top of this, it's said that the recoil of firing even a single gun could reportedly cause the ships to spin out of control with their underpowered engines and propellers unable to set them straight again. This was when seas were calm enough to allow the ships to reliably fire those guns in the first place. The design flaws don't just end there. The circular hull created massive amounts of resistance and drag. And the six outer propellers were found to do little to nothing at all to combat this. The hull shape also rendered the rudder almost useless, and the ship reportedly can take up to 45 minutes to make a full circle. And the flat bottom design didn't help either, causing the ships to act like skimming dishes on the water, offering even less control and steering accuracy. The circular design itself proved to not be a total failure. Surprisingly, in 1880, a similar concept was used for the Russian Imperial yacht Leadia, also the brainchild of Popov. With the yacht counterpart, Popov kept the circular hole, but added a conventional bow and stern. Called a gigantic life-size experiment. And despite having been used only once for her intended purpose as a yacht, the Levardia's design was ultimately deemed a success, having learned from the failures of the Papovkas before her, she was surprisingly maneuverable and decently fast, surprising naval architects during her sea trials with her stability, and they deemed her to be just as efficient as any other conventionally designed ship. Overall though, the theory behind these ships made a decent amount of sense. The supposed maneuverability coupled with heavy armorament, the potential for all round firepower was a solid enough idea, especially when taking into account the limited scope with which these ships were meant to be used essentially as coastal defense and never in a true sea battle. Quickly, it became clear though that factors such as weather, gun recoil, and sea currents had other ideas in mind for these warships, rendering them terribly ineffective, causing them to go down in history as some of the worst warships ever designed. Despite this, the Papovkas would not be fully decommissioned until 1903, a full 30 years after they were launched. Widely considered by many to be the worst battleship ever built, the USS Massachusetts was a class leader of early battleships built for the US Navy. But in an experience would creep into the ship's design and result in its failure. Commissioned in 1896, the Massachusetts was designed with sheer power in mind. At the time, she and her sisters, the Indiana and the Oregon, were the first true modern battleships in the American fleet. And as a result, they came with massive amounts of firepower. All three ships were fully decked out with four 8in secondary batteries amid ships and then two massive 13-in guns forward and aft. These were some of the largest guns ever built at the time, and it was believed that the Massachusetts could potentially be extremely powerful as a coastal defense vessel. Ultimately though, the designers failed to take the weight of all this machinery into consideration, and this would result in dire consequences for the ship. At 350 ft long and displacing around 10,000 long tons, the USS Massachusetts was a comparatively small ship that was simply over encumbered by the weight of the guns and the ammunition that was fitted to her. As a result, when both of her 13-in guns on either side were turned to aim at an enemy vessel or target, the movement would cause the whole ship to list so severely that the entire deck and even the guns on that side of the ship would be plunged temporarily underwater. It's interesting to note that at the time, the US Navy was still a developing power, and it was learning new lessons all the time. The Bureau of Ordinance oversaw the design of the ships, but needed to take input from the builders on what would or might not work. Coupled with a great sense of inexperience was the usual medalsome political machine. This was the first time a Navy had attempted to fit such a huge amount of firepower into such a small platform. And although the ships were experimental and were like prototypes, because of this, it would ultimately lead to their failure as a design. They were small and they were cramped. Massachusetts and her sister ships only had nine line officers, which meant that they didn't have a dedicated officer for torpedoes, secondary battery, and main battery armorament. Even worse, for a combat vessel, they had no margin for officers killed or wounded in action. The failures of the Massachusetts class become quite obvious when you take into account the colossal weight that they were carrying. The four 13-in gun turrets alone weighed 136,000 lb or 68 tons each. And the shells used for these turrets each weighed a massive 1,130 lb or 512 kg. Now, that's not to say anything of the million pounds of coal required for the engines and the hundreds of thousands of pounds of ammo for the remaining guns on board. In her sea and gunnery trials, the unstable ship rolled heavily, unseating both of her main gun turrets, which jumped their retaining rings. They had to be set back, and builds were hurriedly installed on either side of the ship to make her more stable. On top of all of this, the Massachusetts was also woefully underarmed. While she was built with armored sides that measured about 5 in thick at the water line, the armor was positioned too low. This rendered its protection almost null. By contrast, the hull below the water line was left totally unarmored. This oversight led to the Massachusetts nearly being sunk on three separate occasions during her career after hitting submerged objects. Massachusetts was twice decommissioned and then recommissioned due to her flawed design. First in 1906 after an explosion of one of her turrets tragically killed nine aboard and again just a few short years later in 1914 after spending most of her time laid up in the reserve fleet. But finally in 1920 she was decommissioned for the final time scuttled and used maybe fittingly as target practice off the Pensacola coast of Florida. The story does have a somewhat wholesome ending though. In 1993, the wreck of the USS Massachusetts was officially named a Florida underwater archaeological preserve. Even though she spent much of the last century underwater, the wreck is actually remarkably intact and teameming with fascinating wildlife. In fact, she's now become a well doumented artificial reef. and well lit by the sun and resting in relatively shallow sandy waters, the Massachusetts is conveniently positioned as a popular diving destination, giving divers the rare opportunity to get up close and personal with all manner of aquatic creatures, as well as one of history's greatest battleship blunders. Now, there are some warships whose design flaws are largely mathematical or logistical miscalculations and many small factors that all come together to create a costly and embarrassing mishap for the country. They're mainly found under the hood and wouldn't be apparent to your average onlooker. But then we have the OSH, where the failings in her construction are pretty much obvious at first sight. She started out her life already at a disadvantage, having been ordered by the French in 1880, but not coming into service until a full 11 years later in 1891. The French shipyard which built her took so long to complete the project that by the time she was finished, the world had already moved on from ironclads like her. And as such, she was already basically obsolete upon launch. It doesn't take a warship historian to point out exactly what was wrong with the OSH. She was topheavy as all get out due to her very large superructure and her low freeboard. In fact, a superructure was so enormous even for the time that it earned her the nickname of the Grand Hotel. And this decision was made due to the fact that the French desperately wanted their warships to appear foreboating and menacing, hulking above the horizon in an aesthetic known as the fierce face. Her masts were positively massive and her guns were mounted on almost every available surface. But this however led to some seriously unstable ships which had difficulty at times keeping afloat under their own weight. The freeboard, on the other hand, was so low that the ship would struggle in anything but a flat calm and couldn't sail far from the coast without danger of being swamped. Now, this was all compounded by the fact that she was overweight on completion, which meant that the OSH was entirely too unstable to be considered seaorthy by most accounts. And on top of the superructure being altogether too tall, it was also fitted with numerous unnecessary windows, which were considered weak points in the armor scheme of the ship. Even further, the decision to extend the superructure above the turrets was also controversial because damage to this part of the superructure could also damage or then block the gun turrets, thereby reducing firepower. The ship was towering and awkward and not at all suitable for anything much further out from the coast, let alone an allout sea battle. All this being said, the French were not ignorant to the issues presented by the US, and she saw many refits over the course of her career to correct these issues. In 1895, six of her guns were removed to help lighten up some of the heft that she was carrying. And then later, a more extensive refit lasting from 1899 to 1902 saw that the engines and boilers were replaced. The single large stack was brought down to two smaller ones. And then two of her torpedo tubes were removed. But perhaps most importantly, a large portion of the overwhelmingly tall superructure was cut away to lower her center of mass. Her intended water line was restored so that her side armor was now able to effectively keep above the water. And after all was said and done, this behemoth was whittleled down by about 250 tons. And after this refit, she proved to be much more stable. It appears that the French had learned their lesson. Though the Osh would still go on to be remembered as one of the worst warships ever to be put to sea. A lot of design failures we cover on this channel come from the late 1800s, and for good reason. This was an awkward time in warship design when sail had just finally given way to steam. New technology was appearing untested all the time. One German class of gunboat was absolutely hated by its crews and the issues were typified by the class leader. The SMS Vesper was the result of some tactical thinking that dated way back to the age of sail where bombarding enemy forces on shore or at sea was a challenge thanks to the limited range of guns. So, the idea was to fit a powerful longrange gun on as small a platform as possible so that the boat could retreat to shallow waterways where it would be out of the range and impossible to be chased by larger, more powerful enemy ships. In the 1870s, Germany had to defend itself from amphibious invasion. The coastal defense gunboat was just what it needed. But aside from being born of maybe outdated tactical thinking, the Vesper was also conceived under some other unusual circumstances. For example, the naval chief of staff at the time was a former cavalry general, and the Admiral T design office had total inexperience in designing such a ship, and the German steel industry was incapable of producing the steel plating, which had to be eventually imported from Britain for the first four vessels. Vesper, to be fair, differed from other gunboats from the time. Usually, the guns were fixed in place and could rotate only by turning the whole ship. But Vesper improved on this because she was expected to engage the enemy in shallow water, maybe even with her bottom resting on the sea floor. So the gun would need to be trained and rotated on its own. 10 of the Vesper class were built, the first German warships to be built without sails. But it was about here that all the positive innovation ended. The boats were wide, slow, and extremely sluggish. They were hard to maneuver and turn. Despite their width, they had a tendency to heal in the water. This wasn't a huge problem, though, because they weren't expected to stay out in the open ocean, but it still resulted in drawing eye from their crews for their poor seaorthiness. They were heavy, too. The ship's boughs were reinforced with thickplated armor to protect the forward end from where it would be pointed at the enemy. They were also extremely cramped. The ships were meant to be as small a target as practically possible, and the engineers achieved this goal, but at the expense of the crew. It also meant they had very limited range because the boats just weren't big enough to fit a big coal bunker. The crews turned nasty. They called the boats mud bugs and tidal slippers. Some creative insults there. Just how effective these strange little ships were is characterized by the bizarre service history of Vesper herself. She was only commissioned a few times sporadically between 1876 and 1885. But in the end, technology overtook Vesper and her sisters when the first fast torpedo boat was introduced, consigning the German coastal gunboats to the history books. Vesper was sold and became a lighter in 1910. She was finally broken up. In the interwar period following 1918, the world's navies agreed to limit the size and capacity of their ships. This resulted in some pretty unusual designs and for one nation's navy in particular, some poor design choices that would lead to a scandal. During the course of World War I, the Allies comprising the UK, the US, France, Italy, and Japan had all built up impressive naval fleets. But immediately after the war, there was concern amongst the Allied powers of the potential for a naval arms race as this momentum continued. And that would prove costly for countries already reeling from the expenses of war. and unpopular with the public who were clamoring for peace time. In an attempt to appease the public and slow further progression towards this arms race, the Washington Naval Treaty was signed in 1922 among the major Allied powers. Now, as part of this treaty, limits were placed on the size and weight of future warship construction in an attempt to keep any one navy from outclassing the others. But where the other signatures saw an agreement to equalize their navies, Japan instead saw loopholes. In an attempt to circumvent the limitations imposed by the treaty, the Imperial Japanese Navy or the JN came up with the idea to build vessels that were too lightweight to be considered legitimate members of that category as per the treaty, but then outfit them as heavily as vessels twice their size. And by doing so, they were still bulking up their naval power using smaller scale versions of the vessels that they had been producing for the war without sacrificing on the firepower and therefore without technically violating any terms of the treaty. Enter the now infamous and illegal torpedo boat, the Tomzuru. Tomzuru weighed in at only about 600 tons, but was positively overloaded with complex and heavy gun systems. Her high center of gravity also led to serious stability issues in rough seas. Now, it's rather easy to imagine how such a design may cause structural problems, and we now know these issues would sadly prove fatal. In what would become known as the Tomzuru incident in March of 1934 during a routine nighttime torpedo exercise in rough weather, radio contact with the Tomsuru was suddenly lost. Initially, it was assumed to be the result of power loss or radio failure. that 15 minutes later, however, Tomatzuru's lights were completely dark. A search and rescue mission would find the Tomzuru capsized, floating completely upside down some 10 hours later. The ship was ultimately towed to shore, while 16 men somehow managed to survive. 100 sailors, including the captain, sadly perished in the disaster. The Tomzuru incident was ultimately attributed to the myriad design flaws present on the ship. The structure was horrifically topheavy, fitted with far too many heavy guns and munitions for the ship's comparatively small size. Munitions were also fully loaded at the time of her capsizing, which had not been the case during her sea trials. And this also contributed to an even greater instability than originally feared. And with all of these factors taken together, combined with the unfavorable weather conditions, the Tomzuru had been completely unable to keep herself upright. As a result of the incident, a committee was established by the IGN to identify weaknesses across their entire fleet. Many vessels like Tomzuru had been designed with the exploit of loophole in mind and they were summarily declared to be unseaworthy. A total of 14 vessels were found to have potentially catastrophic stability issues. These issues were summarily addressed and corrected. However, this incident would ultimately prove to be a scandal for the Japanese Navy, delaying the construction of new vessels for several crucial years. While they sought to correct the errors in their present-day fleet, guns were downsized and reduced in number, deck heights were lowered, and excess equipment was removed, whilst bulges and ballasts were added to the hulls of the ships for stability. Now, whilst the Japanese undoubtedly believed their design concept was clever and that it would allow the freedom to build up their naval force while also circumventing the limitations created by the Washington Naval Treaty.
