She too was back in action before the end of the year and the ship would go on to see much heavy fighting for the rest of the war. As far as battleship Row went, however, that was it for what could be considered easy wins. The remaining battleships were far too heavily damaged and they would need extensive work to refloat. Arizona, Oklahoma, and Utah were so far gone that it was clear they could never serve again. There were two contenders for salvage, though. USS California sunk at her moorings, and then the other, USS Nevada, bombed out from above and beed in the sand. Clearly, Nevada would need a lot of work. In fact, many argued that she couldn't be saved at all. If an attempt at salvaging Nevada was to be made, it would clearly be a huge undertaking. Instead, for the time being, the salvage division's attention turned away from the battleships and onto the smaller craft which littered Pearl Harbor's facilities. If they could get some of these in action, then maybe, just maybe, they could pull off the impossible and reflat the massive battleships. USS Vestal was a prime target for repair because she herself was a repair ship after all and could be of some serious ongoing use to the operations. Vestal had been alongside Arizona when the battleship detonated. In fact, firefighting parties on Vestal's decks were blown clear by the sheer force of the blast. Aside from that, conventional 250 kg bombs had rained down on Vestal and pierced her heart. One detonated in a metal store room with no serious effect, but the second passed straight through and out the bottom, causing flooding. With the ship settling by the stern and Arizona a flaming wreck, it became clear that Vestal needed to get away from the carnage. A skipper, Cassin Young, had been blasted off the ship when Arizona went up, but he swam back to take control of the situation, famously declaring, "Lads, we're getting this ship underway." When he stepped on board, they cut the ship's lines with axes as the burning fuel oil began to creep closer and closer. With engines turning slow ahead, Vestal limped free as her superructure began to burn, and her flatting grew worse. First, she had anchored, but in the end, Young decided it was safer to beach his ship. She gently came to rest off Aya Bay. It had been a heroic effort on a day of heroic deeds. And Kassen Young was actually awarded the Medal of Honor for his efforts to save his ship and her crew. And Vestal, despite being tied alongside the most horrendously damaged ship of the attack, was never sunk. Instead, her crew had first got to work helping on other damaged ships of battleship Row, freeing trapped men in Oklahoma and others. Then finally, it was their own ship's turn. She was in a unique position. Her own men were skilled repairers of ships. They swarmed about her like busy bees, cutting away ruined steel or welding new plates. In less than a week, all the holes had been patched, compartments were pumped dry, and damaged bulkheads were welded watertight once more. The work of Vestal's crew meant the Navyyard teams could focus on the other ships. But then, eventually, Vestal would need proper repairs below the waterline. She was no giant, so she could easily fit in the harbor's dry docks. She went in for permanent repair and was all fixed up and finished by February 18th, 1942. She went on to provide invaluable assistance to damaged US warships throughout the entire Pacific campaign. And not just damage from the enemy either, but freak Pacific typhoons that tore steel like it was paper. Then there was the USS Raleigh, a cruiser, one of the old-fashioned Omaha class. She was birthed near Utah in a mooring point usually used by the aircraft carriers. And so it was that she, an outdated design, and Utah, a training ship, came under furious attack from Japanese planes that had expected the carrier fleet. Utah had been devastated and rolled over. But Riley's crews were able to overcome the odds and save their ship. The old cruiser was rocked with blasts, first from two torpedoes, which caused flooding and a list, and then from a direct bomb hit, which again passed clean through and exploded below her keel. As Riley began to lift, her men began to free loose weight on the high side to prevent a full capsize while others manned the AA guns to keep the enemy planes at bay, destroying no less than five. Attempts at counter flooding the ship essentially caused her list to ease, and a barge was brought alongside to stop her from rolling or sinking completely. Fortunately, tanks containing thousands of tons of aviation fuel weren't breached, and no major fire broke out. With no deaths among her crew, Riley had escaped serious harm. And her crew had done a mighty job of keeping their ship afloat, earning them accommodation. Like other lightly damaged ships, the majority of the repair work could be completed by the ship's own crew along with the repair ships and tenders. Riley was patched up, entered the Navyyard dry dock on December 22, and was back in San Francisco for full overhaul in February. The old girl lived to fight another day, and fight she did, bombarding shore positions and enemy merchant ships throughout the Pacific. Work continued on with the lesser damaged ships. The sea plane tender Curtis, which had engaged Japanese submarine during the attack and then kind of brought down an enemy aircraft after it collided with her tall crane. Bomb damage meant her repairs were only finalized in May 1942. Then there was USS Helm, a destroyer. The warship had actually made steam to patrol for submarines out of the harbor when she was attacked by dive bombers. The bombs were so destructive even a near miss could be dangerous. Helm suffered damage from a bomb blast alongside that ruptured plating and caused [music] flooding. The repairs were fairly simple and straightforward and the little warship was back in action in no time. So far, the enormous workload undertaken by the men of the Pacific Bridge Company, the Navy itself, and the Navyyard was bearing fruit. But there was an obvious reminder of the real difficulties ahead. Applying simple repairs to bomb holes and ruptured [music] plating on destroyers was one thing, but sitting at the entrance to Pearl was the burnt out, bomb- riddled hulk of USS Nevada. Every single ship that came and went had to steam straight past her. The same was true of California, Oklahoma, and Arizona. These massive ships were a source of pride for the men of the Pacific Fleet. But the sight of them, sunken and broken, had instead become a source of distress to the entire base. The destroyers Shaw, Cassin, and Downs, and the small vessel Oglala were all officially regarded as lost, too, because the damage was so severe. The same was true of the battleships California and West Virginia. They were so badly damaged that originally it was thought they could never fight again. They didn't know it at the time, but the salvage division, recently renamed the Pearl Harbor Repair and Salvage Unit, was about to perform a series of miracles, and these ships were going to return from the dead. USS Shaw was one of those vessels, thought initially to be so badly damaged as to be a complete loss. She'd been at a floating dry dock when she took three direct bomb hits. The resulting fires spread out of control, and she had to be abandoned. At 9:30 a.m., Shaw's forward ammunition magazines detonated in a brilliant flash. Everything forward of the number one funnel was effectively wiped out. The floating dry dock flooded and sank and Shaw's bow sank with it. But remarkably, her stern section remained afloat. It gave the salvage unit an idea. The bow section was cut off entirely and the rest of the ship, virtually undamaged, was towed and morowed at the nearby docks. Here, the Navyyard men got to work on a strange project. USS Shaw got a new temporary fake bow. It would mean that the ship could steam under her own power out of Pearl and over to the west coast of the USA for permanent repairs. It didn't matter that her bridge had just been wiped out. The ship could be steered from her emergency after steering compartments just above the rudder and a simple platform was constructed at top her tripod mast where officers could coordinate her maneuvering. By the end of January, the new bow had been fitted. Everything was rigged up and the USS Shaw was ready for her remarkable voyage. As she left the harbor, there was cheering from the crews as they watched this first seriously damaged ship set to sea once more. It was a minor miracle because Shaw seemed to have returned from the grave. By the summer, Shaw was fully rebuilt and ready for action once more. In August, not even a year since the attack, [music] Shaw returned to Pearl Harbor once again, looking a brand new ship, and she was very warmly received indeed. The sight of USS Shaw gave the salvage crews renewed hopes and vigor, but it couldn't be denied that the task ahead was still enormous. They were incredibly skilled workers. Divers, riveters, carpenters, but there were some jobs that were impossible to pull off. The SS Kassin and DS had been in dry dock together, and repeated bomb hits and fires had caused magazine detonations similar to Shaw. But for these two destroyers, the result was far more destructive. Kassen's hull and [music] keel were warped beyond repair. The whole ship hogged upwards in the middle by as much as 17 in or 43 cm. Downs was similarly twisted and buckled with her bow twisted high and her stern twisted low. Repairs got underway with holes being patched or plugged, pumps taking oil and water out, and cutters removing bent and buckled superructure funnels [music] and deckouses. At first, it looked like Kassan and DS might live to fight again like Shaw had. But there was intense discussion around the viability of this. There could be no doubt that even with corrective action, the two destroyers would only ever really be suited to low impact escort work or simple patrols. But ship's hulls back then were actually relatively simple and cheap to make. It was the engineering machinery that was complex and expensive, and inspections proved that Cassin and Down's engines were in fine condition. The decision was made to scrap the two ships, but preserve their machinery so that the engines could be fitted to new destroyers instead. Over a thousand tons of machinery, pumps, turbines, fans, and many more were removed, restored, and carefully cataloged piece by piece. Most of the original hulls were scrapped through 1942, and by early 1944, the new ships were ready, appropriately named Cassin [music] and Downs. In fact, both vessels undamaged 37 ton stone sections, which still bore their original name plates, had been ceremoniously kept and grafted onto the new holes. They both went on to fight against the enemy that had sent them to the bottom of the dry dock that December 1941 with many battle stars and medals won between them. With Cassin and DS being tended to, the Pearl Harbor repair and salvage unit was now also faced with their most challenging jobs yet. The six battleships that were still sunk or beached around the harbor. These would not be ordinary repair jobs. The ships were monumental in their scale. West Virginia was herself about 22 times larger in displacement than Cassin or Downs. The first contender for salvage work became Nevada. She was beed off hospital point at the entrance to the harbor. And while her damage was severe, she wasn't a shattered Hulk like Arizona, nor was she overturned like Oklahoma or Utah. Nevada had fought like a lion. Early on, she'd been hit by a torpedo, but steamed out under her own power. Japanese pilots attacked her furiously and scored five bomb hits almost all at the same time. Fire ravaged her super structure and then Nevada came gently to rest, intentionally beached to prevent a full sinking. Her bow was in deeper water while her stern touched the shore. Her usual draft was around 28 ft, but now the water rose nearly two stories higher. The damage was incredible. Photographs show her folks deck buckled and bent from bomb hits and fire damage. It seemed incredible that a ship so badly ruined could ever be refloated or put into service again. Even despite the impressive work done to Shore, Cassin and Downs, Captain Homer Wallen, the salvage officer, remained hopeful about Nevada. He thought her older style of reciprocating seam engines would be more easily salvaged than other ships turbine electric machinery. But others weren't so sure. Admiral Chester Nimttz himself, commander of the Pacific Fleet, thought Nevada would never sail again. He had toured the harbor but found the destruction overwhelming despite having read all the reports and briefings beforehand. This is terrible seeing all these ships down. He had simply said it's easy to see why Nimttz thought Nevada was a total loss. It was up to the salvage unit to prove him wrong. Immediately after the attack, Nevada's flooding began to make her settle deeper into the water until her stern came to rest on the bottom with a slight list of starboard. This was actually optimal for the salvage crews who used anchors and lines to hold her in that position until the ship could be patched and refloated. By securing the ship in place, it meant there was no risk of her being carried off by a high tide only to sink in deeper water and block the channel. In early 1942, crews got to work on their biggest job yet. First, the ship would need to be patched. Bomb damage forward in the hull was covered with simple wooden patches that could be driven hard up against the plating with bolts. As the compartment inside was pumped dry, the water pressure itself would then act to hold the patch in place. Other areas of damage along the hull needed more specialist attention. Skilled divers, some of the best in the world, got to work down below in their hard hat diving suits, welding over holes and fixing ruptured plate seams. They came largely from the Pacific Bridge Company, support vessels, the Destroyer Rapid Repair Unit, and even Nevada herself. It was stressful, dangerous work. the ship could shift slightly and send an unprepared diver over the side where water pressure could crush his entire body up into his helmet. That had actually happened to a diver on the Empress of Ireland back in 1914 who fell only 65 ft or 20 m deeper. This incredible danger was faced every day through the course of no less than 400 successful dives and 1,500 hours spent underwater cutting, drilling, excavating, and dynamiting. No diver was injured or lost in the fight to get Nevada seaorthy. Soon it became clear that a huge torpedo hole needed a patch big enough to cover an area of about 48x 25 ft, some 15x 8 m. Now this was in particular quite complex because it was a part of the ship's hull where a torpedo bulge was installed and matching the curvature of the BGE would be tricky. Fortunately though, the overturned hull of Oklahoma provided the perfect template making opportunity because the ship was the near identical sister to Nevada. The patch was made to fit Oklahoma and by nature would therefore fit her sister, but this proved too large even for the skilled salvage crews to handle. Attempts at fitting the patch proved futile, and even after a month of hard work, divers at last gave up. Totally unbeknownst to them, a projection from the hull, blown out by the explosion, was preventing the patch from seating properly and creating the seal it needed to fit. In the end, it was decided that the large hole could simply remain because the internal bulkheads would be reinforced from the inside and then relied on to prevent any widescale flooding as the ship was slowly refated. With patches in place, the moment of truth had arrived. Would Nevada float again? All remaining oil had been pumped out of her tanks, and the ship's weight lessened by removing guns, munitions, heavy equipment, and anything that might keep her fixed to the harbor's silt. With a mechanical roar, the pumps burst to life, and slowly Nevada began to be pumped dry, bit by bit, compartment by compartment. This was not an easy job. If certain compartments were drained faster than others, the ship could capsize completely. Hoses were rigged to suction pumps of all sizes in a complex arrangement. And slowly, Nevada began to rise again, a steady fountain of water bubbling out from the pumps over the side of the ship. As the compartments were pumped dry for the first time in nearly 3 months, teams were sent in to clear them of any contaminants or remnants of fuel, ammunition, or even organic materials like food and paper. It was a hellish scene. The mixture had become like a thick stew which coated every bulkhead and deck head. In particular, there was found an enormous store of what had once been fresh meat, but by that point was entirely rancid. In other compartments still lay the bodies of their fallen comrades, badly decomposed and requiring identification. They were sent off to the Navy hospital. This wasn't just unpleasant work. It also proved deadly. On February 7th, Lieutenant James Clarkson was in a confined space in the steering engine room when he was overcome by gases. A machinistm mate who rushed to his assistance was overcome too and later died in hospital. Analysis showed that the gas was likely hydrogen sulfide, completely odilus and the result of the decaying organic material in water like the paper or the meat. The salvage unit learned their lessons the hard way. A lot of this kind of work was completely uncharted territory. The loss of these two men was a blow, but it couldn't detract from the eagerness of those who had toiled and suffered so much already to get the job finished. From then on, water samples were rigorously tested for dangerous levels of gases, and they would be detected. Salvage men were clad in thick rubber boots and overalls with breathing apparatus like gas masks as they worked inside the refloated ship, hosing away all the oil and grime. To help the men, ventilation was provided with portable fan units, and rudimentary lighting was also rigged up as well, since the ship's own fittings were, of course, non-functional. That's not to say they are all finished for good, though. The ship's wiring was actually found to be in fine condition. It just needed to be dried out. Machinery was taken out for repair and salvage. This was likely thanks to a wonder substance called tectil, the kind of rustreventative. It dried out the components and applied a protective layer of film which would prevent any more corrosion. From then on, tectil became the main weapon for the salvage unit on all the remaining ships like Nevada. In fact, they were so successful at this kind of work that about 95% of Nevada's original electrical machinery was totally repurposed and saved. On February 12th, 1942, the men of the salvage unit beamed with immense pride. They had done it. Nevada was again afloat. A triumphant sight for all of those who'd worked so hard on her the previous weeks. Even Chester Nimttz must have been shocked by the site as the ship prepared to be taken undertoe for dry docking. This itself was no easy feat. If the ship broke her lines, she would not be able to correct her course. And after all that hard work, she could end up sinking or blocking the channel. Everybody held their breath as the small boats wrestled Nevada under their control and they brought the ragged battleship successfully to dry dock number two, only recently completed and the only dock large enough for a ship in Nevada's size. Watching proudly over the whole operation was Nimitz, who had thought the ship to be a complete write-off. He was happy to be proven wrong. Incredibly, the work to restore Nevada was successful. The hulking wreck was transformed by an army of men from the naval yard into something resembling a functioning warship once again. But of course, her first voyage would need to be back to the US mainland for proper permanent repair. The Navyyard workers did their best to get the ship's galley in working order, her machinery and her electrical fittings functional, and the bomb holes patched. Once in dry dock, the magnitude of the damage done to the battleship was clearly evident. No wonder the divers couldn't fit that patch on. On April 22, not even 5 months after the attack, Nevada steamed out in a convoy under her own power for Puget Sound Navyyard. The ship Nimmits and others thought was done for emerged from that yard in October, completely rebuilt. A formidable modernized battleship with a crew keen on vengeance. After a stint in the European theater, including supporting fire at D-Day, Nevada rejoined the Pacific theater for the invasion of Ioima, where a massive guns hurled shell after shell at the enemy. Nevada anchored just 500 m, only 600 yd offshore for maximum destructive effect. It was a triumphant moment for a warship that had been considered doomed for the scrapyard and which had been the place where 52 men had fallen. Now, as Nevada's guns roared with flame and fury, their sacrifice could at last be avenged. The USS California had been morowed in birth F3 at the very front of battleship row, some distance away from her fleet mates when the first Japanese planes buzzed in to begin their torpedo attacks that fateful December morning. While this distance afforded the battleship protection should one of her comrades suffer a similarly catastrophic magazine detonation as the Arizona had, the birth far away meant that she was almost immediately singled out for destruction by the Japanese flyers. In the opening moments of the attack, at around 8:05 a.m., two torpedoes slammed into the port side of California below her imperous armor belt. The first striking forward near a bridge, while the second exploded further back, almost directly under turret number three. Both of these impacts ripped massive holes in the ship's hull and opened her up to the sea. But the flooding should have been stopped by a watertight subdivisioning. Bad luck stepped in to ensure that California sank. Most of California's extensive underwater protections and watertight compartments were rendered useless because the battleship had been left in what the Navy called condition X-ray. Instituted in the leadup to an inspection, condition X-ray stipulated that watertight compartments and manholes were to be left open to allow for easier navigation of the battleship's interior by senior officers and crew. But on the morning of December 7th, the men of California had little chance to transition their ship to a more secure condition. And so the battleship's critical internal defenses could not save her as she came under blistering air attack. Though California's crew had not been able to seal the battleship's watertight compartments, they had immediately rushed their battle stations, breaking out ammunition and heroically opening fire with 50 caliber machine guns and the ship's complement of 5-in anti-aircraft guns. The men fought back valiantly against their attackers, hurling as much ordinance into the air as possible in a desperate attempt to save their ship. But for all their effort, the brave crewmen quickly found themselves running out of ammunition. The impacts from the torpedoes and the resulting flooding had knocked out California's power. The vast quantities of water rushing into her hull had contaminated the battleship's vast network of fuel lines that supplied her generators. As a result, the hoists that supplied the topside 5-in guns were soon out of action, leaving the topside gunners with almost nothing left to shoot at the seemingly endless formations of incoming Japanese bombers. It must have been intolerably frustrating because the crew had the guts and the guns to fight back, but they just didn't have the ammo. With the ship now listing dangerously deport, California's officers quickly issued orders to counter flood in order to bring her back on something of an even keel. This quick thinking prevented California from capsizing completely in the immediate aftermath of the torpedo attack. But as fresh formations of bombers moved in, the ship and her men were not out of the woods. Roughly 25 minutes after the torpedo strike, California shuddered under the impact of several near misses from the bombers. These substantial explosions in the water right next to her buckled and bent the hull, causing even more uncontrollable flooding through the open compartments. But just after 8:45 a.m., one of the Japanese bombs finally found its mark. The bomb, weighing over,700 lb or just over 770 kg and modified from a 16-in naval shell, punched straight through California's deck of midship and exploded deep inside, killing 50 of her crew instantly and setting off one of her anti-aircraft ammunition magazines. The resulting fire spread rapidly and the blaze was totally uncontrollable since the loss of power had rendered the battleship's vast array of firefighting equipment inoperative and totally useless. California was out of the fight during the desperate combat. Scenes of incredible heroism had played out. Three medals of honor would be awarded to California's crewman in the aftermath of the attack and tragically two would be awardedly. Robert R. Scott, a machinist's mate in the forward air compressor room, refused to leave his battle station as a horrid amalgamation of churned up seawater and oil rapidly flooded the compartment that supplied vital compressed air to the 5-in mounts. His comrades begged him to leave, but Scott refused, doggedly saying, "This is my station, and I'll stay and give them air as long as the guns are going." before the rising water eventually consumed him. Further back, Enson Herbert C. Jones demonstrated remarkable courage, rescuing his fellow sailors from the noxious smoke filling California's corridors before taking over and directing fire from one of the ship's 5-in anti-aircraft guns. As the flooding from the torpedo hits knocked out the power to the ammunition hoists, Jones rangle together a group of men to manually haul the 55lb 25 kg shells out of the magazines themselves and up to the guns. The hit from the 1,700-lb armor-piercing bomb left him mortally wounded. And with fires spreading, Enson Jones used his last breath to warn his comrades to keep away moments before the 5-in ammunition magazine went up in a fireball. The only Medal of Honor recipient from California to survive the attack was Gunner Jackson C. Ferris. He'd been rushing to his position when one of the torpedoes impacted directly underneath, launching him right into the compartment's overhead ceiling. But despite being dazed and in severe pain, Ferris worked desperately to pass ammunition to his gun, setting up another human chain to pass the ordinance up from the magazine. And when the order to counter flood came through, it was Ferris who rallied his fellow sailors and directed them to make sure the orders were carried out. Two times he was rendered unconscious by the choking fumes and the smoke, but each time he resumed his efforts to keep up the supply of ammo that was desperately needed topside, while he also brave the rapidly flooding compartments to save his shipmates. In those sort of conditions, inside claustrophobic steel compartments and rooms, every fiber of your being is screaming at you to get out and save yourself. But Ferris and his comrades were able to keep their mind on the job and get it done, saving hundreds of lives in the process. Despite these men's gallant efforts, California was in dire straits with fires spreading rapidly and a perforated hull flooding uncontrollably. Her men did what they could. But as if to make matters worse, from back along battleship Row, a blazing inferno of burning fuel oil was steadily creeping its way along the surface of the water. Thick clouds of noxious black smoke billowed into the air and choked the brave men still left on California's deck as the flaming oil poured out of the ruptured hulls of the other stricken battleships and threatened to engulf them. With fires now all around and their beloved ship sinking out from under them, the crew were forced to finally abandon California and make for the relative safety of Ford Island. The scene that greeted them must have been simply shocking. the sight of vast plumes of smoke filling the skies as they rose up from a sea of burning oil while their fellow sailors desperately fought for their lives amidst the carnage. It would be forever ingrained in their minds, but there was little time to dwell on it. Hurriedly, the men gathered whatever firefighting equipment they could in a determined effort to save their own battered ship. But by the time they returned, California was already listing 8° over, and the massive dreadnaugh gradually settled into the muddy harbor bottom and came to rest. Recovery of the California was going to be a big big job. The ship had suffered even more substantial damage than Nevada had. The two torpedo holes in her hull along with the buckling and rupturing from the near misses meant that she could not just be patched and refloated. California had also sunk in deeper water than Nevada. Nearly 40 ft or about 12 m. meant the water around California reached all the way up to her main deck and her charred and blackened superructure seemed to rise up from the water almost out of nowhere. The salvage teams were going to have to pull out all the stops in order to accomplish what to them must have seemed like a minor miracle. In the days and weeks after the attack, inspection had determined that the greatest threat to California's salvage was the water that was sitting over her hull and submerging her. In order to save the ship from the scrap heap, the men were going to have to hold Pearl Harbor itself at bay. And while that may have seemed like an impossible task, that's exactly what they set out to do. Lacking the time to raise her properly up, engineers devised a clever solution. Using 4-in thick wooden boards and sturdy angle iron, massive coffer dams were constructed around California's hull. anchored to a shear line, that is the curve along the top edge of the ship's hull, the dam in effect served as a vertical extension of the hull itself, like a wooden wall that jutted up and kept water off the deck. Two of these impressive structures were built, one for the stern section, while another possibly more important coffam enclosed her for peak at the bow, which had been blown open by one of the near misses. Though impressive, the coffams presented challenges of their own. The first problem was that the wood itself was inherently buoyant. Bolting large slabs of it to the side of a sunken battleship was not an easy task, especially when you consider that the divers tasked with installing them were encumbered by clumsy helmet diving suits covered in thick oil that still sheened on the surface of the harbor. Secondly, it was feared that as pumping efforts began to dewater the decks, the surrounding seawater would press inward now against the unsupported inside of the coff dams and collapse the entire structure from the outside, flooding California once again and leading to even further damage. To combat this, a series of heavyduty timber braces, similar to the kind used to shore up ships waiting to be launched on the slipway, were added to the interior walls of the dams that would hold back the immense pressure of the water from the outside. Once the coffer dams were in place, pumping began, the clearing of California's decks, having the combined effect of lightening the ship and revealing the damage done to her top side during the attack. With their decks finally free of water, divers could turn their attention to the crippled giants's ravaged hull. It was quickly discovered that the California couldn't simply have her watertight compartments sealed and the water pumped out as had been done with Nevada. The combined damage to her bow section below the water line from the torpedo and the near miss bomb was considerable with a near 40 foot or 12 m long and in places 10-ft tall gash being blasted out of the side of the ship. With the option to simply button her up and pump out the water not being viable and with the immense success of the coffidam solution, it was decided to carry over the principle of the topside structures into the new versions of the underwater patches that had failed to work with Nevada. like oversized bandages placed over massive wounds, these new patches were constructed from the same 4-in thick wood planks and angle iron that had been used topside. Each of the 16 ft sections of timbering had to be curved at the bottom perfectly to account for the shape of California's hull near a build section, while the tops extended well above the ship's waterline. Massive floating cranes were used to carry the patches over from Pearl Harbor's cold dock, where a team of skilled carpenters worked tirelessly. The structures were then lowered down against California's side and sunk using heavy lead weights to counteract the wood's natural buoyancy before finally being bolted to the crippled warship's hull. The act of bolting a wooden patch onto a battleship proved to be a monumental task in and of itself since divers were first tasked with cutting away twisted bits of metal ran apart by the force of the explosions before and then drilling holes into the ship's side into which they would mount the heavy duty bolts needed to support the patch's immense weight. But the divers's struggle did not end there. Once the bolts were inserted, they would have to traverse the flooded labyrinthine corridors of the battleship's interior to place a similar heavyduty nut on the other end of the bolt threads and screw it shut to properly hold the patch against the hull. It was a very daunting job. California's cramped and winding passages stretched pitch black, apart from what scant illumination the gallant men's lights could provide. The danger of this task is difficult to overstate. and so was the bravery of the men who carried it out. But for these men, the notion of simply leaving the ship sunk in the mud or breaking her up for scrap was just too much to bear. California and the other battleships stationed at Pearl Harbor on December 7th, which cherished vessels, their presence instilling a sense of deep pride in all the servicemen of the Pacific Fleet. To see them in such a state, burnt out, bent, broken, and sunk, filled each man with an indomitable will to do whatever it would take to bring them back. And they pressed onward. To ensure that the patches would adequately shore up California's hull before the refloating, gaps between the timber and the steel hull had to be made watertight. The nut andbolt arrangement wasn't good enough. Here again, another ingenious solution was implemented. To seal the patches, long thin canvas sacks filled with oakum, a hemp or juke fiber soaked in pitch were pressed into the gaps. Once packed full and soaked in water, the pliable material was referred to as pudding thanks to its malleability. Although some men joke that the puddings more closely resembled sausages. But regardless, after being wedged in between the hull and the timber, the weight of the water that had earlier threatened the viability of the cough dam solution in the first place now actually worked for the salvage team since it pressed the oakum sacks firmly enough into the gaps to form a very effective watertight seal. Admiral William Furlong, impressed with the creative solution, compared it to a mason jars rubber gasket. With the great patches finally bolted in place and the canvas and oak and pudding sealing the gaps, divers were once more called on to brace the interior face of each patch, similar to what had been done on the cough dams above. Like with those, it was feared that once the water was pumped out of California's hull, the weight of the water on the outside would cave in the wood, keeping her afloat and send the dreadnaugh crashing right back down to the bottom. And so once again, the brave men were called upon to traverse California's flooded interiors. Only this time dragging along cumbersome timbers and heavy steel bracing along with all the tools and equipment required to actually build the bracing to keep the patches intact. With the patches braced and the coffidams keeping the sea at bay, the colossal floating cranes were used to remove every major heavy bit of equipment that could be taken off to lighten the load. the battleship's huge main armament, thousands of rounds of ammunition, and even her towering basket masts. It was all taken off in an effort to lighten the lumbering monster as much as possible before attempting to refloat her. Finally, on the 21st of March, after 4 months of exhausting, grueling, dangerous work, the pumps were turned on and California began to rise from her muddy grave. But almost immediately, there were problems. See, California hadn't only sunk in deeper water than Nevada. She'd also gone down on an uneven patch of sea floor. This meant that as water was pumped out and the ship began to lighten, the irregular positioning caused her to develop at one point a terrifying 20° list. It took three agonizing days for California to come up from the bottom with pumping continuing all the way until April 5th. And that's when the unthinkable happened. At around 1:15 p.m., with California once again floating finally and waiting for a dry dock to open up, another explosion rocked the ship. With a thunderous boom, the massive bow patch over the near miss bomb damage blew out. Thousands of tons of sea water reflooded the spaces that the men had worked so hard to restore. The ship lurched under the added weight, and her bow dipped alarmingly back down into the water. Immediately, the men aboard sprung into action, rigging up two pumps and shutting as many doors and watertight hatches as they could. Their quick thinking saved California as the water ingress from the loss of the bow patch would have been enough to put her back on the bottom in minutes. But with the pumps running and the hatches and doors closed, California stayed afloat. And crucially, at a shallow enough draft to actually make it into the dry dock, a fact which saved the poor divers from having to perform another miracle. With the ship saved, everyone's thoughts immediately turned to what had just happened. Of course, sabotage was immediately suspected. Pearl Harbor and the Pacific Fleet battleships were still prime targets for the Japanese, and even before the war had started, it was feared that Hawaii's significant population of ethnic Japanese would side with their ancestral homeland in the event of war and would either spy or commit acts of sabotage. Now, with the significant explosion aboard California, it appeared those fears might have some merit. But after a thorough investigation, no evidence of sabotage or any kind of explosive compounds were discovered. What was found though was that large amounts of fuel oil vapor along with a high concentration of hydrogen sulfide to gas generated from all the decomposing food, paper, and other organic materials had created an extremely volatile mixture that had somehow found an ignition source and erupted into an explosion powerful enough to mangle deck beams and damage bulkheads. The salvage team got lucky as even with the patch blown out, California's forward compartments now flooded again, the battleship was just barely light enough to clear the entrance to the dry dock. At last, on April 9th, 1942, USS California was gently towed into dry dock number two. The two pumps still attached to her deck were gushing water as they strained to keep the indomitable giant's bow afloat. With the gates closed behind her and the water steadily pumping out, crews descended on the battleship to prepare her for the long voyage back to the United States. Like with Nevada, the interior of California was a scene of indescribable filth and ruin. During the initial salvage, over 200,000 gallons or some 757,000 L of fuel oil had been siphoned out of her. But despite this incredible volume having already been removed, the oil still clung to every surface from the third deck up. And below that, thick, gluey mud had cemented itself in and around the bomb and torpedo damage. Heaps of decomposing food, paper, clothing, [music] and bodies all had to be removed. The mess inside California was so bad, in fact, that after 4 months of grueling work performed by hundreds of men, only about half of the ship had been reclaimed from the filth. There were also all the human touches of life from before the tragedy as well. A band member, LB Lucenbach, had taken his sheet music aboard, but was forced to evacuate the stricken ship as the attack went on. Now, all these months later, Lucenbach, who was lucky to have survived, was able to go aboard and find it. Poignantly, one of the sheets was the score for the stars and stripes forever. As the muck was finally cleared away, scores of metal workers turned their attention to the battleship's ruptured hull. Twisted and bent steel plating was cut away to make way for new sections to be welded in place. Beams were removed, straightened, and then reinstalled. It was found that much of California's damaged hole plating could simply be heated, rolled back into shape, and then reattached. While this work was performed, the extensive topside damage was repaired as well, with the many holes in California's deck and superructure being patched over with new plating. But not all of this work that needed doing was going to be straightforward. Unlike Nevada, California used a turbo electric propulsion system. When Nevada used the steam generated in her 12 massive boilers to drive turbines geared to her propeller shafts, California relied on steamdriven turbines, generating electricity for an impressive set of four electric motors to push her immense bulk through the water. And being submerged in Pearl Harbor's briney water for several months hadn't done them any favors. But under the supervision and guidance of representatives from General Electric, two of the massive motors were removed and completely rewound. miles of copper wire had to be carefully spooled in order to provide the dreadnaugh with enough of its own power to limp its way across the Pacific back to Puet Sound Washington where the rest of her machinery could be overhauled. This massive effort in rebuilding California's beating heart was described by the men from General Electric as largest job of this sort ever performed in [music] the field. While all of this was going on, dockyard workers set to work stripping the battleship's interior down to almost nothing. Furniture and fittings were removed along with the ship's ventilation equipment, while every ounce of wiring was ripped out to make way for newer, more up-to-date systems and switchboards. Compartments, which had been stripped down to bare metal during cleaning operations, were now repainted and restored. And finally, on the 7th of June 1942, USS California left the dry docks at Pearl Harbor on her way to mainland USA to complete repairs and refit the Revenant battleship departing Pearl on October 10th after being reunited with her main 14-in battery. It must have been an emotional sight for the hundreds of men and women who had made it happen. There was California and a coat of fresh blue paint steaming out for the open ocean. A true moment of pride for the teams that had worked day and night to bring this mighty warship back from the dead. But few news rules chattered as California made her way out of Pearl Harbor. The departure had to be strictly secret lest Japanese submarines or aircraft intercept her on route and send her back to the bottom. Seeing once more under her own power, California arrived back in the US to undergo permanent repairs and receive a huge refit, an entire overhaul. When she emerged from dry dock in January 1944, the once aging dreadnaugh was now a lethal and modernized warship. Sporting a new dazzle paint scheme, California bristled with 40 brand new buffers anti-aircraft cannons and just as many 20 mm Erlicon guns as well. She was stripped of her outdated basket masts and also had her armor increased, turning her into a veritable floating fortress. Returning to the fleet in May that year, California would go on to deal out healthy servings of revenge, unleashing her fury on the Japanese forces at Saipan, Guam, and Tinian. But this would not be all, as on October 24th, 1944, USS California would have the distinct honor of joining her fellow Pearl Harbor Revenants Maryland, West Virginia, and Tennessee along with the New Mexico class battleship Mississippi at the Battle of Surawa Strait. This task force laid waste to their opponents, sinking the Japanese battleships Fuso, and Yamashiro along with the destroyers Mijashi, Asagumo, and Yamagumo. California's guns roared and sent over 60 big shells down range, crippling Yamashiro. Meanwhile, Mississippi Salvo would prove to be the last time one battleship would ever fire at another in anger. But California would not emerge from the war unscathed. On January 6th, 1945, while supporting the invasion of the Philippines, she was struck by a kamicazi. The resulting explosion killing 44 of her men and injuring another 155. The damage required her to return to the United States once more for repairs. But she still wasn't done. The old battleship returned just in time to participate in the end of the Okinawa campaign. She'd go on to support the American occupation of Japan in the wake of the Empire's surrender. The much revered battle wagon sailed into the home waters of the enemy that had once crippled her, now stronger and more deadly than ever. [music] Through late 1941 and into 1942, the ships had been slowly writed, pumped, repaired, and sailed off one by one. Each had suffered in the attack, but not equally, and the damage varied from ship to ship, much of it deadly. Each salvage played a crucial role in educating the division for their next job. And the Chard Hulk of the USS West Virginia would again present a unique challenge. She was the most severely damaged battleship to be saved. Morowed outboard of the Tennessee in birth F6, the USS West Virginia found herself in a deadly predicament similar to her fellow battleship Oklahoma because she was morowed directly in the firing line of the horde of Japanese Kate torpedo bombers that swooped in low to attack. During the rapid onslaught, West Virginia acted as a shield for the battleship Tennessee. She shuddered and shook from the near simultaneous impact of no fewer than seven Japanese torpedoes. The warheads ripped the mighty warship's side open as if it was made out of aluminum foil. A further hit would open up her bow section to the sea, while yet another one further aft would blow the massive dreadnaugh's rudder clean off and hurl it off the now sinking ship. But despite the horrific damage at the outset of the battle, the crew of the West Virginia still fought valiantly. Even as fires spread rapidly both aboard the ship and along the surface of the water around her, the ship itself began to list to a terrifying angle, her guns continued to hurl ordinance up at the enemy planes still circling above. To get a sense of just how sudden and rapid the attack came to West Virginia, we turn to the testimony of Commander RH Hillcott, West Virginia's executive officer and her most senior officer to survive the attack, who wrote in his report after the battle, "I was in my cabin just commencing to dress when at 0755 the word was passed, away fire and rescue party." This was followed about 30 seconds later by General Quarters. At the same time, 0755, the Marine orderly rushed into the cabin and announced, "The Japanese are attacking us." Also, just at this time, two heavy shocks on the hull of West Virginia were felt. It seemed as if these shocks were somewhere forward on the port side. By this time, I'd reached the quarter deck, and the ship was beginning to list rapidly to port. I proceeded along the starboard side until just forward of number three turret, when there was a third heavy shock fell to port. The planes on top of turret three caught on fire and there were flames all around the turret top. The quarter deck sentry informed me that the captain had already gone to the bridge. So I remained after to assist the extinguishing of the fire around turret 3 and on the quarter deck. There was another heavy explosion at this time that threw me flat to the deck. During all this time, the ship was continuing to list to port. And at the time of this latest shock, I should estimate that the list was about 20 or 25°. I called to the Sound Power Telephone Watch to tell Central to count a flood, but do not know whether or not this word got through. Luckily though, Hill Cott's words had gotten through to someone. Lieutenant Commander John S. Harper heard the orders and rushed to carry them out. His actions in starting the counter flooding undoubtedly saved the ship from capsizing in the same way Oklahoma had, which had too suffered a devastating barrage of torpedoes and went over like a dog might roll in his sleep. It was only the rising water in his compartment that forced the brave officer to finally abandon his post. In the melee, several bomb hits were also scored on West Virginia, which only added to the chaos breaking out all over the embattled vessel. One struck the fortop all the way at the top of the main mast, piercing through the thin unarmored section with ease before smashing down potentially as far as the second deck where it exploded and ripped apart sections of the ship's superructure. Another bomb struck West Virginia right on the top of her number three turret. The armor-piercing projectile sliced through the armored roof of the turret, but by some miracle it failed to detonate. Instead, the bomb broke up inside the turret and potentially saved the ship from a shattering magazine detonation. However, bomb and torpedo strikes were only the first of West Virginia's problems. The massive oil fire fed by the ruptured fuel tanks of her fleetmates that surrounded her soon engulfed the ravaged battleship. And while Nevada and California had been lucky enough to avoid the worst of those devastating fires, West Virginia found herself in the heart of the blaze. For 30 hours, the once mighty dreadnaugh burned, the heat from the fire reaching temperatures high enough to warp and buckle solid steel deck plating along an astonishing 3/4 of her entire length. Even some of her internal bulkheads deep within the hull were damaged from the incredible heat. The fires were made worse by the fact that West Virginia was almost fully fueled. Her cavernous tank sitting at about 70% capacity on the morning of the attack. It was rapidly becoming clear that the damage control crews, despite their heroic efforts in saving the ship so far, just couldn't suppress an inferno of that scale. And so the order was given reluctantly to abandon ship. Surviving crew and officers leapt into the oilcoated water. Some making their way to the neighboring Tennessee to aid their embattled comrades, while others swam for Fort Island to join other survivors there in helping the wounded and those fighting the fires from land in any way they could. >> [music] >> Salvaging the burnt out and blasted open giant would be no easy feat. Though by now, after the successful raising and recovery of the Nevada and California, the men of the salvage team were not going in blind. Initial dives on the hull revealed the extent of the underwater damage. And it became very quickly clear that a far greater patch than those used on the California would be needed in order to reflow West Virginia. And there would certainly be no getting lucky like they had done with Nevada, which had been refloated without its so-called big patch. Most of the battleship's port side was blasted open. So, it was decided that one massive nearly 150 ft long patch would be constructed in sections and installed along the battleship's midsection where the damage was the most severe, while a second smaller patch would be used to cover the damage from the forward torpedo strike. But for the hit towards her rudder at the stern, it was determined that this kind of damage could actually go unsealed. That simply closing the watertight doors and the bulkheads and isolating the damage would be sufficient to get her off the bottom. Using their experience gained from months of grueling work on the California, it was decided to again employ the highly successful Coffadam style of patch now on West Virginia. With a plan in place, the experienced work crews set about in earnest. Patches were constructed in smaller 13 1/2 ft sections which could then be lowered into the water with the assistance of heavy lead weights and placed next to those that had gone before. Though quickly divers ran into a problem since the damage to West Virginia's hull above her armored belt was so devastating, there just wasn't enough material left on which to bolt the massive coffam structures to begin with. And what was left could hardly be considered battleship hull anymore at all, thanks to the twisting and the mangling from all those violent explosions. To remedy this and give something to secure the patch sections to, the team employed a very simple but brilliant solution. Heavyduty 10-in wide H beams were bolted vertically to the warped but intact armored belt spaced every 8 ft. The beams could then be braced horizontally to provide a sufficiently strong frame to which the patches could then actually be mounted. But this wasn't the only challenge faced by West Virginia's salvage team. The size of the giant main patch meant that the same techniques used on the California to seal the gaps between the coffidan and the hull just wouldn't work on that ship. Smaller coffin dams had been employed to seal off individual torpedo hits which had been sealed with long canvas sacks filled with pitch soaked jute fiber called puddings. Once water logged and stuffed in between the hull and the patch, the simple devices acted like a kind of gasket that prevented water from flooding back into the vessel when she was pumped out dry. Almost Virginia though, since the damage was one giant hole caused by multiple warheads detonating in roughly the same area, it was decided instead to use concrete to seal up the bottom of the battleship's massive bandage. Using the Tre method, a technique in which concrete can be poured underwater using vertical pipes, over 650 tons of special underwater concrete mix was poured in with Tremy pipes installed every 10 ft. The special mix developed by the Pacific Bridge Company for constructing dry docks was poured to depths of around 4 ft along the bottom length of the entire patch. With the hull sealed, the men could then set about lightening the massive dreadnaugh in preparation for refloating. 800,000 gallons or over 3 million L of heavy fuel oil was pumped out of West Virginia's tanks while over 40,000 gallons or 150,000 L of loose oil was skimmed out from her interior and off of her decks. Ammunition, food stores, and fittings were also stripped, while two Japanese bombs that had failed to explode were also carefully removed and sent away for evaluation. The ship's food stores included thousands of pounds of beef and dairy products, the removal of which was a particularly horrendous task considering the battleship had been submerged in oily salt water and left to bake in the beating Hawaiian sun for months. But the men were at least somewhat aided by the fact that before work had even begun, divers had descended into the horrid filth to open all of West Virginia's remaining intact internal doors so that clean sea water could be circulated through the hull to remove some of the mess and clear out pockets of stagnant water and toxic gases. During the salvage efforts, 66 bodies belonging to West Virginia's fallen crew were discovered and removed for burial. Most of them were in a state of advanced decomposition. Their remains left unrecognizable to their comrades after months of intunement within the ship. Hauntingly, there was considerable evidence that at least some of the men had survived for weeks. Trapped inside the dark rooms of the sunken dreadnaugh, barely surviving within tiny air pockets deep within the pitch black flooded compartments, the men would have used whatever they could to pound desperate messages, begging for rescue. But tragically, none came. There was simply no way for anyone outside the stricken behemoth to hear them. And even if they had, rescue for those poor souls would likely have been impossible. Many were found clinging to the tops of steam pipes near the top of the engine room where the air pocket had once been. In total,6 of West Virginia's men tragically met their end during the attack. [music] >> [music] >> Finally, on the 12th of May, 1942, after months of yet more exhausting, dangerous work, West Virginia began to rise from her watery grave. Though almost immediately it was found that the water being pumped out of West Virginia was nearly equal to the amount flooding back in. Even though the massive coffidans were working as intended, the dreadnaugh's hull was in such a sorry state after that immense beating it had taken that a combination of loose rivets, small shrapnel holes, bursts, seams, and other random damage had turned West Virginia's hull into something more resembling Swiss cheese than a proud warship. So once more, the gallant divers were sent down with their tools to patch up the myriad of holes and rents in her side. And 5 days later, on the 17th of May, the water levels within the battleship finally began to fall. But as the water was pumped out, a serious concern began to arise that once the battleship was fully refated, there was a risk that she might suddenly capsize and be lost once more to the harbor bottom, but this time for good. With so much of her hull blasted apart, the ship's weight was terribly skewed to one side. As the water was pumped out of the massive void where her hull used to be, the growing air pocket meant that the battleship was far more buoyant on one side than the other. There was also the fear that with all of the water removed, the immense weight of the sea would cave in the massive coffer dam and everything would be lost. One patch had been blown out on California when a mix of fuel vapor and toxic gas had built up and ignited. But luckily on that ship, crews were able to seal off the damaged section and keep the battle wagon afloat. If a similar incident happened to West Virginia and her giant patch suddenly failed, no amount of heroic effort would save her from crashing right back down to the bottom. Anxiety began to mount because when West Virginia was refloated, there was just no dry dock space available for her, meaning the huge warship was forced to sit idly by and wait, while the immense pressure of the water pressed in on her fragile patches. Even though the coffidam was braced from the inside, just like had been done on California, the length of time the structures were subjected to the crushing force of the sea caused serious concern. The issue was that California was still occupying Dry Do 2 and she couldn't be moved until her repairs were completed. West Virginia simply had nowhere to go. In an attempt to mitigate the risk, several spare patch sections were held in reserve aboard one of Pearl Harbor's massive floating cranes, while teams of men were stationed aboard the battleship to operate the sea valves for counter flooding should the hull become breached. At least then, it was hoped that West Virginia would settle on something of an even keel and the team could just try to reflat her again instead of rolling over like Oklahoma. It wouldn't be until June 1942, nearly a month after the pumps were switched on, that West Virginia could finally be towed into the safety of the dry dog. Thankfully, the reserve patches weren't needed because her sturdy coffer dams and bracing successfully held back the sea and allowed the massive Dreadnaugh to stay afloat. Now finally sealed in Pearl Harbor's cavernous dry dock, the horrid ritual of cleaning the battleship's interior of all that toxic buildup of rotten organic material and thick oil could begin once again. Even with a great volume of the sludge already removed, huge amounts still clung to every surface, and it all needed to be cleared away. And while those with that unenviable task set about their work, and crews of skilled yardsmen tended to the ruined hull, the job of breathing some life back into the old dreadnaugh began in earnest. Like California, West Virginia was a turbo electric ship. Her power plant consisting of four mighty electric motors supplied with electricity from huge turbines fed by steam from a series of eight massive Babcock and Wilcox oil fired boilers. These motors contained miles of intricately wound copper wire. that after being submerged for months in Pearl Harbor's briney waters, these impressive machines would need to be completely stripped down and have every inch of their wire carefully and precisely rewound. But thankfully, owing to the fact that such a massive volume of loose oil and debris had been removed from West Virginia's interior during the salvage work, work crews had been able to descend into the depths of the stricken giant to remove loads of sensitive machinery and equipment from the harsh salt water far earlier on than on California. In fact, before the battleship even entered dry dock, the preliminary steps of removing her massive generators and main propulsion motors had already taken place, as had a thorough cleaning of the engine room. This coupled with a generous coating of the rustreventative product tectil meant West Virginia's vital machinery was able to be recovered in far superior condition when she entered dry dock than California's had been. While this work was being undertaken, the herculant task of rebuilding the dreadnaugh's shattered hull could also begin. But as the water was gradually pumped out of the dry dock, the true enormity of the job that lay ahead became apparent. With the massive sections of coffidane removed, a gaping twisted moore of rent and broken steel greeted the teams of yardsmen and metal workers. Nearly the entire port side of West Virginia had been blown apart by all those hits from Japanese torpedoes. Even her hefty 13 1/2 in or 34 cm thick armored belt was bent and cracked in several spots. Parts of the ship that hadn't taken bomb or torpedo damage had still been affected by the raging fires that burnt unchecked for 30 hours, even after the last Japanese planes had departed. That immense heat had buckled and warped her still both inside and out. And with the vast extent of the damage, massive sections of her hull and armor would have to be cut away and either straightened out or outright replaced. In all, it took hundreds of skilled workers 3 months to restore West Virginia's hull and make the giant warship watertight and seaorthy once again. With dry dock work completed, West Virginia was removed and left PSI, while further work to the battleship's interior spaces was carried out. Wiring was stripped and renewed, walls and ceilings repainted, and furniture and fittings were all replaced. It wouldn't be until May 1943 that this work was finished and finally the mighty battleship could set out for Pearl under her own power once again and make for the Puet Sound Navy Yard in Breton, Washington. Here, like Nevada and California, West Virginia would undergo final repairs and receive an extensive overhaul and modernization. She would emerge from the yard in July 1944, a completely new ship, far deadlier and even more effective than before. From there, West Virginia rejoined her comrades in the Pacific theater, exacting revenge at Muro, Lingian, Iwoima, and Okinawa, and also taking part in the battle of Surugawa Strait. And after Japan's surrender, she was called upon to help to support the massive occupation efforts. But during her combat career in the Pacific, the Japanese would have one last crack at the old girl when a kamicazi struck her during operations off Okinawa. Fortunately, the damage was relatively minor, and she was able to remain on station and continue her duties. West Virginia would finish the war participating in Operation Magic Carpet, the mighty dreadnaugh now acting as a ferry for thousands of American veterans returning home to their families and loved ones after a bitter, long, and hard forward war. By 1947, the aging warship was finally brought out of active duty and decommissioned after 24 years of exemplary service. And in 1959, the mighty West Virginia would finally meet her fate in the scrapyard. The oxy torches of the yard workers, completing that final destruction the Japanese armed forces had never achieved. So far, all the battleships had been returned to service. What remained was essentially a graveyard of overturned and shattered warships. At battleship row, the upturned hull of the Oklahoma sat conspicuously in view as the men toiled away on the other ships. The side of her propellers sticking helplessly out of the water, while her superructure lay smashed against the harbor bottom was a stark and painful reminder of what had happened on the day of infamy. Hers would be the largest and the most difficult salvage of them all. The effort would require the skills and expertise of some of America's best and brightest engineers. On the morning of the attack, Oklahoma had gone to battle stations just like the others around her. her men racing topside, breaking out 5-in shells and belts of 50 caliber ammunition. She had fought back valiantly at first, but she was a stride of Maryland on the outer mooring, and her long, thick hull presented a perfect target for Japanese Nakajima B5NK torpedo bombers. Almost immediately, a heavy barrage of torpedoes smashed into her side, ripping her armored hull apart like wrapping paper. In fact, the exact number of torpedoes that struck the Oklahoma has never been definitely verified, but it's thought that between five and seven torpedoes struck during just the opening moments of the attack. It was an unprecedented, devastating blow. Almost immediately, Oklahoma took on a massive list as water thundered into a broken hull. Within minutes, the battleship had healed way over to a frightening 35° and continued to slip further and further. It was quickly becoming obvious that the mighty warship just wasn't coming back. And the order to abandon her was promptly issued and passed to the crew as they desperately scrambled out of hatches and gunports to escape the rapidly advancing flooding. Men poured over the rolling side of the battleship, plunging into the water, and some swam to the safety of Ford Island, while many made for the Maryland m alongside to assist her gunners in the fight against the marauding Japanese aircraft that still filled the sky. Those who landed on the island quickly set up a collection point for casualties and sent those who arrived uninjured to help in putting out the rapidly spreading oil fires. But as their superructure settled into the mud, more than 450 crewmen found themselves trapped within the upturned hull, fumbling around in the pitch dark as a horrid mix of water and spilled oil quickly overtook the few remaining air pockets. Frantically, the men picked up whatever they could, desperately banging on the battleship's hull with wrenches and hammers, tapping out SOS signals in a lastditch attempt to call for help. Stuck inside the sunken hull, the men trapped had no way of knowing if rescuers had heard their SOS at all. And without a way to effectively talk with the outside world, they were forced to sit in the choking darkness and wait. But as it turned out, someone had heard. Julio Dcastro, a civilian working at Pearl Harbor's Naval Yard, heard the sounds of clanging from within the cap-sized hulls. Knowing this could only mean one thing, he quickly gathered his fellow yard workers and set about trying to open up the Oklahoma's hull to free the trap sailors. Working with Commander EP Cranfelder from the Maryland, who had managed to find a booklet of general plans for the two near identical sister ships, Dcastro and his team worked with pneumatically powered shipping tools fitted with heavy duty chisels to break into the capsized hull. Dcastro and his men worked through the night, the still burning Arizona lighting up their work area as they desperately toiled to rescue as many men as possible before their oxygen ran out. After hours of backbreaking work, one by one, the belleaguered sailors of Oklahoma that could be reached were pulled out of their wouldbe tomb. When one of these sailors told the Castro that several men were trapped in an adjacent compartment, the yard worker simply replied, "We'll get them out." For an hour, fellow dockyard worker Joe Bulgo worked on the bulkhead in the rising water. He made three cuts before calling out, "Look out for your hands, boys." and he set about smashing the wall the rest of the way down with a sledgehammer, freeing 10 more men. All in all, 32 of Oklahoma's trapped sailors were rescued by Diccastro and his brave crew of yardsmen. It had been a magnificent, heroic effort, but tragically for hundreds more men, the battleship would be their tomb. Its upturned hull serving as a giant steel sarcophagus, but not a permanent one. In the wake of the rescue attempt, attention eventually had to be turned to the ship itself. It was clear that Oklahoma was in a very sorry state, though the full extent of the carnage was unknown since her damaged sections were largely inaccessible [music] thanks to either being blocked by the ship itself or buried in the mud. With her hulk resting firmly on the bottom, salvage teams left Oklahoma to rest for the time being. There was little hope that the old girl would ever see service again. And with California and Nevada providing far more hopeful prospects for salvage, workers efforts and Pearl Harbor's limited resources were committed to see these ships restored instead. But with her corpse occupying a valuable birth on battleship row, and her sunken superructure representing a navigational hazard to any ship traversing the channel, by mid1942, the decision was finally made to write her. Getting Oklahoma onto an even keel was an even greater undertaking than the salvage of either California or Nevada. And once more, the skilled men of the Pacific Bridge Company were vital in its success. It was immediately obvious that the previous solutions of coffer dams, patches, and pumps employed on both California and Nevada were woefully insufficient to lift Oklahoma's bulk off the bottom. The battleship was effectively upside down. She'd need to be put right first before any attempt at refloating could be done. But just how on earth do you write a 27,500 ton, 583 ft long ship stuck in the mud? Well, the brilliant minds of the Pacific Bridge Company got to work and their expertise devised a spectacular system that would see Oklahoma pulled right side up. It involved a series of 21 massive writing frames, each attached to the exposed portion of the hull. Heavy duty steel cables were run across to the conveniently nearby Ford Island, where they connected to an array of staggeringly powerful winches using electric motors taken from the tram cars in Honolulu. In theory, as the winches got to work, the cables would slowly be wound up, lifting Oklahoma's exposed side over and riding the ship. But with over 27,000 tons of steel to shift, it was a very dicey proposition. To ease at least some of the strain on the whole arrangement, as much fuel and ammunition as possible was removed from Oklahoma, while divers ventured inside the wreck to close as many doors and hatches as they could to allow air to be pumped into undamaged sections and create pockets that would lighten the ship even more. Thousands of tons of crushed coral was even placed under Oklahoma's bow to provide something for the ship to roll against as she was writed since her bow had gone down in a patch of the same sort of soft mud that had complicated the salvage of the California. With the system designed and set up within months, on March 8th, 1943, the winches were switched on, and ever so slowly, the once mighty dreadnaugh was hoisted upright. The resulting explosion in turn set off the much larger smokeless powder magazine, and the devastating explosion that followed ruptured and blew out the dreadnaugh's hull and blasted her forward sections to pieces. Incredibly, it was captured on film camera. Her sturdy hull and stalwart armor was simply no match for the immense release of destructive energy from within. With her imposing main mass slumped forward, Arizona by now a pitiful and shattered sight, sank further and further into the now oil laden waters of Pearl Harbor. her once mighty and imposing figure reduced to a broken wreck. 1,177 of Arizona's crew were killed in that enormous blast. Enson Douglas Hine, one of the 334 survivors and one of the sailors whose testimony on the morning's events was preserved, later wrote, "I left the junior officer's mess at General Carters. Today, it's only the two ghostly wrecks of the Arizona and the Utah that remain as a testament to the incredible efforts of this gallant team of determined people.
