The ship instead had to resort to blaring its sirens. Others were alerted by the horrifying sight of smoke creeping under their cabin doors. Captain Vic ordered full speed to Aiden, where help would be close by, and the crew focused their efforts on rescuing passengers and fighting the spreading flames. Thick smoke now filled the ship's corridors. Those on board struggled to see or breathe as they attempted to make their way through the stifling heat to the upper decks. The engineers were ordered to cut the power in an attempt to prevent further spreading of the fire through the electrical systems conduits, but it was too late. The lights went out, and terrifyingly, some passengers found the passageways blocked and had no choice but to try and escape through their port holes, and others became trapped in their cabins. Those who made it out onto the deck were met with a distressing sight of lifeboats already a flame, with others requiring hosing down to prevent them from becoming unusable. It was imperative that the remaining lifeboats were launched as quickly as possible. An SOS was sent out around 2:15 a.m. just before the wireless room was completely engulfed. Thankfully, three different ships responded right away to the distress call. A Russian tanker, the Soviet Sky Neft, and two British freighters, the Massud, and the Contractor. Survivors were brought across to the first ship to arrive, the Soviet Sky. In their lifeboats, the burning wreckage of the Gor Filipar loomed behind them. Over 400 passengers and crew members were brought aboard the Russian ship, which remained on station until noon the next day to make absolutely sure that everyone possible had been saved. Captain Vic sustained extensive burns as he attempted to check for any last reachable survivors and was the last to leave the wreck around 8:00 a.m. All the survivors were then transferred from the Soviet sky to the French passenger vessel Andre Lemon, which had arrived and taken to Djibouti. The flaming wreck of the now abandoned Gors Filipar continued to burn as she drifted for a further 3 days before finally sinking on the 19th of May off the coast of Cape Garde. Last seen trying to escape to the water through his room's port hole, the journalist Alber was among the 52 people who were missing and presumed dead, most having been trapped thanks to how rapidly the flames had spread out of control. The press seized on the idea that Lundre's demise could not have been coincidence. and several unfounded conspiracy theories cropped up. One tried to link the assassination of French President Paul Dumeare that had taken place a few days prior to the Gor Philip disaster, though there was no evidence to support any connection between the two. Another theory implied that the report Laundra had been working on believed to be exposing opium and arms trafficking along with the potential Bolevik interference in SinoJapanese affairs warranted being covered up. This theory took hold given that the only people who Laundra was said to have been confiding the contents of his notes to fellow passengers Alfred Langula and his wife Suzanne perished in a plane crash just a few days after having survived the sinking of the Gor Filipar. However, the findings of the investigation into the disaster were more practical, concluding that the fire was owed to the lethal combination of a faulty electrical system throughout the ship and its highly flammable decorative elements, which enabled the fire to spread with fearsome speed. Captain Vic and his crew were criticized for not having responded to the situation quickly enough or for running boat drills and fire drills, but they were ultimately cleared of wrongdoing. New guidelines were put in place recommending the banning of the use of those kinds of flammable materials as well as upgrading onboard firefighting equipment. The inquiry also proposed that the use of direct current caused too much energy loss at high voltages resulting in excessive heat and that alternating current should be used instead. Faulty electrical would also explain why the Gor Filipar was just one of several French ships of the time to be plagued by fire. A lesson had been taught, not necessarily learned, because it would happen again. And it was one that sadly came with the loss of over 50 innocent lives. Thankfully, not all maiden voyage disasters have ended in tragedy. Though, as Reuben Griffiths, a lift boy on the RMS Magdalina, found himself and his crew mates rowing towards the beautiful white sands of Copa Cabana Beach, their experience of the last few hours was far from relaxing, and they were making this trip in a lifeboat. After the Second World War, many shipping companies found themselves in need of new vessels to replace all those that had been lost. One of these was the British Royal Mail Line, who had lost the 14,000 ton liner Highland Patriot during the war. The Magdalina would be her replacement. Ordered in 1946 and built at Belfast by Highland and Wolf, that legendary shipyard, the Magdalina was 17,547 gross registered tons, about 570 ft or 173 m long. She was a combination cargo passenger liner and the first passenger ship built by Harland and Wolf since the war. Completed on the 18th of February 1949, the Magdalina had a distinctive island bridge design separating off the bridge from the passenger accommodations and the rest of the ship's superructure. A style reminiscent of Harland and Wolf's big four built years and years ago for the White Star Line. The Magdalina had a part riveted, part welded construction and featured all the usual watertight subdivisioning as well as a double bottom to help prevent grounding damage. On the 9th of March 1949, she embarked from the King George V dock in London on her maiden voyage bound for Buenes Aerys, Argentina. Captained by Douglas RV Lee, the Magdalina would be his final assignment before retirement. After a successful 40-year long career, the first leg of her journey was without issue. She reached her destination according to schedule and in preparation for her return, she was loaded with a substantial cargo of Argentine beef and then proceeded to pick up a cargo of Brazilian oranges at Santos. Along with her refrigerated cargo, the Magdalina also had 347 passengers on board and 237 crew. She departed Santos on the 24th of April, heading northeast towards her next port of call on the way home, Rio de Janeiro. As they steamed on though, it became apparent they were tracking more north than intended. Captain Lee ordered that they alter course to correct this. First at 6 p.m. and then again at 7. They reduced their speed from around 18 knots down to 13 1/2. All seemed okay. The captain ate dinner in the saloon before returning to the bridge and then turning in for the night at 10:45 p.m. But by 2:30 the next morning, first officer Sirill Senior, serving as officer of the watch, alerted the captain that the Magdalina was now some 2 and 1/2 m north of her course. Her heading was adjusted once more, and the captain returned to his cabin. But just 2 hours later, around 2:30 a.m., the Magdalina was once again off course. Suddenly ahead of them loomed what appeared to be a ship without lights. It was too late to prevent an impact though as it turned out it was not another vessel they're about to collide with. In the early hours of the morning on the 25th of April, the Magdalina had struck the Tucas Islands reef and was now stuck. Passengers and crew alike were jolted awake by the sudden impact. The ship's refrigeration engineer, Bill Harkness, described how the big crunch was so severe it threw me across against my bunk. The collision tore into the number three hold and water began flooding in. An SOS was quickly sent out and it was received by the Brazilian Navy. The Magdalina's passengers were ordered to the lifeboats where they anxiously awaited the arrival of the rescue ships. With nearly 5,000 tons of cargo on board, the decision was made to attempt to unload some of it to lighten the ship in an attempt to refloat her the following day. Some of the 20,000 cases of oranges were transferred to barges. Others were simply jettisoned overboard, and a further 2,000 tons of oil were discharged, all with some difficulty thanks to the increasing swell. Crowds gathered on the beaches on the morning of the 26th of April to watch as the Magdalina was towed towards Rio de Janeiro. But they surely weren't expecting quite so dramatic a show as they ended up getting. The ship found herself caught in a heavy swell approaching a bay. As the onlookers watched in disbelief, the rivets shot out. Topside plating started buckling and finally the shell plating ripped up. The Magdalina was tearing apart. The anchors were dropped and for a second time the abandoned ship order was given, allowing the remaining few passengers and then the crew to get safely to shore. Of course, Captain Lee was the last to leave. And not a moment too soon. With a noise described as being like the felling of a giant tree, the Magdalina had broken in half close to the impressive backdrop of Sugarloaf Mountain. splitting off of that forward bridge section. It was as if she'd been sliced clean through with a knife. The bow and the midship section sank quickly at the harbor entrance with only part of her mass still showing above the water while the stern drifted further towards land, eventually beating itself. But how exactly could this have even happened? The brand new ship well equipped with the latest navigational equipment. Yet her career ended before it had even truly begun. A court of inquiry in London in September 1949 placed the blame on Captain Lee and his first officer for their navigational errors and for failing to take sufficient and timely action. Their certificates were both suspended for 2 years and one year respectively. Up until the 70s, a boy with a bell marked the location of the ship's sunken forpart. Most of the bow section of the wreck has since been demolished because it remained a hazard to any large ships looking to enter the bay in the decades after the sinking. In a far happier turn of events than many maiden voyage disasters though, not a single life was lost in the sinking of the Magdalina. Even some of her jettisoned cargo actually survived the ordeal. The shores of Copa Cabana Beach were littered with washed up oranges and even intact bottles of beer that were found among the ship's scrap. Not so fortunate were the Magdalena's owners who faced the embarrassing and expensive loss of a brand new ship. A blow no doubt softened by the fact that the Royal Mail Lines was awarded an insurance check of around2,295,000. That's around £70 million in today's money. This massive sum made headlines at the time as the largest insurance payout for any marine casualty in British history. Not all ships are destined for long careers, and those with tragic legacies are often the ones we tend to remember the most. Many of today's safety standards are built on the sometimes painful lessons of the past. And we would do well to not forget that rapid innovation can sometimes have dire consequences. A ship's maiden voyage is an exciting time to be sure. It's an achievement by both the people that designed and built her. Yet, there's always a lingering notion of worry and anxiety for the owners and the operators. Fortunately, no big passenger ship has been lost on its maiden voyage since the Hans head to. But it doesn't mean that ship builders and operators should ever become complacent. >> [music] [music]

Dozens of survivors were transported to Saint Vincent's Hospital, which was run by the Sisters of Charity. New York had prepared to deal with the worst case scenario, the likely possibility that all 2200 or so of Titanic's passengers and crew would need urgent care. But instead, only around 700 people disembark Carpathia. In addition to the many medical staff and the transports, survivors on Carpathia were greeted by the Women's Relief Committee with food, clothing, and emergency funds. While the travelers aid society and the council of Jewish women stationed themselves at the pier and guided mostly second and third class survivors to temporary and safe lodging inside the city. It wasn't just government or official organizations either. Locals started to take the steps to make sure that survivors would have what they needed for long-term care and support as well. In fact, the women's relief committee was formed by some of the city's most prominent female figures who took to action at a blistering pace, coming up with a comprehensive plan for providing critical services and resources for surviving passengers, especially immigrants who traveled third class. The problem was that hundreds and hundreds of these people had simply lost literally everything they owned and were now washed up in a foreign country with nothing to their names and nowhere to go. Many had lost husbands, sons, and brothers. News of Titanic's loss crackled through telegraphs around the world. Back in England, the Lord Mayor of London commissioned the Titanic Relief Fund that spring. It aimed to support the families of victims in cities hit the worst with loss of life. In Southampton, for example, no fewer than 549 were lost, a devastating statistic that left hundreds of workingclass families without breadwinners. Virtually an entire generation of Southamptoners was lost that night in the North Atlantic, and those they left behind needed help. Many families received benefits from the council to help them recover. In the end, the fund raised over $161,000 for Titanic survivors and families of the victims, and the British component raised over 2 million. Amazingly, the Titanic Relief Fund operated for decades and actually didn't close operations until 1959, where many of the children the foundation had helped had grown to adulthood and were finally able to support themselves. Many women made widows, but the Titanic disaster were also able to stand on their own two feet, and some had remarried. The charity provided by many countless strangers for Titanic survivors was a dramatic display of human compassion and kindness. While the donations and relief efforts from strangers were overwhelmingly generous and definitely uplifted the spirits of survivors, it didn't mean their ties with the White Star Line were over. In fact, for many, it was just the start of a multi-year journey with Titanic's owners because hundreds were rightfully seeking compensation. When most people boarded a lifeboat that terrible night, they had no thoughts that it would be the last time they'd stepped foot on Titanic. Most thought the evacuation was just a proactive measure. For dozens, it was only after rowing away from the ship that they noticed her bow was low down in the water. Many brought very little with them. When the ship sank, down with her went belongings, artifacts, prized possessions, and family heirlooms. Naturally, the question arose, when a ship sinks and there's a loss of life, how do you determine who's at fault and responsible for that person's passing? Tickets sold for White Starline Voyagers had a broad disclaimer that said, "Neither the ship owner, agent, or passage broker shall be liable to any passenger carried under this contract for loss, damage, or delay to the passenger, or his baggage arising from the act of God, public enemies, arrests, or restraints of princes, rulers, or people, fire, collisions, stranding, perils of the sea, rivers, or navigation of any kind. Even though the loss, damage, or delay may have been caused or contributed to by the neglect or default of the ship owner, servants, or other persons for whose acts he would otherwise be responsible. It's jargon that few migrants would have properly read through if they could read it all. But despite the clause, survivors and families of victims were going to look for someone to take responsibility for their losses. Incredibly, the White Starline filed a petition in the Southern District of New York in October 1912 to limit its liability against any claims for loss of life, property, or injury. The very three things survivors and families of victims would be filing suit over in short order. The company claimed that the collision was due to a so-called inevitable accident. That at the time, Titanic's liability was protected by an 1851 law that stated in cases of unavoidable accidents, the company was not liable for any loss of life, property, or injury. If the captain and the crew made an error that led to a disaster, but the owner was not aware of it, the company's liability was limited to the total of the passengers fairs alone, the amount paid for cargo and any salvaged materials recovered from the wreck. The law was passed to encourage ship building and trade by minimizing the risk to owners when disasters occurred. Under this law, the White Star Line would only be liable for a grand total of $91,85, which amounts to nearly $3 million today. $85,212 for passenger fairs, 273 for cargo, and $4,520 for materials salvaged from the recovered lifeboats. But despite the White Star Lines claiming that the disaster was within the perimeter of the law, individuals seeking payments slowly began to build their cases. They claimed that although the crew had received wireless messages warning of ice, the ship maintained her speed, stayed on the same northerly course, posted no additional lookouts, and failed to provide the lookouts themselves with binoculars. They also faulted the White Star Line, and rightly so, for not drilling the crew properly for evacuation, leading to the launch of partially filled lifeboats. For the time, these were all very fair arguments. In a previous video on this channel, we looked at the break up of Titanic and how dark it was that night. And we looked at the fact that binoculars probably really wouldn't have made a huge difference in these kinds of conditions, but the lookouts should have had them anyway, and it was up to the captain, his officers, and critically the owners to ensure that they were properly equipped. After the White Starline filed its petition, notices were posted in the New York Times between October 1912 and January 1913, asking people who claimed damages to prove their claims by April 15th, 1913, the one-year anniversary of the ship's sinking. Hundreds of claims totaling over $16 million came from people from all around the world. They were divided into four groups: loss of life, loss of property, loss of life and property, and injury and property. Now, the injury and property category stands out in particular because the claims detail the nightmarish experience of many survivors. In nearly 50 claims, survivors describe how they lived through the disaster and the physical and mental injuries they sustained. Anna Maccgawan sailing on Titanic to return home to Chicago wasn't able to get on a lifeboat cleanly, and she was forced to jump. She sustained permanent injuries from the fall, from shock, and subsequent frostbite. Bertha Noon filed suit for more than $25,000 thanks to injuries she sustained after being physically pushed onto a lifeboat and her exposure to the cold water for several hours. She listed a badly injured back and spine that left her unable to wear corsets, severe nervous shock, and a misplaced womb. Additionally, she suffered from recurring congestion in her head and chest that left her prone to waves of unconsciousness for days at a time. The claims for loss of property really emphasized the class differences between different survivors on Titanic. Margaret Maggie Brown, for example, one of Titanic's most famous survivors and today known as Molly, made claims in excess of $27,800 alone. Her claim listed a loss of multiple furs, gowns, capes, dresses, and a $2,000 necklace. Irene Harris, the widow of Broadway producer and theater owner Henry Harris, sought a million-doll claim. Then there was the Carters. As we covered in a previous video on Lost Treasures of Titanic, they had a brand new 1912 Renault on board. Carter filed claim on the Renault with Lloyds of London seeking $5,000 reimbursement from the White Star Line. By contrast, in perhaps the most modest of claims, thirdclass passenger and survivor Yung Hei filed a claim for items totaling just $915. The most expensive thing, a suit valued at two half pounds. Clearly a far cry from a French automobile or fine jewelry and a perfect demonstration of the massive gulf between Eduwardian rich and poor. Hearings for the lawsuits weren't held until June 1915 in the Southern District of New York. Depositions filed with the court through 1913 and 1914 show conflicting reports on who to blame for the disaster. In June 1914, Bruce Isme, White Starline's chairman at the time of the disaster, was once again questioned on the speed of Titanic, the lifeboats, the lookouts, and other issues that may have contributed. Just as he had in the inquiries held in the days and weeks following the sinking, he reiterated that all decisions were made by Captain Smith and he was just aboard as a passenger. A claim which is technically correct, but the real truth is that no chairman of a company could ever truly board his ship and be treated as just another passenger. And of course, Smith wasn't alive to defend himself. Outrageously, the British inquiry held in 1912 had come to its own ridiculous conclusions, particularly the point that there was apparently no structural reason that any class of passengers had less of an opportunity than those from another class to reach the deck and the lifeboats. Even though third class were birthed hundreds of feet away and stories below the boat deck itself, more survivor eyewitness accounts gave more insight into the dramatic and final moments of the ship. While these testimonies continued for several days in June and July 1915, negotiations were being carried on outside of court that led to a settlement with nearly all claimments in December that year. Judge Julius M. Mayor signed a final decree in July 1916 which held the company guiltless of any probability and knowledge and thus not liable for any loss, damage, injury, destruction or fatalities. In the end, the company paid a total settlement of just over $600,000 to be divided amongst all the claimants. A far far cry from the original 16 million. It was one of the great injustices of maritime law. For surviving passengers, the ordeal would never really truly leave them. [music] Some would speak of it publicly, and others would hold it secret, even from their own families. What about Titanic surviving crew members? How could they continue with their lives and their careers? Life at sea had some strange peculiarities back then. One of which meant that their wages stopped as soon as Titanic sank at 2:20 a.m. It was an era of bureaucratic indifference. The most extreme example of this concerns the band. In one very famous case, musician Joe Hume's parents were outraged when CW and FN Black, the agent that contracted musicians to Ocean Liners, sent a note asking after a 14 shilling 7 pence debt for the uniform that had been lost with their son. Instead of paying it back, Jock's father sent the note to the Amalgamated Musicians Union to publish in their newsletter. For most of Titanic's crew, this was the stark reality, and the survivors had to get back to business. Many went to work right away, with some even finding jobs aboard Titanic's sister Olympic. Then there were the officers. After the inquiries concluded, they ended up charting very similar careers. But the spectre of Titanic's loss never really left them. Second officer Lighto was the highest ranking surviving crew member. He lived through the night by balancing on an overturned collapsible lifeboat and was a powerful voice in the Titanic inquiries and correctly testifying that the Titanic did not break into during her sinking and he stayed a devout company man to the last. After the disaster he served as a mate on the Oceanic, returning to duty with the White Star Line and a year later he received a promotion from subleut tenant to full left tenant in the Royal Navy Reserve. He was called up to active duty with the Royal Navy at the outbreak of the First World War. He was shipwrecked again and in 1915 was given his own command, the torpedo boat HMTB 1117. His wartime career was marred in controversy after the sinking of a yubot. Reportedly, his crew fired on German survivors in the water, violating the conventions of war. He was placed on the retired list in March 1919 with the rank of commander. And in retirement, Lightaller took odd jobs like inkeeper, chicken farmer, and property speculator. But he was later involved in the Dunkirk evacuation, charging off across the channel to help bring the boys back. He was a real character, and he died in 1952, having never commanded his own passenger ship. Third officer Herbert Pitman continued to serve with the White Star Line, too, after the Titanic. He served on Oceanic and then Olympic, but thanks to failing eyesight, he was taken from the bridge and made a purser instead. He left the White Star Line in 1922 for Shore Savile, but he also never commanded his own passenger ship. Fourth officer Joseph Boxhall served again in the same position on White Star Lines Adriatic before he was promoted to left tenant in the Royal Navy Reserve in May 1915. He served a year aboard the battleship HMS Commonwealth during the First World War before being dispatched to Jibralta where he would command a torpedo boat. After the war, Boxel returned to the White Star Line in 1919 and eventually signed on as second officer on Olympic. Finally, when White Starline and Cunard merged in 1933, Boxhall served as first and later chief officer of the RMS Aquitania and after 41 years at sea, he retired in 1940. Finally, there was fifth officer Harold Lowe. He served with the Royal Navy Reserve during the First World War as well, eventually attaining the rank of left tenant. Lo returned to serve with the White Star Line before retiring in 1931. But as with the other surviving officers, not one of them ever held their own passenger ship command with White Star or any other line. Such was the cloud that loomed over them. The legacy of Titanic's loss. The aftermath of Titanic sinking is a demonstration of the strange duality of society. Where survivors were lavished with aid by total strangers in the immediate aftermath. On arrival at New York, they were kicked to the curb by courts and inquiries for years after. The British Inquiry didn't even bother to interview a single thirdass passenger. And yet, it came to the conclusion they had just as good a chance as first class at getting into a boat, never mind the fact their survival rate was less than half that of their supposed social betters. For those that survived the Titanic disaster, or those who lost loved ones during the sinking, the sad fact of the matter is that it would be part of their lives forever. Much of it would be under the exposure of the public eye, testifying at inquiries, giving interviews to the press, and filing lawsuits against the White Star Line. But for others, the trauma manifested in private. Survivor Frank Goldsmith couldn't take his children to a baseball game because the roar of the crowd reminded him too much of the screams of the hundreds left behind in the water once Titanic sank. When tragedy strikes, surviving the actual event is usually just one in a long series of harrowing and difficult steps. Survivors are not only forced to recollect the value of their lost possessions, but to try to put a price on the loss of lives. And really, just how is anybody supposed to do that? Before the Carpathia had even reached New York, carrying not only her own passengers and crew, but every last survivor of the Titanic disaster, the wheels had already been set in motion for an official inquiry in the US Senate to investigate the cause of the ship's sinking. These hearings to be conducted by the Senator William Alden Smith of Michigan, beginning at the Waldorf Histori Hotel in New York City, were intended to find not only who was to blame for the catastrophe, but also intended to recommend changes to maritime law and regulations for the future. of those questioned were some of Titanic's most notable passengers and crew members as well as passengers still reeling from the ordeal they had just overcome. The world itself had fundamentally changed overnight. Picking up the pieces and solving the puzzle would be no easy task. The open and public nature of the hearings also meant that a media frenzy would ensue among journalists in attendance who were all hungry to keep chasing the Titanic story and happy to add fuel to the fire to sell papers. The world watched transfixed as the story of Titanic began to reveal itself little by little over the course of the 18-day inquiry. And all the while, questions began to rise about the man at the center of it all, painting a very shaky picture of the American judicial system and their treatment of the delicate situation. Once all was said and done, the resulting testimony given added up to 1,100 pages of text. Some of it contradictory, most of it confusing, and often marred by the witnesses struggling to recall accurate details while still processing immense grief and trauma. But for the first time, the story of Titanic had officially been told. And what a story it was. In the days immediately following the Titanic disaster, US Senator Alden Smith sat in his office pouring over newspaper headlines, all bearing the same grim news. The brand new White Star Liner Titanic had sunk with a great loss of life. For Smith, this news came as not only troubling, but puzzling. While having very little in the way of maritime knowledge himself, Smith had very fond memories of traveling with his son on board the RMS Baltic just 6 years ago, commanded by none other than the venerable captain EJ Smith, who had himself taken command of Titanic just days before and now, it seemed, had perished with his ship. The senator had taken a liking to the wise and old captain during this voyage, having joined him for dinner and a tour of the Baltic. He counted himself quite impressed by both the ship and her captain, who had seemed to be the picture of the reliable old shipmaster who could weather any storm. So now, as the senator gazed down at the headlines spread out before him, the question on his mind was the same as the question on everybody else's minds. What had happened? This wreck cannot have been a consequence of a full hearty and reckless captain because the EJ Smith he had come to know couldn't have been further from that. Senator Smith knew that an intensive investigation would need to take place in order to find the answers. But upon phoning President Taft, he learned that the president intended to do essentially nothing in response to the disaster. He was too riddled with grief over the loss of his close friend and aid, Major Archer Bald Butt, who'd been tragically lost in the sinking. Frustrated and full of unanswered questions, Smith decided to take action. If anyone was going to reveal the truth behind the Titanic disaster, it would have to be Senator Olden Smith himself. With the Carpathia fast approaching the New York docks, Smith knew that if any meaningful action was to be taken, there could be absolutely no delays. Just 2 days after the sinking of Titanic, with the Carpathia still steaming her away, carrying all of those survivors from the disaster towards New York, Smith introduced a resolution to the US Senate, laying out his intent to form a subcommittee to investigate the sinking and used the findings of the investigation to recommend changes to maritime safety. This was a forward-thinking move from Smith, who despised panic legislation and was taking pains to stop such measures before they could begin. He was of the mind that preventing another disaster like that of Titanic could only be possible once all the full story was known and laws could then be passed to address the issues that came to light from the investigation. This was no time for assumptions or guesswork and clearly many agreed. The resolution was passed and Senator Smith got to work immediately ironing out the legalities of subpoenenaing British citizens for an American investigation. Under advisement from the president, it was decided that Smith was well within his rights to subpoena Titanic surviving crew and passengers because the White Star Line was owned by an American parent company, the International Merkantile Marine. Because of this, Titanic was legally an American-owned vessel. When asked by a reporter how Congress could have any jurisdiction over British citizens, Smith replied, "We may not have jurisdiction over the individual, but the American Congress is not without jurisdiction over the harbors of the United States. It is for these men who make use of these harbors to meet the public demand for information in regard to the disaster. After speaking to reporters, Smith made his way to New York Harbor by train where he planned to meet none other than J. Bruce Isme, Titanic survivor and the chairman of the White Star Line on board Carpathia as soon as she docked. It was not for lack of empathy that Smith didn't even allow Isme time to step foot on dry land before being issued the subpoena. Smith's office had intercepted several curious telegrams sent under the clever code name Yampsy or Isme spelled backwards requesting that the White Star office hold the RMS Cedric so that Isme and the remaining Titanic crew members could return home aboard her to England as soon as possible. For the sake of Smith's investigation, this wouldn't do. He couldn't very well have his most important witnesses being whisked off across the Atlantic before the investigation had even begun. Upon boarding Carpathia in New York, Smith found his way to the cabin of the ship's surgeon, where Isme had been staying, and ignoring a handwritten sign on the door, which read, "Please do not knock," Smith burst in. Philip Franklin, vice president of the International Merkantile Marine, answered the door and informed Smith that Isme was far too ill to accept visitors. But unwilling to take no for an answer, Smith simply said, "I'm sorry. I shall have to see that for myself." A half hour later, Smith reemerged from the cabin, having gotten what he came for. And upon leaving Carpathia, he was met by a crowd of reporters who had got wind of this intense conversation with Isme. Smith informed them that Isme, the White Star chairman, would be appearing the very next day at the Waldorf Historio Hotel for questioning alongside Titanic's four surviving officers. The investigation was officially about to begin. But despite seeming business-like and collected on the surface, though, as Smith left Pier 54, the senator was beginning to realize the immense gravity of the disaster he was grappling with. He'd witnessed panicked families begging him for more information on the whereabouts of their loved ones. He'd heard the hysterical wailing of grief blended with the joyful laughter of those being reunited. It was a jarring experience that he'd found to be deeply disturbing. It was enough to put him on pins and needles. The weeks ahead were about to be long and painful, but the truth of the Titanic needed to be discovered once and for all. The very next morning on April 19th, a massive crowd had assembled itself out the front of the Waldorf Atoria Hotel. The doors opened promptly at 9:00 a.m. and within 3 minutes, the east room of the hotel was filled to the brim with reporters, photographers, and anxious spectators, all packed shoulderto-shoulder, all desperate to know the truth behind the historic disaster. An hour later, Senator Olden Smith arrived, accompanied by Senator Francis Nuland of Nevada and Steamship Inspector General Oola. Now, the first witness called to give testimony was, of course, J. Bruce Isme, a man whose character was already being called into question by the very fact that he had survived the sinking at all. Isme was seated at the large conference table situated in the center of the hall, flanked on either side by White Star Vice President Philip Franklin and Titanic's highest ranking surviving officer Charles Lighthaller. Senator Smith began by asking Isme a few preliminary questions, and immediately the frantic flashing of cameras and the popping of bulbs filled the room, but the media free-for-all was over as quickly as it began. With Senator Smith shouting, "Get those photographers out of here." With this interruption aside, formal questioning could finally commence. Isme took the stand and faced his first round of intensive questioning. Two more would follow in the coming weeks, and for Senator Smith, it was vital that his line of questions leave no stone unturned. Isme was, after all, the most obvious and convenient villain for this disaster, being the wealthy English gentleman who had fled the sinking ship while so many women and children perished behind him. But even worse, rumors were quickly spreading that Isme had directly ordered Captain Smith to attempt a record crossing, ultimately speeding the vessel into an ice field that had sunk it. This could be an easy win for Smith and a death nail for Isme's reputation. But Isme, it seems, had heard the rumors and was ready to address them head on. When asked about his role in loading the lifeboats, Isme was quick to put the allegations to rest. He said, "I assisted as best I could getting the boats out and putting the women and children in. I stood upon the deck practically until I left the ship in the starboard collapsible lifeboat, which is the last boat to leave the ship, so far as I know. More than that, I do not know." Later in Isme's testimony, he described exactly how he found himself in a lifeboat despite the order being given for women and children. First Smith asked him, "What were the circumstances of your departure from the ship?" I asked merely that, but Isme cut him off. He said, "The boat was there. There was a certain number of men in the boat, and the officer called out asking if there were any more women, and there was no response. There were no passengers left on the deck." Smith asked, "There were no passengers on the deck." As said, "No, sir." And as the boat was in the act of being lowered away, I got into it. Now, this bit of testimony would prove to be very important in Ismay's case, as rumors of his misconduct throughout the evening had spread since the news broke of the sinking, including accusations of cowardice, Isme jumping into the very first lifeboat to be lowered, and even wilder accusations of Isme disguising himself as a woman to gain entry into a lifeboat. Another common misconception that prevails to this day suggests that Isme had put pressure on Captain Smith to increase the ship's speed in order to reach New York a day earlier. A decision which would have had dire consequences as the ship sped her way through the ice field. But Isme's testimony paints a different picture of those events. Smith asked him, "Did you have occasion to consult with the captain about the movement of the ship?" Isme said, "Never." Smith asked, "Did he consult you about it?" And Isme said, "Never." Perhaps I'm wrong in saying that. And I should like to say this. I do not know that it was quite a matter of consulting him about it. Of his consulting me about it, but what we had arranged to do was that we would not attempt to arrive in New York at the light ship before 5:00 on Wednesday morning. Smith asked, "Was it supposed that you could reach New York at the time without putting the ship to its full running capacity?" Isme said, "Oh yes, sir. There was nothing to be gained by arriving at New York any earlier than that." Now, Isme may have been bending the truth a little bit here. He and Captain Smith had at one point discussed the ship's speed. They were overheard by a passenger in the vessel's reception room, and Isme was noted to observe that they were on track to beat Olympic's crossing time on her maiden voyage. Now, while some may point to this as a gentle nudge to the ship's captain to possibly push the engines a bit harder, the decision to do so always rested with Captain Smith and Captain Smith alone. Even still, with such prominent passengers on board, such as Isme, the ship's owner, as well as her designer, Thomas Andrews, Smith very well may have felt an unspoken pressure to pull off a notable crossing for Titanic's maiden voyage and his final outing before retirement. The bosses were, after all, watching. Now, throughout the proceedings, Isme asserted that he was more than willing to cooperate with what was happening to whatever extent was necessary. But after defending himself at length for hours, upon leaving the conference room, he was quick to bring the legality of the hearings into question before the press. A move that at this early stage only really served to make the scapegoat of Titanic look even more undignified. Having already once attempted to secure passage home on the Cedric for himself and Titanic surviving crew members before the inquiries had even begun, Isme was once again frustrated at his inability to leave American soil and felt it unlawful that British citizens should be detained. While his complaints wouldn't seem so incendiary as the hearings continued, his decision to speak out against the hearings to the press seemed to many to be a tactless move, especially for a man actively working to clear his own name. Unfortunately for Isme, the reputational damage would haunt him for the rest of his life. Despite multiple attempts to clear his name and many of the allegations against him having been proven false, he would never outlive the public smear campaign that resulted the sinking. The public needed to believe somebody was to blame for Titanic and the picture the press painted of Bruce Esme was unfortunately a very easy cell. The same day Titanic second officer Charles Loller was called to testify. He started out by describing his role in the ship's trials and testing with Smith grilling him to describe each process in detail. Now Loller was a notorious company man with a penchant for playing his cards very close to his chest. and his evasive responses quickly became an annoyance for Senator Smith, who continually needed to press Loller to be more specific. Once the senator was satisfied with Lightoall's accounts of the ship's testing, the majority of the remaining testimony in that first day was focused on recounting Lighto's actions during the sinking, most notably the loading and lowering of the ship's port sideboats. Now, many of the boats on that side of the ship had been lowered away before being filled to their complete 65 person capacity. and Lightoall's decision to not fill these boats completely had come under heavy scrutiny in the days immediately following the sinking. Senator Smith took the opportunity to press the officer for more answers. Now, initially, Lola claimed he simply didn't realize the extent of the emergency and said he was more concerned about the 70ft drop from the deck to the sea than about filling the boats completely. Once it became clear that the ship and her passengers were in mortal danger, Loller admits that he took more risks loading the boats with some 35 passengers, still well below capacity, but he claimed the boats didn't seem safe when filled beyond that point. With the first day of testimony complete, the subcommittee retired to review their findings so far. Many felt that Lola had not presented all of the facts, and the White Star was attempting to supply only the bare minimum evidence in order to speed through the hearings and see their employees brought back home to England. Now, beyond this was the issue of Bruce Isme's appeal to be excused from the remainder of the hearings and be sent home to be with his family, a request which Senator Smith continued to deny. Rumors continued to circulate about the possibility of negligence aboard Titanic prior to her sinking. And while the blame for this negligence may not have lain with Isme alone, he would be called for further testimony to address the concerns publicly. Isme along with the ship's surviving officers and crew were to remain in the United States for the remainder of the hearings. The next morning's hearings were held in the much larger Myrtle room given issues with the crowding and harsh echoes experienced in the Waldorf Histori's smaller east room. Now this second day saw testimony given by Harold Cotm Carpathia's wireless operator and Harold Bride from Titanic. Cotm's testimony transfixed the crowd. The 21-year-old appeared not much more than a boy, described his harrowing experience as man in Carpathia's wireless room from Sunday night right up until Wednesday afternoon without stepping away or sleeping, say for a few hours, in which he admits to inadvertently drifting off in front of his instrument. He was then relieved by Harold Bride, who despite his own extensive injuries from frostbite preventing him from even walking, had taken over Cotm's duties to allow him to rest. Cotton described in detail the messages he sent and received on the night of April 14th in regards to the imperiled Titanic leading up to the moment that the ship finally went dark. It was at this moment that Senator Smith called Harold Bride to testify and a somber atmosphere settled over the room. The severely injured young man was wheeled into the room, bandaged and clearly exhausted, his expression showing all of the weight of the tragedy he was now bearing. There was little room to maneuver a wheelchair through the crowded room, though, so Bride needed to be carried to his place at the conference table and seated in a large chair near the senators who now needed him to relive in detail the night he nearly lost his life. He gave his age, just 22 years old. After reviewing the finer points of his experience and duties as wireless operator, Bride was questioned on the messages he sent and received the night of the sinking. It was here that an interesting, uncomfortable point arose. In desperation and trying to keep the lines of communication open with rescue ships, Bride's colleague, Jack Phillips, had been frustrated by the German liner Frankfurt for cutting in and asking, "What is the matter with you?" Bride recalled that Phillips called the German a fool in response and essentially told him to shut up. The Germans did not take kindly to this perceived slight and pointed to this interaction as British inefficiency at sea, claiming that it's likely the Titanic disaster may have claimed far fewer lives had the Frankfurt not been sidelined. Now, this is of course completely untrue. The Frankfurt was too far away to help. But Bride defended his colleagues actions on the stands and essentially pointed out that this was a matter of course. He and fellow Wireless Officer Phillips knew for certain the Carpathia was on her way and Frankfurt's attempts would be simply too little too late. While finishing up the second day's proceedings, Senator Smith concluded with an announcement that a number of Titanic surviving officers and crew, including managing directors Bruce Isme and Philip Franklin, would be subpoenaed and to appear in Washington DC on Monday for the next round of hearings. Those not subpoenaed were free to return home at last, and some 172 British survivors of the disaster were finally free to return to England on board the SS Lapland on Saturday, the very next day. This was despite Isme's repeated requests that he and the surviving officers be allowed to return home to England as soon as possible. With this new round of subpoenas, Smith was making it clear he was in it for the long haul. Isme's hands for now were tied. The venue was changed from the Waldorf Histori in New York City to the caucus room of the Russell Senate office building in Washington DC on Monday, April 22nd. The room was as fresh and new as Titanic had been on boarding day. Dubbed the throne room by the first few people to step inside, this massive and ornately decorated room had never been used before until this very morning. The spotless room was immediately flooded by a throng of enthusiastic and curious ladies carrying sack lunches and crowding shoulderto-shoulder, eager to witness the day's events. Now, this did not sit well with Senator Smith, who had to shove his own way through the crowd of photographers and spectators just to get to his seat. After rejecting a number of those, overcrowding the room, Smith began the day's proceedings with this announcement. We are not at all concerned about the convenience of visitors upon the hearing. We are concerned primarily in obtaining the truth and I desire each person here to understand that they are here solely by the courtesy of the committee that the inquiry is not for their entertainment and that any expression of any kind or character will not be permitted. With that line drawn in the sand, the first to take the stand for this next round of questioning was Philip as Franklin, the vice president of the International Merkantile Marine Company. It was now Franklin's turn to explain this egregious oversight. Smith said, "I ask you whether you know anything about the sending of that message or by whom it was authorized or from whom it emanated." Franklin said, "I do not, sir." And since this was mentioned at the meeting in New York on Saturday, we've had our entire passenger staff in number nine Broadway office asked, "Then we cannot find out who sent the message." Throughout Franklin's testimony, it becomes more clear that he and the rest of the White Star officers were operating under the assumption that Titanic had survived and was making for Halifax based on rumors circulating in the press and their own confidence in the supposed unsinkable ship. Now, it wasn't until 6:30 p.m. Monday evening, a full 14 hours after Titanic had sunk, that the reality had become painfully clear. He said immediately that telegram was received by me. It was such a terrible shock that it took us a few minutes to get ourselves together again. Then at once I telephoned myself to two of our directors, Mr. Steel and Mr. Morgan Jr. at the same time sent downstairs for the reporters. I started to read the message, holding it in my hands to the reporters. I got off the first line and a half where it said the Titanic sank 2:00 a.m. and there was not a reporter left in the room. They were so anxious to get out to telephone the news. I want to say this that during the entire day we considered the ship unsinkable. And it never entered our minds that there had been anything like a serious loss of life. We of course thought there might have been something in transferring passengers or handling the passengers, but it never entered our minds that there had been a serious loss of life until we got this hadock message at 6:30. Called next to testify after Franklin was Titanic's fourth officer, Joseph Boxell. Smith asked, "You say you fired these rockets and otherwise attempted to signal her?" "Yes, sir," Boxall said. She got close enough, as I thought, to read our electric moore signal, and I signaled to her. I told her to come at once. We were sinking. Smith. And did you get any reply? Boxel, I cannot say I saw any reply. Some people say she replied to our rockets and our signals, but I did not see them. Smith went on. From what you saw of that vessel, how far would you think she was from the Titanic? Boxel, I should say approximately the ship would be about 5 miles. It seemed as though over the course of the Titanic's short life, testing of safety equipment and the drills required of the crew had been something of an afterthought. And in that drill that did occur at Southampton, only two lifeboats were actually tested. The officers and crew all seemed conflicted on the number of passengers that could be safely loaded into a boat at all, and the women and children first rule was heated differently on each side of the ship. The lack of training and the coordination caused significant confusion in an already dire emergency and very likely resulted in further loss of life. Now, this was not a show of negligence on the part of Titanic's crew, though. Everything from the number of lifeboats available to the necessary testing and boat drills was dictated by the British Board of Trade, whose standards by this time were hopelessly outdated with massive steam ships like Titanic. The most unfortunate part of all was that it took a tragedy the magnitude of Titanic to force a muchneeded overhaul to these requirements. The inquiries would also suffer from no shortage of interpersonal drama. Senator Smith had successfully subpoenenaed citizens of a foreign country to remain in the US to give their testimonies regarding the disaster. But for many of them, patience was beginning to wear thin. 172 of Titanic surviving crew had successfully returned home on April 20th. But a select few, namely the highest ranking officers and White Stars management, had been prevented from returning home thanks to this new subpoena by Senator Smith. The British government was not taking kindly to the senator's insistence upon detaining its citizens on foreign soil, and Bruce Isme was very vocal in his displeasure that his repeated requests to return home were being denied. In a letter to Senator Smith dated Thursday, April 25th, Isme wrote that if the committee wishes to examine me further at the present time, I hope it may be found convenient to do so promptly in order that I may go home to my family in view of my experience at the time of the disaster. And subsequently, I hope that the committee will feel that this request is not unreasonable. In a reply dated the same day, Senator Smith wrote, "As I said to you in New York on Friday evening last, when you asked to be permitted to return home and again on Saturday night when you made the same request, I shall not consent to your leaving this country until the fullest inquiry has been made into the circumstances surrounding the accident. This information can be fully detailed by yourself and other officers of your company and the officers and crew of your ship. I am working night and day to achieve this result and you should continue to help me instead of annoying me and delaying my work by your personal importunities. Trusting you will receive this letter in the spirit in which it is written. I am very respectfully WMEN Smith. In the eyes of the survivors, their families, the press, and foreign governments, Smith was beginning to rapidly lose credibility. His lack of understanding of the subject matter at hand also showed through in his lines of questioning such as his apparent morbid curiosity as second officer lighthaller described the collapse of the forward funnel. Smith asked, "What was this that fell?" Loller said, "The forward funnel." Smith, did it strike the boat? Loller, it missed the boat. Then what? Well, it fell on all the people that were alongside of the boat if there were any there. Injure any of them seriously? Smith asked. Loller said, "I could not say, sir." Smith, did it kill anybody? Lightaller, I could not say, "Sir." Later on in the same testimony, though, Smith seemed to have a strange interpretation of how Titanic's watertight compartments were meant to be utilized. I mean, as a place to die, I'm quite unable to say, sir," said Lighthaller. Now, this particular gaff earned Smith no small amount of ridicule in the press along with the nickname watertight Smith, further cementing his public persona as a clueless politician out of his depth when it came to nautical and maritime knowhow. On day five of the hearings, while questioning the notoriously feisty fifth officer Low, Senator Smith attempted to truly get at the heart of the matter when he asked, "Do you know what an iceberg is composed of?" Low, smirking, said, "Ice, I suppose, sir." Meanwhile, the British press was having a field day with Smith's apparent incompetence, not to mention their fellow citizens being held against their will at the mercy of a man who seemed to be making a fool of himself at every turn. A particular incendiary piece was published in the London Globe, calling Smith a gentleman from the wilds of Michigan who is possibly compelled by the exigencies of electioneering to be as insulent as possible to Englishmen. The British newspaper Daily Sketch published a short editorial column from its New York offices on April 27th which read, "British criticisms of Senator Smith and his methods of investigation appear to be fully concurred in by the majority of Americans." And it would not be too much to say that the senator is the laughingtock here as he seems to be in England. But the American press was quick to counter this sentiment with their own moral grandstanding. The New York Herald printed that nothing has been more sympathetic, more gentle in its highest sense than the conduct of this inquiry by the Senate Committee. And yet, self-complacent moguls in England call this impertinent. This country intends to find out why so many American lives were wasted by the incompetency of British seaman and why women and children were sent to their deaths while so many in a British crew have been saved. The Philadelphia Press published their own op-ed in the situation, maintaining that Senator Smith's inquiries have brought out and placed on permanent record the circumstances and conditions under which the great catastrophe took place. If incidentally the examinations disclose that the chairman of the committee is not an expert in nautical matters and asked some questions that caused the seaman to smile, what does it matter? The value of this investigation is not in the questions but in the answers. The hearings officially concluded on May 28th when Senator Smith presented his final report to the committee. Now, these findings took particular aim at the British Board of Trade as well as the general standards of seafaring on the day, recognizing that the testing and training protocol of the ship's safety equipment was hopelessly inadequate. The crew were unprepared to deal with an actual disaster at sea, he found, detail which ultimately resulted in needless loss of life. Passengers had been given no indication that there was an emergency, were unsure whether to proceed to the lifeboats or stay on the ship until it was too late for many. Orders from the crew and officers were conflicting when they were given at all, and it took far too long for the evacuation to get underway in earnest. It was also found that Titanic's Captain Smith had not done enough to heed the ice warnings received from nearby ships, which could have had as much to do with his confidence in his vessel as it did with his confidence in his own seafaring. But now this confidence seemed misplaced. It was also thought that the Californian had played its own role in the catastrophe, having failed to come to Titanic's aid despite being within sight of the ship as it went down. The lack of aroundthe-clock wireless contributed heavily to this critical misstep, as did Captain Lord's rather laxidasical attitude towards sighting the distress rockets in the distance. Possibly most damning of all, the horrendously outdated British Board of Trade lifeboat requirements meant that while Titanic met and even technically exceeded these standards, she lacked proper lifeboat space for about half of the ship's complement of passengers. Now, these regulations had been set for any ship greater than 10,000 tons. And of course, Titanic dwarfed this at over 46,000. It seemed that protocols and regulations had barely even attempted to keep up with the rapid progress made in naval engineering in the latter part of the 19th century. And what may have been possibly adequate for ships half of Titanic's size in decades past was now woefully out of date for these massive steam ships carrying thousands of people across the sea. These oversightes came at the cost of 1,496 human lives. As a result of the Titanic inquiry, it was recommended that all ships carry enough life-saving apparatus to accommodate all of those on board. New emphasis would also be put on more lifeboat drills and inspections so as to prevent the confusion experienced on the night of Titanic sinking. The International Convention for Safety of Life at Sea or Solass was drafted in response to this disaster, overhauling almost every aspect of maritime safety practices. Now though it wouldn't officially pass until 1914 and was ultimately brushed to the side with the outbreak of the First World War. In the weeks and months following the Titanic disaster, almost every major transatlantic passenger carrier updated their lifeboat requirements accordingly. The SS Californian's role in the disaster brought about its own changes to maritime law. The botched response to Titanic's distress calls had been at least in part caused by a lack of aroundthe-clock wireless since the Californian's only wireless operator had already retired for bed when Titanic's messages of distress came through. The Radio Act of 1912 was passed in direct response to this. The act along with the provisions in Soloulless called for 24/7 wireless operation on all passenger ships along with backup power for the wireless apparatus in case of emergency. With this, it was hoped that no future distress call would ever again fall on deaf ears. Also placed on more comprehensive patrol and reporting of ICE, especially on the North Atlantic tracks, which passenger ships routinely followed. In the immediate aftermath of the sinking, the US Navy dispatched ships and large cutters to patrol for ice in the vicinity of Titanic's final position. But it was found that action on a larger scale was necessary to ensure that all checks were in place. Now, up until this point, it had been largely the responsibility of a ship's crew and captain alone to monitor for ice at sea and report their findings to other ships. In response, the International Ice Patrol was founded as an arm of the US Coast Guard with the purpose of reporting dangerous ice conditions in the North Atlantic. This organization still exists and operates to this day, though they now make use of aircraft rather than ships for increased visibility over larger swades of sea. The construction and design of ships was also altered in the wake of the sinking. Double bottoms like the type Titanic had were now expanded on many ships like her sister Olympic into full double holes which now extended all the way up to the waterline to further reinforce the sides of the ships. Bulkheads were also extended to reach all the way to the top decks, making them fully waterproof. In Titanic's case, we know these bulkheads only extended to about 10 ft above the waterline, making it impossible to fully seal them. The results of the Senate inquiries showed that much of what transpired the night of April 15th, 1912 was largely preventable and was ultimately the result of lacks and outdated safety regulations, improper handling of ICE warnings, and simple hubris. The idea that the ship was a lifeboat unto itself was proven to be little more than an Edwwardian fairy tale. And it took the world's largest maritime tragedy to that point to see changes made to this backwards mentality. The American Inquiry did a pretty decent job of separating a lot of the truth from the myth in the days immediately after the sinking. But it was felt by many and it was very obvious that the British would need to hold their own inquiry as well. But with over 25,000 questions asked over the course of 42 days of total questioning, more than double the length of the American hearings, this is obviously a topic for another day. Despite a contentious press that looked to lambast Senator Smith's actions through the investigation at almost every possible turn, by the end of the hearings, a column printed by the New York Times conceded that he has brought out what we all wanted to know and had a right to know about the loss of the big ship and enabled us all to form a clear idea as to where the responsibility, direct or indirect, for that loss lies. The world now knew some of the truth of the Titanic, for better or for worse. And with that, important progress could now be made in hopes that there would never again be a tragedy as painful and avoidable as the loss of the RMS Titanic. 59 Buckingham Gate, London. Rows and rows of wooden chairs are packed as heads crane for a view of the witness who stands next to an enormous half model of an ocean liner. The model itself is about the size of a small rowboat. The witness's voice echoes through the galleries and the towering space called the London Scottish Drill Hall for the regiment at headquartered. A panel of seriousl looking men watched the witness intently from behind their solid wooden desks. Do you still think, asks one of them, that it was natural not to think about going back and saving some of those people? The witness thinks for a moment before he responds carefully. I think it was still natural, but I concede that it would have been a very splendid thing if it could have been done. The witness is talking about why his lifeboat, barely full, did not return to help the hundreds of people crying out after their ship had slipped beneath the waves. It's Monday, May 30, 1912, day 11 of a 36-day inquiry into the loss of Titanic, which now rests nearly 4 km deep on the bottom of the ocean. Just how it got there, the complicated series of events that led to the sinking and the persons or parties at fault is at the core of this investigation. Just after Titanic survivors had landed at New York, an American inquiry was hastily called that to many in Britain seemed little more than political theater. Now the government and the public hoped to find out the real truth. What had happened that night Titanic sank? What changes had to be made to ensure it never happened again? Unfortunately for all of its solid material findings and recommendations, the British W Commissioner's inquiry into the loss of Titanic would prove to be its own political theater, too. A kind of whitewash which diverted attention away from the dark truth of how and why the newest and greatest ship on Earth had sunk. Ladies and gentlemen, I'm your friend Mike Brady from Ocean Liner Designs, and this is the story of the British Titanic Wreck Inquiry. News of the loss of Titanic, as well as the nearly 1,500 men, women, and children that succumbed in its sinking, was initially slow to spread. In the immediate aftermath of the tragedy, headlines were a tangled, ugly mess of misinformation, causing mass confusion among a public that was desperate for answers. Some news reports claimed the ship had been involved in a minor collision was making for Halifax, with all souls accounted for. But later that same day, the grim truth was revealed. Titanic was lost, marking the most staggering maritime tragedy the world had yet seen. In Southampton, there was massive grief. Most of the crew had come from there. And across the world, telegraphs chatted with fantastical tales of panic in the final moments, men dressing as women to escape, the captain sacrificing himself to rescue a baby. Just what exactly had happened out there on the cold Atlantic was shrouded in mystery. And even as the ship's victims were still bobbing in their life jackets on the ocean's surface, moves were being made to hastily convene an inquiry in the US. The Americans were quick to jump at the opportunity because Carpathia had landed the entire load of survivors at New York in one go. Officials only had a tiny window to subpoena witnesses who could explain how so many people, many of them Americans, had died. Senator William Olden Smith of Michigan oversaw the inquiry, having accosted White Star Chairman Bruce Isme to ensure his cooperation with the investigation before Isme had even had a chance to step foot from off the Carpathia when she'd arrived. His authority came with backing from the White House. President Taft had lost a close friend and confidant in the Titanic sinking, Major Archbold, but and the disaster had devastated him. With the witnesses hastily gathered and proceedings underway, the whole thing was marred with controversy. Seeking out answers in the wake of the disaster was all well and good. But tension between Titanic's surviving crew and Smith, himself, no seaman, boiled over into outright open hostility. The crew, many of whom had lost virtually all that they possessed, were now kept as prisoners in New York until the inquiry was finished. Officers like Lightor were presented with questions, many of them seemingly nonsensical that wrankled them. They gave half-hearted answers or ignored questions outright, deeply resentful that the crew of a British ship were being investigated by an American inquiry that seemed little more than the political theater Smith needed to curry favor with his president. By the end, the investigation concluded the ship's loss was the consequence of Captain Smith's flippant attitude towards the ice warnings he had received, and the tragic loss of life was primarily the fault of inadequate emergency drills, as well as having too few lifeboats and a lack of organized emergency response. But almost at the same time the Americans launched their investigation into the disaster, the British began laying the groundwork for proceedings of their own. Titanic being a British flagged vessel, it was only logical that the British Board of Trade investigate the sinking of their ship. The Board of Trade was a government body that oversaw commerce, trade, and industry, everything from farming to merchant shipping. It was a vast scope of authority headed by Sydney Buckton. As far as shipping was concerned, it had been responsible for outlining all the regulations British ships had to follow in order to operate legally. To help with this, it had advisers who provided insight into how shipping companies actually worked. Many of the advisers being managers and directors from the big shipping lines themselves. Buckston called for the inquiry himself and asked the Lord Chancellor to appoint a wreck commissioner to oversee the events. And the man chosen for the job was a certain John Bigum, the Lord Murzy. Murzy was an interesting character, a lawyer and a QC who tried his hands at politics unsuccessfully before presiding over a handful of obscure but important bodies. He was the son of a wealthy merchant from Liverpool. Crucially, early in his career, he'd worked in merchant shipping cases and naturally developed an interest in the subject. Murzy's appointment wasn't without controversy and already cast a small shadow of doubt over the authenticity of the upcoming inquiry. He'd been a guest at the ship rights company, a professional ship builders club whose members included Weiss Sarine's own Bruce Isme and some of the senior leadership from the yard that actually built Titanic, including Lord William Perry. He had frequent dealings with the big shipping lines and felt strongly about Britain's dominance at sea. At a dinner for the Chamber of Shipping in February 1908, he had proposed a toast saying that those connected with the industry had to see that nothing was done by legislation or in other ways which would decrease the carrying power of this great country. This judge who had regularly sided with the big shipping lines over pay disputes and strikes was the man adopted as the head of the so-called independent tribunal. Britain's Prime Minister Aswith declared that the Board of Trade had absolutely no power to direct the course of the inquiry, but it's difficult to swallow the idea that Murzy was an independent and neutral leader in the proceedings. At the House of Commons, the Prime Minister was challenged by Irish politician Edward Carson. Does the right honorable gentleman imagine Lord Murzy will be influenced by the Board of Trade? He had asked. It was a fair thing to ask, but inevitably it called the man's honor into question. No, sir, said the prime minister. It's an insult to Lord Murzy to suggest it. So it was that the inquiry would be headed by a man who had Britain's shipping interests very very much at heart. Advised by a team of officials who unlike their American counterparts came equipped with actual maritime experience and knowledge. There was the chair of naval architecture at the University of Glasgow, an admiral from the Royal Navy, a senior engineer assessor, a senior captain and representative of the Trinity House Organization, and another assessor, a commander of the Royal Navy Reserve. It was hoped that they'd avoid the embarrassing pitfalls experienced by US Senator Smith as he fumbled his way through awkward lines of questioning during the Senate inquiry. Second officer ligher later wrote that the American hearings were quote such a contrast to the dignity and decorum of the court held by Lord Murzy in London where the guiding spirit was a sailor in essence and who insisted that any cross questioner should at any rate be familiar with at least the rudiments of the sea. With the board of trade having called for the inquiry and appointed the commissioner, this meant they were essentially investigating themselves and their own interests. Compared to the American investigation which took place over the course of 18 days, the British inquiry amounted to a whopping 36. Whether that's a testament to the thoroughess of the investigation or the consequences of long-winded and meandering questioning is a debate for another day. But the hearings began on May 2nd, 1912 at the London Scottish Drill Hall, a venue chosen specifically for its size. Unfortunately, every word uttered in the cavernous room echoed and reverberated to the point where many in attendance complained that much of what was being said was completely inaudible. Despite even Lord Murzy himself in agreement that the venue was unsatisfactory for their purposes, the hearings wouldn't be moved to a new location until their second to last day. They covered everything from Titanic's installed safety equipment like the lifeboats and their testing to the ship's wireless communication capabilities, her overall design and accessibility, and of course, the protocols surrounding the evacuation on the night of the sinking. The hope was that by answering these questions, the court could paint a clearer picture of the ill- fated maiden voyage and better understand the reasons behind the loss of the ship. They accepted the questions and with the last formalities in place, the investigation could officially get underway. Lookout Archie Juel, who hadn't even been on watch when Titanic hit the iceberg, and sailor Joseph Scarat. In fact, those first few days focused mainly on Titanic's lower decks with fireman George Bchamp and Frederick Barrett called on day three. Clearly Murzy and the panel wanted to establish a clear understanding of exactly what had happened to Titanic when it hit the Berg. When the court adjourned for the weekend, Lord Murzy and the others toured Olympic, Titanic's near identical sister ship to better understand the layout, the safety equipment, and the construction. In their mind's eye, it placed them right there on the night of Titanic sinking. Of particular interest was the Maronei wireless set. The operator even called up Cape Ushant Station in France for a demo. Back at the Scottish drill hall and leading stoker Barrett painted a compelling picture. Down in the dimly lit boiler rooms, the red light on the stoking indicator flashing red in the middle of his watch before the furnace dampers could even be shut came the grinding impact and the rush of water 2 ft above the deck plates. Even this formal inquiry wasn't without its moments of levity, though. Where did the water come from? asked the solicitor general, John Simon, who represented the board of trade. Well, came Barrett's reply, "Out of the sea, I expect." So concerned was the Board of Inquiry with the impact that the first week was almost entirely devoted to what had happened down below the waterline, having witnesses specify where they saw water entering the ship and cross referencing with the enormous half model of Titanic installed at the hall for demonstration purposes. But who the board really wanted to speak with were the ship's officers. But by the end of the first week, they were still on a ship on their way over to Britain. As the man quite literally behind the wheel at the moment Titanic collided with the iceberg, his testimony was deeply important. But the line of questioning taken with Hitchens highlighted one of the British inquiries huge flaws. Like many ships of the day, Titanic's wheelhouse was completely closed off and darkened by blinds at nighttime. The quartermaster, the man at the ship's wheel, simply responded only to verbal commands from the officers of the watch outside. It meant that Hitchens had a unique perspective of the disaster in that despite being at the helm at the time of the collision, he couldn't see anything of the outside world. He indicated as much early on in his testimony when he was asked by Lord Murzy, "Was the speed altered before the collision?" To which Hitchens said, "Well, the crash came immediately." "I know it did. Had the speed been altered before? Murzy continued. No, I could not say, my lord, because I could not see the officer on the bridge. I'm in the wheelhouse. I cannot see anything, only my compass. Despite this, he continued to be pressed on this point when he was questioned by Attorney General Sir Rufus Isac, who asked Hitchens, "While you were remaining at the wheel until 12:23, could you see what was going on on board the vessel?" Hitchens, I could not see anything. Later in the same questioning, Isaac's again pressed the issue. Could you see the watertight doors being closed? Hitchens, I could not see anything but my compass. Isaac asked again. Where you were, you were not able to see it. Hitchens, no. And again, when questioned by Sir Robert Finlay, representing the White Starline, could you see ahead at all through the wheelhouse? I could not see anything. You would not be able to see the iceberg, even if it had been quite clear. Is that what you mean? >> No, I could not see it. On no account whatever could I see it. This type of repetitive questioning seemed to plague the entire inquiry with witnesses asked to recount the same information over and over to one official after another resulted in a kind of endless bureaucratic line of interrogation that saw inane questions asked again and again that seemed to dance around the point rather than striking right to the heart of it. Murzy and the others might have argued they were just being thorough, but you still wonder why. On day 21, after White Starline's chief marine superintendent had explained thoroughly that 18 of his 30 years as an officer and captain had been with that company, Murzy asked if he had ever been to sea.
