"I might have said that," said Lord with regard to the steamer, but I did not say that the steamer was a passenger steamer. Murzy cuts in here. He says, "You do not give answers that please me at present. You just said now as plainly as possible that you answered the third officer, I think it was, and said, "The only passenger steamer near us is the Titanic, but you now suggest that you do not remember whether you said it or not." Captain Lord lamely responded with, "I do not recollect saying anything to him about it, my lord." While the captain admitted to being in the vicinity of Titanic and spotting a ship in the distance sending up rockets, he still denied that the ship could have been the sinking Titanic. The attorney general asked, "We know from the evidence in this case that the Titanic did send up rockets for some considerable time." Lord says, "Yes, so as far as I understand from you, you do not know of any other steamer which on that night and about this time sent up rockets?" I do not. Does not it strike you now that the steamer you saw sending up rockets must have beamed the Titanic? No. It was all to do with Titanic's reported position. During the sinking, Fourth Officer Joseph Boxell had taken a celestial reading that the Wireless Met broadcast as the ship's sinking position. In the event Boxel was wrong and put Titanic sinking about 10 mi further west of her actual spot. Despite Lord's testimony and the stated position of his ship during the sinking, Murzy simply determined he was wrong and Boxhall was right. This put Californian much closer to the reported Titanic sinking position and it damned Lord and his men for their inaction. But striking right at the heart of the matter, Mr. C. Robertson Dunlop, representing the Leland line, owners of the Californian, questioned Lord on his ship's ability to render aid any sooner than the Carpathia. Assuming, he asked, that she sank somewhere between 2 and 3, could you, in fact, if you had known at 1:15 in the morning that the Titanic was in distress to the southward and westward of you, have reached her before, say, 3:00 a.m.? Lord said, "No, most certainly not." Could you have navigated with any degree of safety to your vessel at night through the ice that you in fact encountered? It would have been most dangerous, Lord responded. Would the attempt, from what you know now, in fact have succeeded? I do not think, Lord said, we would have got there before the Carpathia did if we would have got there as soon. It was in Lord's best interest to defend himself and his ship from blame. So, it's no surprise that he plays up the danger here, but he's not wrong. Unlike Carpathia, Californian had been stopped for the night because of the ice, and she already found herself surrounded by Bergs. The ship would have had to have crawled its way ahead, groping through the darkness, lest she fall prey to an iceberg as well. That point was lost on Murzy. And while Lord wasn't prosecuted for his crew's supposed inaction, the disaster was a black stain on the 34year-old's career that would haunt him for the rest of his days. Meanwhile, where the American inquiry had questioned some 21 surviving passengers of the disaster, the British hearings heard the testimonies of just two aside from White Star Chief Bruce Isme. And those were first class passengers, Sir Cosmo and Lady Lucille Duff Gordon, questioned on day 11. The couple had famously escaped in lifeboat number one, one of the ship's small emergency cutters, which was lowered away with just 12 people aboard despite having capacity for 40. With survivors in the water fighting for their very lives after Titanic had disappeared, those aboard Lifeboat One ignored their cries, supposedly because the passengers aboard were terrified of being swamped. Rumors began to spread in the wake of the disaster that the inaction was also, thanks to a bribe, of £5, around £730 today, almost £1,000, offered by Sir Cosmo Duff Gordon to the sailors manning the lifeboat on the condition that they declined to return to try to rescue anybody. At the inquiry, he faced the attorney general, who asked, "I must ask you about the money. Had you made any promise of a present to the men in the boat?" Duff Gordon said, "Yes, I did." "Will you tell us about that?" Duff Gordon explained, "There was a man sitting next to me, and of course, in the dark, I could see nothing of him. I never did see him, and I do not yet know who he is." He said to me, "I suppose you have lost everything." And I said, "Of course." He says, "But you can get some more." And I said, "Yes." Well, he said, "We've lost all our kit and the company won't give us anymore. And what's more, our pay stops from tonight. All they will do is send us back to London. So I said to them, "You fellows need not worry about that. I'll give you a fiverr each to start a new kit." That, he said, is the whole of that £5 note story. Clement Edwards, representing the dock laborers union, examined Sir Duff Gordon and attempted to understand why exactly those aboard Lifeboat One declined to aid survivors in the water, but failed to come up with a satisfactory answer. "Do you think?" he asked. It was natural then not to think of rescuing those people who were drowning. It's a difficult question to answer. Duff Gordon said if you put it like that [music] at the time I saw no possibility. I thought there was no possibility of doing so. Edwards pressed him. I will put it this way. Do you still think that it was natural not to think about going back and saving some of those people? I think it was still natural, Duff Gordon said, but I concede that it would have been a very splendid thing if it could have been done. The uncomfortable truth was that more first class men had survived than thirdclass children. The Duff Gordon's reputation never recovered, and the questions about the supposed bribery loomed large. It was a mystery the inquiry never quite got to the bottom of. But just why a civilian passenger was being grilled about why his boat did not return is in itself a bit of a mystery too considering Duff Gordon was not an employee of the shipping line or actually in charge of the lifeboat. The whole thing smacked of theater. With the inquiry now stretching into its second week, the first of the ship surviving officers had arrived. He was the most senior Charles Laller. second officer and he was finally called to testify. [music] What resulted was a brutal barrage spanning around 2,000 questions over the course of 2 days with Loller's testimony filling the entirety of day 12 by itself. Later, Lola would write of the experience, "I know when it was all over, I felt more like a legal doormat than a mailboat officer, and I don't blame him one bit." Loller was questioned on every move he made throughout the night of the sinking. From his brief conversation with Captain Smith on the bridge regarding visibility prior to the collision to the loading and lowering of the lifeboats to his rescue on Carpathia after braving the elements balanced on top of an overturn collapsible throughout the entire night. Most interesting of all was Lola's adamant claim the Titanic could not possibly have split in two despite what was reported by other survivors. The solicitor general asked him, "I do not know whether you can help us at all in describing what happened to the ship. You were engaged and had other things to think about, but what did happen to the ship? Can you tell us at all?" Loller knew what he was getting at. "Are you referring to the reports of the ship breaking in two?" "Yes," answered the solicitor general. "It is utterly untrue," Loller said. "The ship did not and could not have broken in two." Later, as the two-day bombardment was coming to a close, Murzy himself offered Lighto an opportunity to revise his statement, but instead he doubled down. It is suggested, Mury said, that perhaps you, being in the water, would not see that writing of the after part of the ship at all, and that you possibly only saw her after she had got in that position and was going down. Lola refused to budge. I should not think, after once she had shown a tendency to break and was weakened, she would ever have the strength to write again. Murzy said, "You do not give credit to those witnesses who say that the afterpart of the ship, having once been up in the air, rided itself." "No, my lord," he answered. "I do not." On the topic of Stanley Lord and his claim that he had mistaken Titanic's distress rockets for company signals, Lola was quick to dismiss this as highly improbable. The solicitor general asked him, "If you had seen those signals, like those sent out from another ship, would you have known for certain what they were? I would have seen them and known immediately. Lolla said, "We've heard something about company's signals," the solicitor general pressed. "Do they resemble those at all?" "In no way, to my knowledge," answered Loller. The officer was heavily criticized for his actions during the evacuation, having reportedly stuck to a strict women and children only policy rather than women and children first, resulting in many of his lifeboats being lowered away with sometimes half as many passengers as the boats were rated to carry. When questioned by Solicitor General Sir John Simon on why those lifeboats were lowered with so few passengers, Loller explained that the fully loaded boats being lowered from the 60 ft height might compromise the integrity of the boats, causing them to buckle. Loller explained that he had planned instead to lower the boats partially full only as far as the gangway doors located down the ship's side where more passengers could be safely loaded in. Here is a boat with only 42 people in it, the solicitor general asked. And when it's waterborne, everybody agrees it would safely carry more then. Yes, answered Lighthaller. Did you give any orders with the object of getting more people into it when it was in the water? Yes, I see what you're alluding to now, Lightoall said. The gangway doors. I'd already sent the boatwin and six men and told the boatsmen to go down below and take some men with him and open the gangway doors with the intention of sending the boats to the doors to be filled up. So with those considerations in mind, I certainly should not have sent the boats away. The plan was of course unsuccessful. The boatsman and his mates were never seen again. Murzy was quick to point out a fundamental flaw in Lightoall's reasoning on the night. It appears to me, he said, that you would be very unlikely to order the forward gangway door to be opened. You might get the head so deep in the water that she might ship water through that gangway door. Of course, my lord said, I did not take that into consideration at the time. There was not time to take all these particulars into mind in the first place. At this time, I did not think the ship was going down. Now, we have to be fair to Lightoraller because he's right. Titanic sinking was still in question for most of the night and confronted with a sudden and unexpected evacuation. It would be so easy for the mine to overlook even obvious logic issues. For example, not one of Titanic's officers realized that Captain Smith's original plan to lower the boats to ADC to take passengers on there was impossible because the ship, unlike Olympic, had big screens with windows that were wound shutting off half the prominard. and it made escape impossible until somebody could find the handle and wind them all down. Because passengers were unable to board any of the boats through the gangway doors, several lifeboats were lowered away without being filled to capacity. Loll has cpped some criticism over the years for his handling of the evacuation. But the truth is, he like Titanic's other officers were suddenly presented with the nightmare scenario and very little time to coordinate an effective escape. He was hopelessly underprepared because the system didn't require the crew to coordinate a realistic evacuation drill beforehand. Lightaller had overseen lifeboats being lowered, all 16 of them, in fact, at a test in Belfast. But actually lowering empty wooden boats is a very different thing to coordinating an effective evacuation for hundreds and hundreds of people. [music] The passengers had no idea where to go, and the officers had to just do the best with what they had. White Starline chairman Bruce Isme was finally free to return to England a month to the day after the Titanic disaster on May 15th, 1912. Just a couple of weeks after, as the British hearings were rounding out their 16th day, having questioned mainly sailors and stewards, Isme was called as the day's final witness. With his reputation already in tatters publicly, is took to the stand once again as he had already done during his grilling before the American inquiry. But the battery of questioning was perhaps unsurprisingly nowhere near as brutal as what he'd experienced before the US Senate inquiry. Murzy seemed eager to dig into the accusations that would implicate Isme directly in the disaster, but in doing so, it gave him an opportunity to try to clear his name. One of the major issues first raised was Isme's supposed role in increasing the ship's speed once it entered the vicinity of ice. Nuri and the other officials questioning him seemed focused on cornering their witness to admit he had directed Captain Smith to speed Titanic towards the ice field, though Isme himself admitted he had no knowledge of ship navigation. The attorney general asked, "According to your view, what do you say as to the weather conditions?" So far as I could judge, Isme responded, "It was a perfectly fine clear night." The attorney general, "So that on a perfectly fine clear night with the expectation that you were coming within the region of ice, your view was that the captain would be justified in increasing his speed?" Isme answered, "I do not see any reason why he should not, so long as he could see sufficiently far to clear the ice." While it seems as though his may was appearing negligent here, his viewpoint was a surprisingly common one shared by many involved in navigation at the time, most notably Captain Smith himself. See, the idea of maintaining or even increasing your speed in the region of ice was apparently considered the done thing by many White Starline captains who often prided themselves on their ability to keep their ships on schedule even in the most difficult of circumstances. Later in the inquiry, Captain Ranson, master of the White Star Line at Baltic, was questioned on this same point by Sir Robert Finlay representing the White Star Line. And his answers also unsurprisingly aligned with his boss's opinion. Sir Robert Finlay asked, "With regard to your speed, you know the practice in the Atlantic. If the weather were clear and ice reported, do you keep up your speed?" Ranson said, "We keep up our speed." Finlay, is that your invariable practice? Ranson, it has always been my practice. But on the other side of this argument was Sir Ernest Shackleton, the legendary explorer famous for his expeditions to the Antarctic. An important distinction is that unlike the other captains mentioned, Shackleton had never been the master of an ocean liner before, and he had little concern for things like weekly schedules and speed. To him, reaching his destination safely was preferable to reaching it quickly. And to this end, he was very well-versed on navigating the threat of ice. As a man with expertise in the matter, he was called upon during the final days of the inquiry to present his ideas on how a ship like Titanic might have been better handled when faced with the threat of icebergs. The attorney general asked, "We've been told that none of these lighters slow down, even though they know they're about to go through an ice region. That is to say, a region where there are icebergs. Shackleton said, "I've been in a ship which was specially built for ice, but I took the precaution to slow down because you can only tell the condition of any ice you see. There may be projecting spurs, and you may suddenly come across them." The attorney general asked, "So, what was the speed of the boat you were in?" Shackleton says she was only 6 knots at full speed. She was 40 years old. The attorney general said, "Do you mean to say that you slowed down a vessel of six knots?" Shackleton answered, "Yes, I always did." We know now that the practice of proceeding through an ice field at full speed is dangerous at best and catastrophic at worst, but apparently this didn't seem so obvious to skippers back then. Instead, ocean liner captains maintained a focus on reaching the other side of the Atlantic swiftly, which kept their passengers happy and booking their ships for future crossings. Most importantly of all, it kept their bosses happy, even if it meant every soul on board would potentially be put in harm's way to do it. Another point which helped to doom Isme's reputation was that while on board Titanic, he was handed a maroneagram by Captain Smith, which contained the now infamous ice warning from the nearby White Star Liner Baltic. Now, with this warning in hand, Isme was accused of sharing the information contained with a fellow passenger, Mrs. Emily Ryson and allegedly explaining to her that he had directed the captain to speed the ship up through the ice field in an effort to reach New York a day early. This of course was vehemently denied by Isme in America and then again here in the British inquiry. The attorney general asked, "Do you know a Mrs. Ryson of Philadelphia?" Isme said, "Yes, I met her on board the ship." And she, the attorney general went on, was one of the two lady passengers to whom you mentioned the maronogram in the afternoon. That is true. You showed her the wireless message, did you not? I read it to her, I think. Now, I want to put it to you like this. Did she say to you, "Of course, you will slow down." And did you reply, "Oh, no. We will put on more boilers to get out of it." Isme certainly not. We may never know for sure what information was actually exchanged during the course of this conversation between Isme and Ryson. But in a letter dated April 18th, 1913, just over a year after the sinking, Ryson wrote, insisting that Isme had in fact alluded to the ship increasing speed arriving in New York early despite his claims to the contrary. She wrote, "I was on deck in the afternoon of April 14 between 5 or 6:00, and Mr. Risme came up and inquired if our stateaterooms were comfortable and the service satisfactory etc. and then thrust a marodoggram at me saying we were in among the icebergs. Something was said about speed and he said that the ship had not been going fast yet but they were to start up extra boilers that afternoon or evening. The telegram also spoke of the Deutseland a ship out of coal and asking for a tow. And when I asked him what they were going to do about it, he said they had no time for such matters. Our ship wanted to do her best and something was said about getting in Tuesday night. The strong impression which was left in my mind was that they were speeding the ship up to get away from the ice and that we would probably get in late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning. Mr. Isme's manner was that of one in authority and the owner of the ship and what he said was law. At the end of the day, the fact remains that Isme was never in any position to direct the ship's speed or navigation. And Captain Smith knew this as well. Whether or not he gave anyone the impression that he had this authority, he was still traveling as a regular passenger and had no say in how the ship was meant to be handled. Murzy extended a kindness to Isme and put it on record that had Isme not hopped into a lifeboat at the end, then his death would only have added to the tragic loss of life. But an indignant public was outraged that the company chairman had sought escape when 1500 or so of his customers remained behind. Isme's reputation was forever sullied by the allegations of the rest of his life. He almost never spoke again of Titanic or her sinking even to his closest friends and family. Of course, one of the most important topics addressed during the inquiry was the fact Titanic had gone to sea equipped with far too lifeboats to accommodate all the passengers on board. This, it was quickly found, was thanks to outdated board of trade standards for lifeboat accommodations that were based on gross tonnage of ships, that is their sheer size rather than the number of people actually on board. In point of fact, Titanic really sailed with six more lifeboats than what was even really required according to the Board of Trade standards. Now, here is where the Board of Trade could be actually called to account. The lifeboat standards were hopelessly outdated, but perhaps not without reason. The board was advised in part by owners and senior leadership of the big shipping companies who might have borked at the idea of fesoning their modern steam ships with dozens and dozens of lifeboats. Of course, Murzy, who had British shipping and its reputation very much in mind, wasn't particularly interested in finding the Board of Trade at fault. While questioning Sir Walter J. Powell, marine director of the British Board of Trade. No small amount of confusion was stirred up while trying to understand the archaic protocols around lifeboats. But this brief snippet of conversation between the attorney general and Murzy showed that this mentality was still alive and well even in the wake of Titanic. The attorney general asked, "I've already indicated to your lordship that the argument which I shall use will be that it is much more important to make your ship as near as unsinkable as you can than to provide boats." The commissioner said, "Of course it is." Despite this, it was blatantly obvious to everyone in the room that the lifeboat standards put forth by the Board of Trade almost 20 years ago were in desperate need of an update. But to what extent was the question? The last amendment to the protocols was back in 1894 when the 13,000 ton Cunard's Lucania and Campania were the largest ships at sea. But now 1912, ships were exploding in size up to nearly 50,000 gross registered tons. There was no denying that the standards were costing lives. During the course of Howal's questioning, a letter he wrote to the Secretary of the Merchant Shipping Advisory Committee of the Board of Trade just 5 days after the Titanic disaster was read aloud and its contents, well, they were very telling. It said this. The committee fully recognized that the proved impossibility of keeping such a vessel as the Titanic afloat after a collision with the ice until the arrival of outside sucker has it created an entirely new situation which was neither in the contemplation of the border trade nor of the committee in the consideration of the extension of the existing boat scale in regards to vessels of 10,000 tons and upwards. It seemed that as ships grew in size, so did the apparent belief that they were also becoming more and more unsinkable to the point that it seemed almost silly to equip them with any more lifeboats than what was found on ships five times smaller and almost 20 years older. It seems like excuse making and hindsight is, as they say, 2020. But how could some of the greatest minds in shipping not have foreseen a scenario just like this? Some did. I mean designers like Axel Wellan who engineered the Davits specifically to take on two rows of boats. Then there was even Titanic's own designers especially the likes of Alexander Carlilele. Murzy grilled him about the number of boats Titanic carried and uncovered a shocking revelation. Murzy asked, "Did you think there ought to be 64?" Carlilele, I thought there ought to be three on each set of davits. How many would that make altogether? Murzy asked. 48 boats, Carlilele said. Murzy asked, "You thought there ought to be 48?" Carlile simply said, "Yes." Far from being some kind of inconceivable issue, it seems the engineers and designers were in fact planning for the worst. It's just that at the time, 48 boats on a liner of that size might have really seemed excessive. That and the boats added a huge amount of costs, weight, and clutter. The loss of Titanic was a very violent wakeup call for the shipping world. And unless changes were made quickly, it should have seemed clear that a similar disaster would be unavoidable. But even then, several witnesses still stood firm on the belief that equipping a ship with enough lifeboats for all passengers would lead to the decks becoming cluttered, [music] making it difficult for the crew to even ready them. Lord Murzy himself, after hearing several weeks worth of testimony by this point, still remains skeptical at the idea of increasing lifeboat capacity for vessels to accommodate everyone on board. He said, "I have at present serious doubts whether it should be a wise thing to direct lifeboat accommodation for every soul on board. I have serious doubts about it. It never has been done. It's quite true that the loss of the Titanic appears to point to the probability of it being wise to increase the lifeboat accommodation. Now, this back and forth around the lifeboats continued through much of the latter half of the proceedings, and a number of Board of Trade surveyors and officials were called up to give opinions and guidance. Everyone seemed to agree that more lifeboats with the obvious recommendation, but most of them actually stopped short of recommending lifeboats for everybody on board. On July 3rd, 1912, the final report of the rec commissioner's inquiry into the loss of Titanic was handed down. It included the answers to the 26 questions put to the court on day one of the hearings concerning everything from the ship's construction to the events of the voyage up until the disaster to the treatment of ice warnings, the precautions taken when approaching the ice field and ultimately the events surrounding the tragedy when the ship took her final plunge. Among the answers to those 26 questions, it was found that Titanic's speed around 22 knots approaching the ice field was in fact excessive given the warnings that had been received. At least eight lifeboats were lowered with space on board for more passengers and that the nearby ship Californian failed to render aid when Titanic was visible from their position and firing distress signals. In one section of the final report, the board concluded that quote, "The disproportion between the numbers that the passengers saved in the first, second, and third classes is due to various causes, among which the difference in the position of their quarters and the fact that many of the thirdass passengers or foreigners are perhaps the most important. And yet just a few lines down when asking the question, "Was the construction of the vessel and its arrangements such as to make it difficult for any class of passenger or any portion of the crew to take full advantage of any of the existing provisions for safety, the report simply answered no." Totally ignoring the fact that the thirdass passengers were birthed far away and below the boats in endless twisting corridors that all looked the same with no direct access to the boat deck at all. In many cases, nobody came to help them or tell them where to go. No thirdass passengers were even asked to give their testimony at the British inquiry, even though more than 500 of their number had died on the night. An outrageous emission that by itself, in my opinion, casts a massive shadow of doubt, over the entire proceedings. The report and the inquiry itself had been thorough, frustratingly so at times. And yet, while it seemed to take pains to get to the bottom of some of the most intricate details, it merely glossed entirely over other big issues. Conflicting evidence from firemen and stokers that painted very different pictures of the amount of water actually flowing into the boiler rooms. [music] Then there was the obvious difference in positions given out of Titanic's final resting place. The fact that many saw the ship break apart in their final moments. None of it was given much credence at all. A cynical mind might suggest that Murzy was trying his best to paint the situation with as positive a light as possible. Yet, it had been a tragedy that was certain. But it was a story of outdated regulations and mere oversight. Absolutely not an indictment on British ship building itself. The question of why Titanic's watertight bulkheads only rose slightly above the water line and not all the way up the hull as they had on the great ship Great East over half a century earlier wasn't really considered either. Still, like in the American hearings, there came a set of recommendations for much needed updates to the board's protocols. It was suggested that changes be made to the height of the watertight bulkheads. It was also recommended that more care should be taken with regard to those consistent boat drills, that the drills should be manned appropriately by members of the crew, the ships should follow more careful navigational steps when encountering ice, and that 24/7 wireless communication should be made available on all ships while at sea. Now, none of that is much of a surprise. The most major consideration seemed to be with regard to the lifeboats. It had been that hot button issue during the testimony phase of the hearings. And while many witnesses who were questioned and Lord Murzy himself initially stood firm in the belief that having ample lifeboats for all passengers was unnecessary even in the wake of the disaster. The final report relented and included recommendations that the accommodation should be sufficient for all persons on board with however the qualification that in special cases where in the opinion of the board of trade such provision is impracticable the requirements may be modified as the board may think right. So Murzy and the others got their little caveat in that and the provision of lifeboat and raft accommodation on board such ships should be based on the number of persons intended to be carried in the ship and not upon tonnage. This seems frustratingly obvious today. A 20,000 ton tanker with 20 people on board doesn't need as many lifeboats as a 20,000 ton liner with 1500. But as we've seen, change didn't tend to come easily at this point in history. Then there came the matter of the Californian. Remember that over the course of both the American and British inquiries, Captain Lord had maintained that the vessel he spotted nearby was too small to be Titanic. That he had no reason to believe the ship he saw was in any danger, assuming the flares simply to be company signals of some kind. But the report disagreed. It said the Titanic collided with the Berg at 11:40. The vessel seen by the Californians stopped at this time. The rockets sent up from the Titanic were distress signals. The Californians saw distress signals. The number sent up by the Titanic was about 8. The Californians saw eight. The time over which the rockets from the Titanic were sent up was from about 12:45 to 1:45:00. It was about this time that the Californians saw the rockets. At 2:40, Mr. Stone called to the master that the ship from which he had seen the rockets had disappeared. At 2:20 a.m., the Titanic had founded. It was suggested that the rockets seen by the Californian were from some other ship, not the Titanic. But no other ship to fit this theory has ever been heard of. And to Lord's argument that they could not have rendered aid to Titanic thanks to the ship's comparatively slow speed and the presence of nearby ice, the report gave the following rebuttal. When she first saw the rockets, it said the Californian could have pushed through the ice to open water without any serious risk and so to have come to the assistance of the Titanic. Had she done so, she might have saved many, if not all of the lives that were lost. That was a damning final note and probably a deeply unfair one. To suggest that Californian could definitely have pushed through ice to the open water is an incredible leap in logic and well into the hypothetical. A very important note was made around Captain Smith's failing to slow the Titanic down as it approached the ice field despite having received multiple ice warnings throughout the day. Now, this was a point of debate throughout the duration of questioning as others with decades experience as masters and officers like Captain Ransen of the Baltic agreed with Smith's decision to maintain speed despite the danger of ice. But the rec commissioner's view was rightfully at odds with the practice and the final report stated that the question is what ought the master to have done. Why then did the master persevere in his course and maintain his speed? The answer is to be found in the evidence. It was shown that for many years past, indeed for a quarter of a century or more, the practice of liners using this track when in the vicinity of ice at night, had been in clear weather to keep the course, to maintain the speed, and to trust to a sharp lookout to enable them to avoid the danger. This practice, it was said, had been justified by experience. I accept the evidence as to the practice and as to the immunity from casualties which is said to have been accompanied by it. But the event has proved the practice to be bad. Its route is probably to be found in competition and in the desire of the public for quick passages rather than in the judgment of navigators. In these circumstances, I am not able to blame Captain Smith. He was doing only that which other skilled men would have done in the same position. The evidence shows that he was not trying to make any record passage or indeed any exceptionally quick passage. He was not trying to please anybody, but was exercising his own discretion in the way he thought best. He made a mistake, a very grievous mistake, but one in which, in face of the practice and of past experience, negligence cannot be said to have had any part. And in the absence of negligence, it is, in my opinion, impossible to fix Captain Smith with blame. It is however to be hoped that the last has been heard of the practice and that for the future it will be abandoned for what we know now to be more prudent and wiser measures. What was a mistake in the case of the Titanic would without doubt be negligence in any similar case in the future. Now this is an incredible statement. Never mind that Smith had failed to post additional lookouts forward to assist in the spotting of ice, something that Captain Rostan Carpathia did that very same night. Never mind that Smith had final say over the course, speed, and operation of his ship. Titanic had met its demise under Smith's command. And yet, the captain was found entirely free of blame. In a similar maritime court over a decade earlier, a Captain Watkins of the SS Paris made a slight mathematical error and ran his ship onto the rocks off Cornwall. The inquiry found that his error alone constituted negligence, and despite his many years at sea, his career was over. Meanwhile, in the case of Captain Smith, a kind of distinction was drawn between simple mistakes and negligence that Watkins was never afforded. The difference was that Watkins had been captaining a liner over a decade old that had actually survived the event, while Titanic, the newest and finest ship afloat, had cast a paw over the entire British ship building industry and merchant marine with its sinking. To suggest that Captain Smith was to blame would cast scrutiny over every British captain and their employers to boot. Better to suggest that Smith had made a mistake, but was also somehow not to be blamed. Now, just how those two conclusions managed to coexist peacefully in the mind of the board of inquiry is a mystery. But von Luckn wasn't in the business of executions. In fact, he seemed to find this whole escapade amusing, and he simply sent Banister down to the prisoners quarters to join the others. The British captain, perhaps dreading what kind of hellish, damp build tank he was about to spend the next few weeks in, was likely pleasantly surprised by what he found instead. These prisoners quarters were comfortable and luxurious. They were given plush bunks, provided with books, magazines, and a gramophone to help stave off boredom, and even enjoyed champagne dinners up on deck with the captain. Those who chose to help out with chores were rewarded a fair wage for their efforts. Plus, they didn't even have to stay on their quarters unless there was an active battle situation of foot. Most of the time they were free to roam the ship and even reportedly helped keep lookout for new targets on the promise that whoever spotted the next ship would bag themselves $50, courtesy of the captain. Seadler's days in the North Atlantic had netted two valuable prizes. Now it was time to swing south into the relatively narrow gap between Africa and the eastmost tip of Brazil. Ships bound for Australia, South Africa, or Argentina would need to pass through here. And Luckn felt pickings would be good. His instincts, it would be proved shortly, were absolutely right. The coming weeks would see Seard Lamett with great success. Each time the captured crew was transferred over to her, and they could do nothing but watch as their ship, along with their precious cargo, was sunk. They were prisoners, but to Von Lucknner and his men, they were also guests. The German skipper earned the nickname the sea devil during the war, but owing perhaps to his own notions of hospitality and chivalry, he would go out of his way to be welcoming and courteous to his guests. The truth was von Lucknner was a tragic anglophile who used typically British phrases and loved spending time with the British officers aboard ship. Extraordinary photographs show him sitting with his prisoners, enjoying drinks in the sun as if they were on some kind of cruise instead. One captured British captain even referred to von Luckner as a gentleman of the high seas. For 10 days, no more ships were spotted after Glattis Royal and Lundy Island. And Luckn have thought his luck had just run out. But then they came. The French sailing ship Charles Gnord on January 21st. Then the small 364 ton schooner the P, a big 3,000 ton French bark Anton in after a thrilling chase under sail. and then the 1800 ton Italian sailing ship Wenos Aris after that. But then on February 19th, 1917 off the coast of Argentina, Seadler encountered a surprising quarry. Luckn couldn't believe his eyes. It was the old Pinmore, a fourmastered English bark he had gone to sea on as a youth. That was the voyage that had taught him many of the hardships of life on the ocean. But it also provided a home for him as a young runaway. So when the seadler ran her down and the pin wars crew had been transferred over, Llner found himself unable to resist one last trip down memory lane. He took a boat over to the captured ship and tracked down his old bunk along with the rail on which he'd carved his then name Fairlax Lloydiger all those years ago. Dwindling supplies provided the perfect excuse for the now captain to sail on the Pinwor one last time. He decided to take her on a final last risky trip to Rio de Janeiro. Again, he was lucky coming away from the neutral port undiscovered, reuniting with the sailor 3 days later with fresh supplies. While Pinmore had been loading, Luckn posing as the Norwegian Nudson, struck up conversation with a British officer. His ship, the cruiser Glasgow, was out to hunt down and destroy a mystery raider. reported somewhere out on the Atlantic. Clearly, Seardler's exploits were beginning to stir up the eye of the Admiral T. They couldn't have imagined the mystery raider was in fact a sailing ship any more than the British officer could have imagined that the gruff Norwegian in front of him was the very enemy he was supposed to be hunting. But for now, aboard Seardler again, Von Luckner was confronted with a terrible duty. With the explosives being planted in the old Bark's holds, Von Luckner went below into his cabin and shut the door to wait for the dreaded boom. By Joe, Lucker had once said, I could sink a steamer and laugh as she takes her last dive. Sinking a sailing ship was different, let alone one that had carried him as a lad. These were the last of a dying breed. To sink them was like killing endangered animals. But Luckn had his orders. With a crack, the Pinmo's holds were blasted open, and she dropped with a whoo of white mist into the abyss. Life was good for Seardler's crew. Late February saw the ship take the sailing bark British year whose cargo had included a lot of live chickens and pigs much to the delight of Saddler's crew who'd yearned for a more varied diet. Then came the French sailing ship Laros Fuko and then the Dupri. The captain of that ship came aboard dismayed because some of his friends also captains had warned him of raiders in the area. You can only imagine his surprise when they came up to greet him because they'd also been captured. Hey, cried Dup please captain. All of France is here. By early March, Seadler had captured and sunk over 22,000 tons of enemy shipping. The raiders ruse was working flawlessly and all those ships had been captured and sunk without loss of life. That all changed on the 11th when Luckn and his men encountered the British steamer Horngarth. This was Sadler's most dangerous adversary. As it drew closer, the captain realized to his horror that this steamer had its own gun, a 5 iner that could handily punch holes in the Clipper's hull. But worst of all, it boasted the unmistakable heavy wires that could only have been the antenna of a wireless set. Both would need to be dealt with if they're going to stand a chance at capturing the vessel and living to tell the tale. Von Luckner tried the old trick and signaled for chronometer time, but there came no response from the dark British steamer. Then he tried something new. He staged a fake fire and signaled for distress. Flames were climbing, smoke billowing out from the sadler's deck, shouts of alarm echoing as the crew struggled to contain the fire. Or so it appeared. In reality, it was just a set of chemical pans that had been ignited. Perfectly controlled, and the crew were just making use of their acting skills once again. One man, dressed as the captain's wife, running back and forth on the deck, distracted the crew of the other ship, who gathered to watch with amusement. Unable to ignore these apparent cries for help, the Horngarth turned back to offer assistance to the innocent looking sailing ship. And then it happened. The distress signal was replaced with a German enson. And a great ugly 105 mm gun was run out to point directly at them. Hornath's captain instantly recognized he'd been tricked. Instead of helping a vessel in need, they now found themselves under attack. There were seconds to lose. He ordered his men forward to swing their own 5-in gun around. Von Luckner, meanwhile, directly targeted the steamer's wireless shack. There would be no opportunity for the Horngarth to signal for help or to reveal the Sadler's true identity. The guns pounded away and smashed the wireless office with a direct hit that turned it into matchwood. But now there was still the 5-in gun to contend with. The Horngarth's captain was already rallying his gun crew to their posts in retaliation. Von Luckner needed to think fast. A single hit on his ship could doom her. He called to his crew and clear English for the benefit of his target to make the torpedoes ready. At point blank range, these would take the British ship to pieces. They surrendered suddenly and desperately. Of course, Seadler had no torpedoes. It was another brilliant ruse, and it worked. Unfortunately, the sudden action had one tragic consequence. One of the crew, a 16-year-old apprentice named Douglas Paige, had been hit with shrapnel and killed. Von Luckner made sure he was buried at sea with full military honors and draped in the Union Jack. By mid-March, Seadler was getting full up with almost 300 prisoners aboard down in the holds. Von Luckner needed to figure out what to do with them all. Capturing more ships would mean more prisoners, something they couldn't manage unless they first cleared some room. On the 21st, Luckn got his chance. The French Bark, the Cambon, was spotted and captured in the usual way. But then her captain was given surprising news. His ship wouldn't be sunk. She would instead become a prisoner transport. Lucker appointed the master of the Pinmore, Captain James Mullen, the most senior skipper of the lot, as Camberon's temporary commander. They would set out for the safety of Rio de Janeiro, but he had to swear he would not speak to any other ship of Sadler's antics until then. That and Cam Brun's progress was hampered as Luckned her top gallant masts taken off and additional spars and sails destroyed. By this point, the world had no idea there was a wind jammer out hunting down merchant vessels in the Atlantic. But unfortunately for Lucker and his men, releasing prisoners would blow their cover. But there was no other choice. They had a farewell feast before Captain Mullen and his crew of Saddler's former prisoners departed with handshakes, cheers, and a salute to one another. Mullen would keep his vow, and Luckn had his head start, but still time was of the essence. Even with the Cambon being slowed, owing to the fact she could now only make use of her lower sails, the Seardler would have to get away fast to ensure she remained undiscovered. Her time on the Atlantic was up. Once news spread of a strange clipper ship hunting merchantmen, the Royal Navy would send cruisers to catch her and sink her. And that they did. A Toronto Lancaster and Orbiter made steam to catch Seardler. And the race was on. Lucknied his charts and looked hopefully towards the freedom of the Pacific. But the journey there would not be easy. What stood in their way was Cape Horn, the southern tip of the American continent. Rounding it would be the quickest way to reach the Pacific from Europe. Cape Horn is notorious for its storms and particularly treacherous for a tall ship. Not to mention, they'd be going against the prevailing winds. Sure enough, news headlines soon cropped up, alerting that a quote, "neew German raider had slipped past the British warships on guard in the North Sea and reached the South Atlantic, taking down 11 merchantmen on the way." The men of the Cambon had reached port and word was out. The Royal Navy immediately dispatched patrols to go after the Seardler, but they weren't quick enough. The Wind Jammer was able to outrun the Navy's cruisers. It seemed that her head start had actually been enough. Seadler had first stumbled straight into a hurricane and Luckned the Cape well south, but the ship slipped past the British once again. As a lastminute ruse, he ordered property from the prisoners marked with the name Seardler to be thrown overboard. It might trick the British into thinking that the German raider had been lost in the storm. So with sails set, she swept into the wide expanse of the Pacific on April 18th to begin a new hunt. April became May, then May became June. Seardler patrolled first off the coast of Chile before swinging northwest to run parallel with Peru and the western coast of Mexico. This was not the bustling ocean highway of the North Atlantic. This was the Pacific, an unimaginably vast stretch of ocean of Sadler's port bow. Australia was nearly 7,000 m away. Prowling along the equator, they went weeks without sighting a single ship. The US entry into the war in April 1917 would offer up some new targets. Seardler received news by June that the long neutral country had at last entered the frey against Germany. It would also make things trickier for the raiders. Though neutral ports far from guaranteed a warm welcome, there were now even fewer available to the Kaiser's pirates. It wasn't until the summer that the Seardler would manage to take down three small American trading schooners in fairly short succession. the little 529 ton AB Johnson, the 673 ton RC Slade, and the 731 ton Manila. On July 8th, among their new prisoners was apparently a pet opum. But then again, weeks stretched on with no new sightings. It seemed that the Seardler's run of good luck couldn't last forever. They'd been at sea now for over 7 months. They had covered some 30,000 m and captured 14 Allied ships, taking hundreds of prisoners and destroyed millions of dollars worth of cargo. The tall ship was starting to look a little worse for wear. They were running low on supplies, and morale began to suffer. Simply put, the crew were bought. They had been months without docking anywhere, and the thrill of capturing a new ship was getting rarer and rarer. Without the thrill of action, the crew's daily routine consisted merely of maintenance and tending to the prisoners, now 29 in number, while Seardler sailed day after day through an empty ocean. The boredom was crippling. It got so bad that the men became creative. If von Luckner is to be believed, they even experimented with using baited hand grenades to fish for sharks. But worst of all, the effects of scurvy and berry berry had now begun to set in. Without access to fresh fruit and vegetables, the crew would become weaker, and so would their ship. Her underside, after months at sea, was by now caked in slimy marine growth that slowed her badly as she sailed and checked her speed. VonLa decided it was time to give his crew and his ship a break. Seadler made its way to the French Polynesian island of Mapellia. A beautiful coral atal full of lush greenery, blooming flowers, and plenty of food and fresh water. It must have seemed like a dream come true for the seaweary sailors. Maybe their luck was on the turn again after all. They spent a few short, sweet days on shore, feasting on lobster, coconuts, wild pig, and eggs, picnicking on the white sands, and fishing in the crystal clearar, warm waters. But what happened next on August 2nd, 1917 is still shrouded in mystery because suddenly, unexpectedly, Seardler met her end. Von Luckner told it like this. Anchored just off the island, the crew of the ship were preparing to head for another blissful day on shore when far in the distance, he noticed a strange shape getting larger and larger. Dismissing it at first as a mirage, the imposing shape was getting closer and closer, too close to ignore. This was no mirage, he said, but a tidal wave. Some undersea earthquake had brought this immense danger directly at them. They were trapped with nowhere to go between this terrible 40 ft high swell and the shore. The helpless Seardler was grasped as if by some gargantuan otherworldly hand and hurled against the coral reef with enough force to smash her into pieces. Huge 100 lb chunks of coal raining down on her crew like grenades. Miraculously, no one was hurt. Seardler, however, was not so fortunate. She was completely wrecked. The hull, already in need of repair prior to reaching the island, was embedded with fractured coral, peppered with holes. Her masts were snapped. She lay sadly grounded on her side against the reef. The sea devil and his men were now castaways in the middle of nowhere. While Luckn's story is fantastical, but the American prisoners who'd recently joined the Seadler had a very different version of events. As magnificent as Mopelia appeared, beneath the island's veil of paradise lurked hidden perils, a belt of treacherous reefs and rocks that circled the place and threatened to tear the bottom out of any ship that came too close. Conditions were especially unsuited to a tall ship just like Seardler. Currents were very strong and there wasn't much in terms of shelter from the elements. Anchorage was poor. This was unfamiliar territory for the German town. A sailor would know full well that where you choose to anchor should be greatly dependent on the wind direction and strength. But the German count underestimated the way winds and currents on the Pacific can change at a moment's notice. To von Lluckner, conditions appeared calm. What harm could there be in anchoring by the reef while they enjoyed another one of their picnics on the beach? But Luckn's boldness had seen the Seadler through a hugely successful wartime patrol. Now it would doom her. The wind of course changed abruptly. It seized the ship's towering masts and rigging. Even though there was no canvas set, it swung her bulk around and smashed her directly into the very reef that she was anchored to. After all of Saddler's daring escapades, all that the raider had achieved and seen, the plucky wind jammer was wrecked by a completely preventable mistake. It was hardly a dignified end for the world's last ever sailing warship. No doubt this is why the proud and admittedly ego-driven captain would insist until the day he died that it was a tidal wave, not his own embarrassing blunder that had wrecked his ship. It's probably needless to say that there are no other known records of any tidal wave occurring in that region on that day, only the insistence of Von Luckner and his crew. Either way, the outcome was the same. And Lucknner and his party were marooned on the island. The situation was bleak. Mapellia is smack in the middle of the South Pacific Ocean. The closest land of any significant size was Tahiti, about 300 m east and south. An easy journey in one of the lifeboats. But Tahiti was part of the French Empire, and that would mean surrender. While the captain plotted his next move, the stranded sailors and prisoners all got to work. From the wreckage, they built a makeshift village out of timbers and canvas, naming their own streets after those back home, like Broadway in Pennsylvania. They even set up a chapel. The group still had plenty of supplies, including rifles, ammunition, and dynamite, as well as tobacco, and even wine from the earlier capture of the French bark Charles Gnau. Plus, the island didn't leave them wanting for food. But this is Felix von Luckno we're talking about, and he was not a man who was happy to just sit back and wait until a ship might just happen to pass. Besides, that could take months. After just 3 weeks of waiting, Luckn's nerves had had it. He and his crew rigged up one of their remaining lifeboats and fitted her with her own mast and sails. Only 6 m, that's 19 ft long, and with a crew of six packed in, it seemed impossible to think this tiny lifeboat would survive the open seas. But at least the hurac season was over. No doubt the rest of the party left behind on Mapellia probably expected to never see them again. They christened the small boat Crown Princess and Cecilia, the name of a giant German luxury liner in some irony and set off. Von Lucknner decided to try for Fiji via the Cook Islands, planning to chance upon a sailing ship and capture it to pick up his stranded group. Despite the lack of space, they managed to load their tiny boat with rifles, pistols, and a machine gun. Now, they set off into the unknown in their little wooden boat and hope for the best. For 28 days, the group survived on hard tac and rough pemacan, having to constantly bail out water with no real shelter from the harsh sun and the weather. Spirits were kept up by singing German folk songs and reading from a book they allowed themselves to bring along for the journey. as their one luxury. They covered a staggering distance, over 2,000 miles of open ocean, all the while thrown about by big waves and buffeted by wind. After just 3 days at sea, the boat had reached the tiny island Atu, where a New Zealander resident had greeted who he thought was a bunch of Dutch Americans on a kind of crazed round the world cruise. He provided them with fresh food and water and sent them on their way. A stop at another island, Autaki, was aborted after a resident there became suspicious and a crowd of dozens of locals circled the small boat. Approaching Raratonga in the Cook Islands, Von Lucknet thought he spotted the lights of a big cruiser in port and he turned away. Storm season rolled in. The little boat was tossed around like a toy and let in bucketfuls of water. The mattress became soden and had to be thrown overboard. Sunburn and chafing were immersed in salt water that stung fiercely. Finally, after nearly a month at sea, they reached Wakaya, a small island just off the Fijian mainland, and stepped wearily ashore. This time, they pretended to be shipwrecked Norwegians. But one of the residents of the island, a man named McFersonen, didn't buy it. He ran to the nearby police station, and a local lad, set out on a boat to ask for help from the mainland. With another tropical storm brewing, he arrived and rushed to warn sub inspector Harry Hills, a New Zealander who was alarmed to hear that a strange party had arrived in a boat with thick European accents. He was told by his superiors that he could take a group of Fijian policemen, but they couldn't be armed. Hills was only allowed to take his service revolver. A local steamer, the Amra, had arrived on a regular scheduled voyage, and Hills and his tiny force chartered it to take them to Wakaya. Meanwhile, von Lluckner was ship shopping, eyeing the vessels at anchor around Wakaya with glee. He settled on one, a brand new twin engine schooner, and was making plans to capture it. First by asking for a tow before revealing his crew's German uniforms and storming the vessel by force. Their lifeboat got underway, but just then the Amara arrived plotting into the bay where she stopped and a boat was lowered. Hills stood at the prow. Stop! He shouted. That steamer has you covered with her guns. Von Lluckner froze. He could try to fight his way out, but the narrow confines of the bay would see his boat taken to bits. There was no choice but to surrender. Hills took the men into his charge, and Von Lucknner even handed him his pistol as a formal declaration of capitulation. It was only then that he might have noticed that the tiny Amara mounted no guns at all and the Sea Devil, a master of disguises and ruse, had himself been outf foxed by the police inspector. Fiji was not set up to hold prisoners of war and so von Lucknner's little crew were instead taken to an internment camp in New Zealand who were brought to Oakland in October and divided. Von Lucknner and his second in command, Carl Kachis, were brought to Muihe Island, while his other men, being deemed lower ranking internes, went to Som's Island. Muihei was definitely the better deal. An internment camp might make you picture Von Lucknner being locked up and surrounded by barbed wire and dingy conditions. But this was far from the case. Internes at Motohei were largely given the run of the island during daylight hours, free to go fishing, swimming, bake cakes, pick fruit, and tend gardens. Sometimes they were even allowed to follow along on shopping trips to Oakland. It was a far cry from the experiences that millions of other prisoners of war across the world during the Great War were suffering. The island setup was in itself an effective security measure and its openness meant that they didn't really face the usual issues of disease spread through overcrowding. The former guard on Muihei remembered it as quote a happy little camp. The war never seemed to enter that kind of place. Many of the internes were just ordinary New Zealand citizens of German descent. To an extent, these people were being kept there partly for their own protection thanks to the anti-German sentiment present across the country at the time. Along with these civilian attorneys with the governor, the other officials from German Samoa. So, it's safe to say there weren't exactly high-risk prisoners in need of constant watching either. Charles Harkort Turner, the commonant of Motohei's internment camp, had led the camp in this laid-back fashion for several years without issue before meeting Vonluck. He had always established a certain sense of trust with his internes and was well known to be a kind of friendly, generous man. Upon vanluckner's arrival, Turner was promoted to left colonel and would be required to regularly call over to headquarters in Aland to check in and affirm that everything was okay. He was also provided with an increased guard and a new moat launch to use for patrols. It seemed for now at least that the left tenant colonel had a lot to be thankful towards his new German prisoners for. But never one to go long without some kind of adventure, Von Luckner wasn't content to stay put on Moduhei despite its comforts. He set his eyes on the camp's motor launch, the Pearl, the same launch that would occasionally take the internees on day trips to Oakland. He would need to recruit some other able-bodied prisoners to help out with his plan. A group of marine cadets from German Samoa were the perfect candidates. Under the guise of staging a Christmas play where they had reenacted the battle of Jutland, the party started to make preparations. Gathering supplies slowly so as not to raise suspicion, creating realistic prop weapons and crafting themselves a German flag from a painted bed sheet. One of the recruits had been assigned maintenance duties for the motor launch. The perfect excuse to stow away supplies while he worked on the boat. They even managed to persuade the camp to provide them with a map. All for the play, of course. It really does sound crazy that they could get away with this, but boredom was common on Moto, and attorneys were encouraged to find ways to fill their time. Besides, a play would be entertaining for the camp's officers as well. One of the Marine cadetses, Walter Van Zatski, even improvised an incredible working sexant out of an old camping stove, a safety razor, and some brass hinges salvaged from an old rudder. You can actually still see it in the Museum of New Zealand's online collection. Really is an impressive creation. The final flourish would see von Lucknner use his acting skills once more. Over the course of several weeks, he started to limp, feigning a strong bout of rheumatism and supposedly relying on the use of a walking stick. After all, who would suspect a man struggling to walk of making a run for it? By December 13th, 1917, everything was ready. The Pearls bulkheads were stashed with food and weapons. Soon to be runaways cut the phone lines connecting the little island to the mainland and set up a diversion by lighting one of the barracks on fire. A fire breaking out on a small island was a big deal. So, more or less all of the camp's personnel ran out to help put it out. All except Von Luckner and his party of escaped. That is, although they did make sure to hang around in the thick of it long enough to be noticed by Lieutenant Colonel Turner as being present and helping. It should be noted that this fire seems to only take place in Volutner's account of things. Eyewitnesses on Motohei instead reported that Turner was distracted by his daughter visiting the camp and so he just simply didn't notice that the pearl had been stolen. A less traumatic version of events, but possibly an even more humiliating one for the left tenant colonel. Later on at roll call, it was discovered that 11 of the camp's internes were gone, including arguably its most important prisoner, Count Felix Von Lucknner. By the time the escapes were noted as being missing, they were already crossing the Hierarchy Gulf. There was a significant delay in alerting the mainland to the unfolding crisis thanks to the cut telephone lines. To say this was a source of embarrassment for New Zealand at the time is a bit of an understatement. Prime Minister William Massie even reportedly declared it to be the most regrettable thing that has happened since the war began. This was bad news for Lieutenant Colonel Turner's career. He was immediately suspended for negligence and later caught marshaled then dismissed from the New Zealand Defense Force. The next camp commander aunt at Muihei would run a much stricter regime. Headlines all over New Zealand ran with stories of unluckners's escape and it led to plenty of civilians searching for them on the shores in their own boats. Government also assigned the steamship Iris specially fitted with their own gun just for the occasion to go after the runaways. They had been planning to capture the first suitable vessel they came across and head for the Keradec Islands where they could restock on supplies before heading on further. Von Luckner and his crew did manage to make it there, having successfully captured a scale named the mower. But the little scow wasn't nearly fast enough for their needs, and the Iris beat her to the Kerdex, where they'd correctly predicted the Germans would head. After 9 days on the run, they'd been caught once again. Allegedly, all Van Lucknner had to say for himself was, "You left the door open. You cannot blame me for walking out." It seems his charms still proved useful, though, despite his blatant breach of trust. When the men were taken to a prison camp on Riapa Island, which he wasn't much a fan of, Von Luckner managed to persuade officials to relocate him back to the much more appealing Motohei. Understandably though, security measures there had been tightened and Turner's successor stripped back many of the previous privileges of the camp. There would be no more escape attempts and Verluckner would live out the rest of the war at the camp. As for the rest of the Seardler's crew and the American prisoners that were left behind on Mapellia, they also managed to get away safely. Around two weeks after von Luckna had departed the island, French merchant schooner, the Lutess had spotted the wreck of the Seadler and came over to investigate. This was an unfortunate move for them because the German crew captured the ship and took it for themselves, leaving behind the Lutess's crew as well as the American prisoners from the Seardler. Those left on Mapellia were later rescued. The Lutess was in bad shape, suffering from severe rot. So the German crew could only make it as far as Easter Island where they were then run. They were taken to Chile where they would stay until the rest of the war, which point they were repatriated to Germany. Very unusually for a story from this period of history, this is one where they all made it out alive and well. And it's rumored that the old crew of the Seardler even had a reunion back in Germany years later. After the war, Vanluckner would become something of a folk hero, respected for his determination not to take any lives and his gentlemanly conduct during the raids. Though still refusing to conform to the typical lifestyle of the German nobility, Vanluckner seems to have thoroughly enjoyed his newfound status as a celebrity, writing books and going on tours around the world to further spread the word of his many maritime adventures. Vanluckner was an easily recognizable figure with his signature captain's hat and his pipe. He was tall and strong enough to bend pennies, which he gave out to people as good luck charms. He was a prolific autograph signer. He had a booming fogghorn-like voice and his very own catchphrase by Joe. >> Life was good, but in the leadup to the Second World War, the Nazis would attempt to exploit his status for propaganda purposes. However, von Lluckner had always liked to do things his own way and was far from cooperative. He'd been awarded an honorary citizenship by the city of San Francisco in 1927, something he refused to renounce. And it said that he also helped a Jewish woman to escape Germany by procuring a passport for her. Ever the opportunist, he did go on what was effectively a Reich sponsored world tour in 1939 on a ship aptly named the Sedtol, meaning sea devil. But it seems he was more interested in going on one last pleasure cruise before retirement than in doing the Nazis bidding. According to the reports of a spy who'd been placed on board to keep an eye on the Maverick captain once he got out onto the ocean and his new lugger, von Lucknner promptly ordered that all the Nazi propaganda pamphlets be ditched overboard near the Panama Canal. Unsurprisingly, the Nazi party wasn't best pleased with his actions. He became an exile and he was no longer welcome in Nazi Germany. He would retire to Sweden where he lived out the rest of his life with his wife passing away in 1966 at the age of 84. The story of Count Felix von Lluckner's life certainly read like fiction at times. He was a born storyteller, a type that could take any old dull day and turn it into an adventure of epic proportions. He was known, of course, and largely respected in his time for his chivalry, his courage, his zest for life, and his distinct code of ethics. His fondness for embellishment does make it a little hard to distinguish the man from the myth at times. But what we do know to be true of his life at sea truly does seem worthy of a Hollywood blockbuster. Seardler's remarkable role in the war and the success of her raiding campaign went against all odds. Rapid technological shifts in the 19th and 20th century meant that the time when sailing ships had dominated the seas was long gone. Steam ships allowed for fast, reliable transport and expanded trade routes. No longer did crewmen have to rely on the unpredictable weather. Steam power allowed them more control and enabled them to be better prepared to face whatever rough conditions might be thrown at them. And yet, there's just something so charming about a classic sail ship and all the history it represents. In Vanluckner's own words, "They are the last survivors of the golden age at sea. The shipyards are not building many of them anymore. The day of the schooner, the Bark, the Clipper, and the Bantine is fast passing. I have an alltime sailman's love for sail ships." The fact that a tall ship was able to wreak as much havoc on Allied merchant shipping as the Seardler did, all while largely avoiding bloodshed whenever possible is a testament to both the ship builders and sailors of old. This was a different way to wage a war, one that targeted cargo rather than people and when prisoners were treated as friends. When Luckn supposedly once told the anthropologist Scholer Jones that one cannot go out in search of adventure and always find it, adventure will find you if it comes at all. It symbolized the days gone by of swashbuckling pirates and the age of sail. It was a far far cry from the bleak mechanical horrors of the trenches. Titanic existed in an incredible, bizarre, heady place in time when companies raced to outdo one another at breakneck pace with the newest, latest technology. The size and the shape of the iceberg below the waterline, for example. But given Titanic apparently just grazed the Berg, Steven says the margin may have been so slim that an extra 11 square ft of rudder area could, this is very much playing in the realms of hypothetical here, have made the difference. In his professional opinion, things could have played out very differently. Remember when we mentioned Titanic's central propeller washed directly over the rudder? Well, it's thought that when the ice was spotted, her bridge crew had rung down to stop the engines. And that central propeller came to a standstill. Because it was a flat plate, Steven says, rather than an aeraf foil as we'd use now, it was rather inefficient. In fact, much of the turning force normally would be generated by the directed thrust from the center propellers. As steam to this had been cut off, it would have started coasting and would have begun to slow down. In any case, Steven continues, it would not have been providing the maximum amount of thrust. So the conjecture is what if they'd kept the turbine energized with the slight extra kick that the center propeller could have given eased the stern around? It's a tantalizing question, one we'll probably never know the answer to, but it would appear to Dr. Payne that Titanic's rudder size might, given those exceptional circumstances, have made a difference. Myth busted? Not exactly. How's that for a plot twist? Look, there's no way that any one of these factors led to Titanic's demise. It's a story with so many layers and multiple failure points that just all happened to align in the kind of Swiss cheese model that air investigators talk about. Titanic's rudder was technically too small and it could in the event and speaking purely theoretically have made the difference that night. But did Titanic sink because its rudder was too small? No way. I don't think so. Titanic story is a breeding ground for wild and wacky conspiracy theories and myths. Everything from the curse of a mummy traveling in the cargo holds to the raging coal fire apparently consuming the ship from within, weakening it so that simply touching the iceberg was enough to send her below. Join me next time as we once again dive on in and try to bust some of the most egregious zombie myths about Titanic that refuse to die. [Music]
